TUESDAY, 21 OCTOBER 2014
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 10.30 a.m.
Prayers.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have to report that, accompanied by members, I waited upon His
Excellency the Governor-General at Government House yesterday when I addressed His
May it please Your Excellency—
In obedience to Your Excellency’s request, the Hous e of Representatives, in the
exercise of its undoubted rights and privileges, has proceeded to the election of a
Speaker, and, as the subject of its choice, I now present myself to you and submit
myself for Your Excellency’s confirmation.

items.speaker: To which His Excellency replied as follows

items.text: Mr Speaker, it is with much pleasure that I approve the choice by the House of
Representatives of you as its Speaker.
I congratulate you on your election to this distinguished office, marking as it does the
appreciation of the House of Representatives of your impartiality and ability.
The Speaker reported further that he also addressed His Excellency as follows:
I humbly thank Your Excellency for your confirmation of the choice by the House of
Representatives of me to be its Speaker.
I have now, on behalf of the House, to lay claim to all its privileges, and especially to
freedom of speech in debate, to free access to Your Excellency whenever occasion
may require it, and to the most favourable construction being put on all its
proceedings.

items.speaker: To which His Excellency replied as follows

items.text: Mr Speaker, I confirm all the rights and privileges of the House of Representatives
which have ever been granted. I assure you that the House of Representatives shall
always have ready access to me, and that I will at all times place the most
favourable construction upon its proceedings.
I desire to repeat my respectful acknowledgment to the House of the high honour that
has been done me in electing me to be its Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received the following authorisation from His Excellency the
Governor-General to administer the oath or affirmation prescribed by law to be taken or
made by members of this House:
Mr Speaker, I present you with an authorisation for you to administer the oath or
affirmation of allegiance to members of the House of Representatives.
Signed Jerry Mateparae
Governor-General
20 October 2014
Julie Anne Genter was presented to the Speaker, made the affirmation required by
law, and took her seat in the House.
10 Obituaries 21 Oct 2014
David Murray Hereora

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I regret to inform the House of the death on 5 August 2014 of David
Murray Hereora, a Labour Party list member of Parliament from 2002 to 2008 and
chairperson of the Māori Affairs Committee from 2005 to 2008. I desire on behalf of
this House to express our sense of loss that we have sustained and our sympathy with
the relatives of the late former member. I now ask members to stand with me and
observe a period of silence as a mark of respect to his memory.
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect.
MIHI

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I now call on a long-serving Māori member to give a mihi.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: E Te Pika, e te Minita Te
Ururoa, e ngā mema Māori mai i ngā hau e whā, tēnā koutou mō tēnei wāhanga māku ki
te tuku mihi. E tika ana me tāpiri atu tēnei mihi maioha ki tērā o tō tātau nei hoa a Dave
Hereora. Ahakoa kua ngaro i te tirohanga kanohi, e kore e warewaretia. Nō reirā e Te
Whare, kua riro tēnei hōnore ki a au kia tuku mihi mō tēnei Pāremata e 51.
E tika ana me tīmata mā te whakanui i tō ekenga ki te tūranga teitei o Te Whare, e Te
Kaihautū o Te Whare. E Te Pika, nāu te mahi nunui ki te whakawā i  ngā taupatupatu
ahakoa he ringa kaha mā te mahi a Horomona e whakapai ai te wairua o tēnei Whare.
Nō reira tēnā koe.
Ka huri te whakaaro ki a koe Te Pirimia, John Key. Kua whakaae te motu mōu te
mahi nunui hei kaiārahi mō tēnei whenua o Aotearoa/Niu Tīreni, kia tuia ō tātau kāinga,
te whenua motuhake kei waenganui i te hāpori o te ao whānui, arā, kia piri tata ki ngā
motu o Te Moana Nui-a-Kiwa i ēnei wā toimaha. Nō reira, nei te mihi, nei te mihi atu ki
a koe.
Huri noa ki ngā pāti tōrangapū, ngā kaihautū  katoa, ko te tūmanako kia ū ki ngā
kaupapa matua mai i te rangi ki te whenua.
Ki ā tātau tamariki me ngā tāngata katoa, kia piri tata, kia ratarata i raro i te mana o
Te Tiriti o Waitangi hei painga, hei oranga mō tātau katoa. Nō reira, e Te Whare tēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[My thanks to you, Mr Speaker,  Minister Te Ururoa,  and Māori members from the
four winds for this part you have given me in regard to delivering the opening address.
It is fitting that I add this affectionate tribute to that colleague of ours, Dave Hereora.
Even though he is no longer before us he will never be forgotten. And so to you the
House, this honour to acknowledge the 51st Parliament has been bestowed upon me.
It is fitting that I begin by magnifying your elevation to the highest position of the
House, Mr Speaker. Yours is a huge role, in terms of adjudicating debates, ruling with a
firm hand, and being wise like Solomon in ensuring that the tranquillity of this House
prevails.
I cast a thought in your direction,  Prime Minister John Key. The nation has acceded
that your most important role is to be the leader for this country of Aotearoa New
Zealand in terms of intertwining our homes and the special ground between
communities of the world at large so that they are closer to the islands of the Pacific
Ocean in these times that weigh heavily upon us. I therefore salute and congratulate
you.
I turn now to all the political parties and leaders. The hope is that primary proposals
from the sky above to the ground below are firmly fixed.
21 Oct 2014 Mihi 11
And now to our children and everyone, remain close and friendly to each other under
the mandate of the Treaty of Waitangi as a source of sustenance and well-being for us
all.]
Waiata

GOVERNOR-GENERAL’S SPEECH

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I desire to report that when the House did
attend His Excellency the Governor-General this day in the Legislative Council
Chamber, His Excellency was pleased to make a speech, the text of which was handed
to me by His Excellency, and I now lay such text on the Table of the House. The text of
the speech is:
Honourable Members of the House of Representatives.
E nga Mema Honore o te Whare Paremata o Aotearoa, tenei aku mihi mahana ki a
koutou, tena koutou katoa.
Following the General Election, a National-led Government has been formed with a
majority in the House on confidence and supply.
Confidence and supply agreements have been signed between the National Party
and, respectively, the ACT Party and the United Future Party. A Relationship Accord and
confidence and supply agreement has been signed with the Māori Party. These
agreements will enable the Government to operate in an effective, stable and inclusive
manner.
Honourable Members, the Government has a comprehensive policy agenda and a
substantial legislative programme that it will put before the House in the forthcoming
session.
The Government is focused on returning to surplus and its long-term fiscal objective
remains to reduce net core Crown debt to 20 per cent of GDP by 2020. Around $1 billion
of the operating allowance in each Budget will be used to increase spending, with the
remainder set aside for tax reductions and further debt repayment, depending on
economic and fiscal conditions at the time.
ACC levies will be reduced in 2015, and more reductions are expected from 2016, as
the three levy accounts are now fully funded.
The Government’s plan to build a more productive and competitive economy,
supporting more jobs and higher incomes, is set out in the Business Growth Agenda. This
contains around 350 individual initiatives. These initiatives will be progressed, and more
will be added, in this term of Parliament.
The Government will continue to pursue high-quality trade agreements, including
negotiations with Korea and the Trans-Pacific Partnership, while ensuring that New
Zealand’s best interests are always served. More investment will be made in New
Zealand Trade and Enterprise, to expand the number of businesses it works with and
increase its international footprint.
The Government will continue to provide the environment and incentives to increase
business-led research and development, with a goal of raising this to 1 per cent of GDP
by 2018. More funding will be provided for the R&D grant programme. The Government
12 Governor-General’s Speech 21 Oct 2014
will also establish a Food Safety Science and Research Centre, as well as four additional
Centres of Research Excellence, with one of the Centres focused on Maori research.
The Government will progress legislation to increase flexibility and fairness in the
labour market, extend flexible working arrangements and improve collective bargaining.
The enforcement of New Zealand’s minimum employment standards will be
strengthened, and paid parental leave extended from 14 weeks to 18 weeks by 2016.
Legislation to improve health and safety at work will be progressed.
The Government will complete the implementation of the Financial Markets Conduct
Act, and will progress legislation to strengthen competition laws, and improve the
accounting and audit industries.
The overhaul of Inland Revenue’s business systems and information technology will
continue, which among other things will make tax compliance faster and easier for
businesses.
Net migration to Australia has dropped considerably and the unemployment rate in
New Zealand is lower than that across the Tasman. The Government will arrange job
fairs for New Zealand employers in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, to recruit skilled
expatriate New Zealanders to return home and work in areas where there are shortages.
Job fairs will co mplement the Government’s skills training programme here in New
Zealand, which involves strengthening and improving foundation learning, vocational
training and tertiary education. Additional investment will be made this term in training
more engineers, creating 2,000 more places in Maori and Pasifika Trades Training, and
launching three ICT Graduate Schools.
The Government will continue its programme of investment in modern infrastructure.
In this term of Parliament, a number of projects in the Roads of National Significance
programme will be completed, including the Waterview Tunnel, the Tauranga Eastern
Link and the Mackays to Peka Peka route north of Wellington. The Government will
progress the remainder of the Roads of National Significance programme, together with a
package of state highway projects in Auckland and across the regions. New funding will
be allocated for urban cycleways.
The Ultra-Fast Broadband programme will be extended to reach 80 per cent of New
Zealanders. In addition, $150 million will be set aside to improve mobile coverage and
broadband connectivity in rural and remote areas.
Honourable Members, the Government believes that balanced and sensible
management of our natural resources can meet environmental responsibilities while
creating economic opportunities.
The Government will continue to encourage petroleum and mineral exploration while
adhering to strong environmental and safety provisions. This approach includes
investment in new data acquisition projects such as aeromagnetic surveys and petroleum
basin analysis.
Investment in regional water infrastructure will continue, to help these projects get
underway. New water storage and irrigation projects can make land more productive and
boost exports, while at the same time providing positive environmental outcomes.
The Government is committed to improving water quality and the way fresh water is
managed. Water reform will continue through advancing the recommendations of the
Land and Water Forum. The Government will also introduce a requirement for dairy cattle
to be excluded from waterways by 1 July 2017. Coupled with this, the Government has
set aside $100 million to voluntarily buy and retire areas of selected farmland next to
important waterways to create an environmental buffer.
Legislation will be introduced to amend the Resource Management Act to provide
more certainty, timeliness and cost-effectiveness around resource allocation decisions.
The Environmental Reporting Bill will also be progressed.
The Government will introduce legislation to improve the responsible use,
management and conservation of New Zealand’s ocean environment. This legislation will
21 Oct 2014 Governor-General’s Speech 13
allow for a wider range of marine protected areas, including recreational fishing parks in
the Hauraki Gulf and Marlborough Sounds.
The Government will work with international partners to put in place a comprehensive
new global agreement on climate change by the end of 2015. It will also continue to
participate in international research programmes, with particular emphasis on the Global
Research Alliance on agricultural greenhouse gases. The Government will invest
additional funding to encourage and support new forest planting, and will continue to
focus on managing New Zealand’s emissions.
Honourable Members, the Government will continue to deliver high-quality public
services. It will remain focused on getting results, seeking new and better ways to deliver
public services, and continuing to contain and reduce costs.
The Government has 10 priority goals and targets in the areas of long-term welfare
dependency, supporting vulnerable children, boosting skills and employment, reducing
crime and improving interaction with government. Good progress is being made on these
targets, and two of them – in the areas of crime reduction and educational achievement –
will be made more challenging.
The Government is committed to helping more people get off a benefit and into work.
It will work to reduce the number of people receiving a benefit and reduce the lifetime
costs of the welfare system. Legislation will be introduced to extend the Youth Service
approach to 19-year-old sole parents, and to many other 18- and 19-year-old
beneficiaries who need more support, or who are at risk of long-term welfare
dependence.
As agreed with the Māori Party, ongoing investment will be made in Whānau Ora. The
Government will continue to have a focus on poverty, especially child poverty, and will
coordinate cross-government activity in this area through the Ministerial Committee on
Poverty.
The Government will also have a focus on housing in this Parliamentary term.
More special housing areas will be created – and therefore more new housing
developed – as a result of Housing Accords signed between the Government and local
councils. Changes to the Resource Management Act will assist housing supply in the
longer term.
The new KiwiSaver HomeStart Grant will be introduced next year to double the
support a first home buyer can get if they are buying or building a new home, which will
encourage the supply of more affordable new housing. House price limits around the
country will be increased. Legislation will also be introduced to allow first home buyers to
withdraw their KiwiSaver member tax credit to put towards a deposit. The Government’s
extended home insulation scheme will make another 46,000 low-income households
warmer and healthier.
The Government will continue working to ensure that vulnerable New Zealanders have
access to good quality housing, whether those houses are owned by Housing New
Zealand or by community housing providers. The Government sees community housing
providers playing a greater role in the provision of social housing over this term of
Parliament.
The Government will extend free doctor’s visits and prescriptions to children under 13.
More will be invested in lifting the number of elective surgical procedures, particularly hip
and knee operations, and in creating new, primary care multi-disciplinary teams to help
people in pain from bone, muscle and joint conditions.
A new cancer treatment target will be introduced, for 90 per cent of patients to receive
their first cancer treatment within 62 days of being referred by their GP. And the
Government will invest extra funding to allow hospices to expand their care and services
across the wider health system.
As agreed with the United Future Party, the implementation of the National Medicines
Strategy will continue, including the enhanced role of pharmacists in medicines
management and primary care.
14 Governor-General’s Speech 21 Oct 2014
The Government will extend the Enabling Good Lives approach so that disabled
people have more choices, controls and flexibility over support and funding in their
everyday lives.
The Government will this term implement its initiative to raise teaching quality and
school leadership to deliver a better education to every student. This will keep the best
teachers in the classroom, and establish new teaching and leadership roles to spread
best practice across communities of schools.
The Government will also provide more in-class support to special needs students, by
funding up to 800,000 more teacher aide hours each year. More funding will be supplied
to support deaf and hearing-impaired children, and a contestable fund will be established
for schools to establish or enhance Asian language programmes.
The Government will continue its work to lift participation rates in early childhood
education, with a target of 98 per cent of new entrants in school having previously
attended an early childhood centre. The Government also has a target of 85 per cent of
18-year-olds achieving a minimum of NCEA Level 2. Significant investment will be made
in new schools and classrooms, including major projects in Auckland and Christchurch.
As agreed with the ACT Party, the Government will further develop the model, and
expand the trial, of Partnership Schools to improve educational outcomes for
disadvantaged students.
The Government will continue to focus on crime prevention. The crime rate is at a 35-
year low, and violent crime, youth crime and re-offending are all declining. Across law
and order agencies, a stronger response will be developed to prevent family violence,
including a focus on gangs and gang lifestyles. The Government will progress legislation
to address cyber-bullying, organised crime and online child abuse. It will progress the
Parole Amendment Bill, introduce a Public Protection Order Bill, and intends to progress
reform of the Privacy Act.
Every publicly managed prison will be made a working prison by 2017, so prisoners
can take part in a 40-hour week of rehabilitation and reintegration activities. Specialist
after-care will be delivered for those released or paroled prisoners who have undertaken
a drug treatment programme while in prison.
Honourable Members, the Government recognises that Māori face unique
opportunities and challenges in maximising their economic potential. This is reflected in
the creation of a new ministerial portfolio of Maori Development. Reforms to Te Ture
Whenua Māori Act will be progressed, so Maori land can be governed effectively and
profitably for all its owners. The Government will also continue to resolve outstanding
Treaty of Waitangi settlements, and intends for all willing iwi to have deeds of settlement
Starting next year, New Zealand will take its place on the United Nations Security
Council for a two-year term. This will be a challenging time for the Security Council and
New Zealand is determined to make a positive contribution and in particular to represent
the perspective of small states.
The Government is committed to a strong security and intelligence community which
operates within a clear legal framework and with the security of New Zealanders at its
heart. Under legislation passed last year, a review of the intelligence and security
agencies, their legislation, and their oversight, will commence by 30 June 2015.
The Government has already commenced work on a review of settings in relation to
foreign terrorist fighters taking part in, or returning from, conflict zones. The rapid rise of
the Islamic State of Iraq and Levant poses international, regional and local risks which the
Government will respond to in a responsible way.
As has been well-signalled, the Government will put a possible change of New
Zealand’s flag to a public vote this term. There will be no presumpti on of change, but
there will be a very open process which will welcome and encourage full public input and
debate.
Honourable Members, the Government is continuing to stand beside the people of
Canterbury as good progress is made on the earthquake rebuild. The rebuild will continue
21 Oct 2014 Governor-General’s Speech 15
to occupy a great deal of Government attention in this term of Parliament. Big strides will
be made this term on anchor projects and horizontal infrastructure. Next year, the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority will be brought into the Department of the
Prime Minister and Cabinet, and a transition plan developed to hand over CERA’s
responsibilities and powers in an orderly way.
Honourable Members, over the course of the forthcoming Parliamentary session,
other measures will be laid before you.
The Government is privileged to have won the trust and goodwill of New Zealanders
for a third Parliamentary term, and will seek to re-earn that trust and goodwill every day
over the next three years.
Deputy Speaker

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That Chester Borrows
be appointed Deputy Speaker. Mr Borrows is a well-regarded member of this House,
having been a member since 2005. Prior to that, he had a very long political
apprenticeship as he came to understand the ways of this Parliament well before being
elected to it. As a former police officer and a former lawyer, he has a fine understanding
of the justice system in New Zealand and the principles of justice. He has the ministerial
experience of having been an Associate Minister for Social Development as well.
I think his strong associations across the House, and the recognition of him as the
affable gentleman that he is, will afford him considerable scope for his administration of
the House in your stead, Mr Speaker, and I am sure that his general appreciation of
parliamentary matters will ensure that he does fill the role of Deputy Speaker according
to the wishes of this wider Parliament.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: On behalf of the Opposition can I
endorse the resolution and congratulate Chester Borrows on his elevation to the role of
Deputy Speaker. I know that many of us will have worked with him in the select
committees. He has previously chaired a number of select committees for Parliament,
and we have found him to be a fair and balanced chair, and I look forward to him
bringing those skills to the debating chamber.
Motion agreed to.
Assistant Speakers

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That Lindsay Tisch be
appointed Assistant Speaker. Mr Tisch has been a member of this House since 1999. He
has very considerable political experience that goes well beyond the years he has spent
in this House. He has also been part of the Speaker’s team since 2008. During that time
I think he has developed a level of credibility and acceptance among his colleagues that
will fit him very well to serve in this role in the coming Parliament. He is highly
regarded by his own caucus, and I know that many others sitting in this Parliament who
have been in this House while he has been presiding have attested to his competence
and fairness in the exercise of the Assistant Speaker’s role.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Can I also endorse this resolution and
congratulate Lindsay Tisch on his re-election as Assistant Speaker. I would also like to
note that following the departure of H V Ross Robertson, he is now the longest-serving
presiding officer of the House in the current Parliament, and of course holds the record
as being the only presiding officer to withdraw and apologise during the last term of
Parliament. We welcome his re-election.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The last thing that New
Zealand First wants to do is to introduce a discordant note so early in proceedings, but
16 Appointments 21 Oct 2014
we are talking about parliamentary appointments and it would have been courteous,
surely, or polite, or properly parliamentary to approach other parties on this matter of
appointments. The least we could have expected was to be consulted, because we are
being asked, as members of Parliament, to abide by the rulings of the Speaker, the
Deputy Speaker, the Assistant Speakers, and other people. Surely, in a parliamentary
sense, therefore every parliamentary group in this House should have been consulted. I
am not certain about the Greens. I am not certain about the Greens. All I can say is that
we were not. It is all very fine to regard the matter as of no importance because
obviously certain members over there do not understand the importance or the
paramountcy of Parliament. But just to assume that you are going to get the support on
an appointment because you have got what you suppose is the majority in the House is
not good enough. We in New Zealand First believe—
Denis O’Rourke: So much for inclusiveness.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: So much for inclusiveness —exactly. So much for
grand Westminster traditions. Yes, you could even go on further and say that it
bespeaks of an awful arrogance. I do not want to go that far, surely, but let us please in
the future have the decency to consult all of Parliament if you want every member of
Parliament and every political party to abide by rulings coming from these officers in
Parliament.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I realise that the procedure
here is for there to not be a debate on these matters, but I think it does a huge disservice
to the balance of Parliament if there is not some response to the rather ridiculous
comments that have just been offered to this House by Mr Peters. For a start, for the last
6 years every ef fort has been made to make Parliament’s Business Committee far more
relevant than it has been in any Parliament prior to that. Second, this morning the
Business Committee convened for a second time this week, simply to accommodate
New Zealand First’s organ isational dysfunction, and was then told that New Zealand
First members still had not managed to make up their minds. If anyone is to talk in this
House about disrespect for Parliament, it would be every parliamentarian other than
someone who sits in New Zealand First.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will put the question. The House can decide. The question is that
the motion be agreed to. Those of that opinion will say Aye, to the contrary, No. The
Ayes have it.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: As I move this next motion I
hope the last discordant moment is not some sort of a portent of what is about to
happen. I move, That the Hon Trevor Mallard be appointed Assistant Speaker . I did not
think that I would ever be in this House moving a motion like this. If it were not for the
fact that I have been reminded by the honourable gentleman over there that this is a
parliamentary occasion, I may well have quipped that should he be successful, the Hon
Trevor Mallard may be the first Speaker in the Chair to remove himself from the House.
But appreciating the comments Mr Peters has made to the House, I will simply say
that I have worked with Mr Mallard on the Business Committee and in his role as
shadow Leader of the House over a number of years, and I know that he is, at heart, a
true parliamentarian.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha,ha!

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, his colleagues, of course, may find it hard to
believe that anyone on their side of the House has a heart, but the reality is that Mr
Mallard is a gentleman who does appreciate the procedures of Parliament and does
respect the procedures of Parliament. Certainly over his political career he has enjoyed
21 Oct 2014 Appointments 17
the theatre of Parliament as well. I think his broad experience in that regard will equip
him very well as an assistant to you in your role, Mr Speaker, and we look forward to
supporting him.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Where to start?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Where to start! Can I also endorse this resolution and
congratulate Trevor Mallard on his elevation to this role. I think many would agree that
there are few people in Parliament who know the Standing Orders inside out and back
to front in the way that he does. As the Leader of the House, Gerry Brownlee, has just
acknowledged, he has played a very constructive role in the proceedings of the Business
Committee over the last couple of terms of Parliament, and we are confident that he will
be a good, fair, and impartial referee of the House’s proceedings.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Although we have no particular
objection to the nomination that has been made, and we look forward to, I guess, the joy
of watching Trevor Mallard as Assistant Speaker —it will be an interesting Parliament
with him in that role —I would note for the House and for the public that no women
have been nominated for any of these positions. Yet again —yet again under this
Government—no women have been nominated for the positions of Speaker, Deputy
Speaker, or Assistant Speaker. At a time when the New Zealand population is
increasingly supporting and promoting women into positions of authority, when
yesterday this Parliament saw the Commission Opening of Parliament by three women
justices, we now have a situation in this Parliament where Parliament itself is behind the
country in making sure that women are in positions of authority in our own Chamber. I
think that is a disappointment. I think it is a disappointment for all of us that we have
not made sure that more women are promoted into positions of authority in this House
so that we too represent the population of this country, which is increasing women’s
representation in positions of authority. It is worth noting, and I hope it will improve in
the future. Thank you.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I also specifically welcome to the team of presiding officers the
Hon Chester Borrows, Lindsay Tisch, and, particularly, the Hon Trevor Mallard. All the
members selected for these jobs have, in the time I have been here, shown a very high
regard for the dignity of this House, and I think that all three of them will bring a very
special expertise to the running of this Parliament. Thank you.

As Parliaments transition, all the legislation before the previous Parliament, in
theory, ceases to exist, and a Government gets to choose, when it is re-elected or
elected, which should carry over. In this instance, we wish to reinstate all of the
business that is on the Order Paper. I would note that there is one bill under members’
orders of the day in the name of a member who is no longer present. That bill is also
being reinstated, but I wish to simply report to the House that in your role as Speaker
you will determine how that bill is to be allocated or to which member it is to be
allocated, as you are faced with a circumstance that has not been faced by any Speaker
before. I am sure you will work through that in a very fair manner.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: The Labour Opposition will be
supporting the motion, but for the record and in the interests of civility —and, again, for
the record in the new life of the Government —it is worth noting that this motion is
supported in order to enable adequate scrutiny of these entities, especially those assets
that now form part of the mixed-ownership model, given that those assets are not
subject to the Official Information Act and given that there is, because of their new
status, less parliamentary scrutiny. So although the Opposition does support this motion,
it supports it not in respect of any notion that those assets should have been sold or that
it is supportive of the Government’s stance in regard to the scheme of arrangement that
it embarked on before the election, when, as we noted repeatedly, the New Zealand
people were in a position where they lost value. The $7 billion to $8 billion that was
trumpeted as being a Government achievement fell well short, in the order $4.8 billion.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Stick to the motion.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: So although we welcome this motion, we welcome
it for the reason —and I am sure the Leader of the House would agree with me —that
even though at least half of these assets fall outside collective community ownership,
there should be adequate scrutiny on behalf of taxpayers by members of this House and
members of this Opposition. I give notice to the Government that we will be embarking
on strenuous and detailed scrutiny, especially as the Government continues to use those
proceeds in rather dubious ways that fall outside the future investment model.
Finally, I note in supporting this motion that the Government has said in the previous
Parliament that it would not be selling any other assets, but, sadly, we note that there is
now some notion of selling billions of dollars’ worth of State houses.
Motion agreed to.

MOTIONS
United Nations Security Council—Election to Non-permanent Seat

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without
notice in relation to New Zealand’s election to the United Nations Security Council.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? There appears to be
none.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House recognise New Zealand’s election to
the United Nations Security Council for the term of 2015-16. Obtaining 145 votes
against two highly respected and much larger nations is a major achievement. The
overwhelming support in the vote on 16 October in New York is a testament to New
Zealand’s reputation as an independent principal foreign policy contributor and an
acknowledgment of our record at the United Nations over the past 69 years. It is also a
strong affirmation of the important role that a small State like New Zealand can play on
the Security Council.
We ran a very strong campaign over close to a decade. I would like to acknowledge
the Rt Hon Helen Clark, who launched our Security Council campaign, and the
commitment of successive Governments to it. There are several other people I wish to
26 Motions 21 Oct 2014
acknowledge as well. They include the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Murray McCully,
for his leadership and dedication to the campaign; His Excellency Hon Jim McLay and
his team for their work at the coalface of the campaign in New York; the special envoys
Rt Hon Sir Don McKinnon, the Rt Hon Jim Bolger, Colin Keating, Amanda Ellis, Sarah
Dennis, and Lucy Duncan; and the Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson, David
Shearer, for his assistance with the campaign. We were able to run a bipartisan
campaign, and this was well received by the international community, and I think it
counted significantly in our success. I would also like to commend the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs and Trade, including our missions around the world, which worked
tirelessly on the campaign.
We thank all those countries that supported us. We had strong friends and advocates
in every region in the world—in Africa, the Caribbean, Latin America, the Middle East,
and Eastern and Western Europe. I would also like to pay particular tribute to our
friends in the Pacific and Asia, who stood solidly behind our campaign.
Throughout this campaign New Zealand has gained a new level of profile on the
international stage and strengthened our reputation as active global citizens. We look
forward to serving alongside Spain on the council, and I would like to acknowledge
Turkey’s commitme nt to its campaign and the United Nations system. We also made
new connections with a diverse range of countries, and Security Council membership
will allow us to increase our international engagement even further.
This is a once- in-20-years opportunity fo r New Zealand to sit at the world’s top
table. We look forward to again making a meaningful contribution to the important
work of the Security Council. I remember when I went to speak to the United Nations
and the permanent representatives, I had an opportunity to go and speak to the African
congress and the African Union members. At the time, the indication from the chair was
that there would be no questions; I would simply make an intervention and leave. After
I made my intervention, the permanent representative from Rwanda put up her hand and
asked the chair whether she could make a statement. The chair obliged, and the
permanent member got to her feet and said to the members of the African Union that
they should look around, that they should be all voting for New Zealand, that it was the
representation of New Zealand that saved literally millions of people from Rwanda, and
that this was a small country that showed significant influence on the other members of
the council. She put it to the members of the African Union that if it was not for New
Zealand’s contribution, the situation would have been very different.
A small country can make a big difference on the world stage. I think the
bipartisanship shown over the last 10 years and the efforts of our ministry and a great
many other people have contributed to New Zealand once again being given an
opportunity to represent those who are in the greatest of need. Over the next few years it
will be a challenging time for the world. New Zealand’s contribution will be valued.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: The Labour Party supports the
Government’s motion to recognise our election on to the United Nations Security
Council. More than any other place, it is where New Zealand can contribute to peace
and security in the world, and we are living in very turbulent times.
The emphatic victory of 145 votes out of 193, against pretty formidable competition
in the form of Turkey and Spain and without spending that sort of money, is a testament
to a number of things. First of all, it is a testament to our standing in the world. We are
perceived as fair-minded, a country with a principled foreign policy, and an independent
country, one that is a firm supporter of the UN principles.
The quality of our campaign was very important. As the Prime Minister said, it
started 10 years ago under a Labour Government. I acknowledge too the team that
existed within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, those various envoys who
21 Oct 2014 Motions 27
travelled the world, and the formidable team in New York headed by Jim McLay.
Having seen Jim’s work on the ground, I believe he has the respect, the standing, and
the moral compass to be an excellent representative on the council in the years ahead. I
want also to acknowledge the work of this Government and the Prime Minister, but
particularly the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Murray McCully, for spearheading that
effort as well. As the Prime Minister said, it very much is and was a bipartisan effort.
Lastly, our message to those countries that we met —it resonated—was we would on
the council stand up for small States and give them a voice that they often did not have,
to listen and to judge each issue on its merits when it comes to us making a decision,
and that we would be persuaded by the case in front of us, not just by other pressures.
We have an obligation now to make sure we see that through. That might mean taking a
stance against some of our bigger trading partners or perhaps our traditional allies as
well. That is the duty we are given, and that is the undertaking we now have to see
through.
The Prime Minister talked about Rwanda. I remember our last stint on the United
National Security Council. I was a much younger and more “haired” aid worker in
Rwanda back in those days, and I remember Colin Keating giving one of his speeches
in the Security Council where he talked about people around the Security Council
having blood on their hands. I was living and working amongst many of those
Rwandans, and as a person doing that I felt very proud to be a Kiwi who was recognised
by those people around me as standing up for them.
That is the legacy we have, for which we are remembered and on which our
reputation is also based, and it flows through to so many other aspects of how New
Zealand is perceived. The challenge before us in the next 2 years is to make a real
contribution to making this world a more peaceful and safer place, and, in doing so,
further enhance our standing as a country.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: The Green Party also supports the
Government motion around New Zealand attaining the United Nations Security Council
seat. It is a major achievement for a small State. Congratulations to all of those who
were involved in achieving it. On behalf of the Greens, I would also like to thank all of
those countries that voted for New Zealand to hold that seat.
The question now is what we do with the position that we now have, and what we
should do looking forward. It seems to us in the Greens that we need to show leadership
as a country on some of the big global issues, and, in particular, on climate change.
When we ran our campaign we said we would be a voice for the small States on the
Security Council and at the United Nations. There are many, many small States across
the Pacific whose very existence is under threat as a result of sea-level rise as a result of
climate change. If we are to be true to our campaign slogan —that we would be a voice
on the United Nations Security Council for those small States —then we need to show
leadership on climate change.
Climate change should be recognised by the United Nations Security Council as an
international security threat, and New Zealand should support that position. The
Pentagon, just on Monday, released a report asserting decisively that climate change
poses an immediate threat to national security, with increased risk from terrorism,
infectious disease, global poverty, and food shortages. This should be recognised by the
United Nations Security Council. Moreover, if New Zealand is to provide leadership on
climate change, as it should, and if it is to stand up for small island States, then we must
also take action to cut our own greenhouse gas emissions. New Zealand plans to
increase our net greenhouse gas emissions by 50 percent in the next decade. That is a
grossly irresponsible position. Other States and small States, which we say we are
representing on the Security Council, will not thank us for it and it will undermine our
28 Motions 21 Oct 2014
credibility on the UN Security Council if we take that position. We should provide
leadership on climate change on the UN Security Council.
Secondly, and this is to reflect partly also David Shearer’s contribution, we need to
have an independent foreign policy. The Prime Minister’s more recent state ment, that
we should get into a new war simply because our traditional allies are doing so, is the
antithesis of an independent foreign policy. If we are to have an independent voice on
the UN Security Council we need to be independently minded and have an independent
foreign policy. That is what we promised to do in our campaign to be on the Security
Council, and it is very important that we do that.
We asked to be on the world stage, and now we are there. We were not thrust on to
it. We sought it, which is fair enough. Our small country will be judged on how we
exercise our responsibilities to the rest of the world, both those alive today and those
who are yet to come, and how we exercise our responsibilities to the environment of
planet Earth. I look forward to New Zealand exercising those responsibilities in a way
that makes us all proud.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand First wishes to
acknowledge the very significant achievement of New Zealand winning a seat on the
United Nations Security Council in 2015 and 2016. This is a result we welcome, as it
enhances New Zealand’s international standing and reputation. Winning a Security
Council seat was the result of a sustained and effective campaign involving the current
and former Governments. New Zealand First recognises and salutes all who have
contributed to this result. Ministers and many of our foreign affairs staff have played
their part in securing this notable victory. So to all who played a part for New Zealand,

items.speaker: New Zealand First says
items.text: “Well done. You have served the country well.” New Zealand
faced some serious challenges in its bid, as you know, from countries with much greater
resources at their disposal. New Zealand had to be smarter, not a bigger spender, than its
competition.
Having said all that, there is a widespread and deep concern at how effective the
United Nations actually is in confronting the issues facing the international community.
The task is now for New Zealand to use its opportunity of a Security Council seat to
bring about some real reform. As a small country with very modest defence capability,
New Zealand has much to gain from a stable and secure international order. It is very
much in our national interests that the UN is an effective organisation. For 2 years New
Zealand will be sitting on the Security Council, at the summit of world affairs. This is a
great opportunity to make real improvements in the UN —an institution that serves all
peoples around the world. New Zealand has done exceptionally well to gain a seat on
the Security Council, and if it is not too grandiose to say, we must now use this special
opportunity to make the world a better place.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe Mr
Speaker, kia ora tātou katoa e Te Whare. Ko tāku ko te whaiwhai haere i ngā kōrero a
Te Pirimia, ki te mihi ki ngā ringa raupā i kawe nei i tēnei o ngā kaupapa ki mua i te
aroaro o te United Nations, ka mutu, tēnei o ngā kaupapa ki tōna taumata. Ka mihi rā ki
ngā tāngata pēnei i a Murray McCully, ki a Jim McClay, ki a David Shearer ka nui te
mihi ki a koe, ka mutu, ki ngā Pirimia o ngā tau kua h ipa, ki a Helen Clark, ki a Jim
Bolger, ko rātou katoa, ngā ringaringa rāweke i te pepa kia eke tēnei o ngā kaupapa ki
tōna taumata, otirā, ngā mea i āwhina nei i ngā kaikōrero ki te kawe i ēnei moemoā o
Aotearoa, ā, ki tāwāhi.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to us all in the House. My address follows the
sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister. I congratulate the team that worked to put
forward this of the bids before the United Nations, which ultimately was a successful
one. I acknowledge those involved, particularly Murray McCully, Jim McClay, and
21 Oct 2014 Motions 29
David Shearer. A big thank you to you, and, furthermore, to former Prime Ministers
Helen Clark and Jim Bolger, all of them—all the people who played a part in preparing
the document that enabled this of the bids to be successful, those indeed who assisted
the presenters to convey these dreams of New Zealand abroad.]
I also just acknowledge the other gentlemen and ladies who have been mentioned
earlier and the contribution that they made in terms of presenting New Zealand’s case to
the United Nations.
When the UN Secretary-General, Ban Ki-moon, spoke at the University of Auckland
just recently, I am told that he talked about the powers of connectivity in creating
enduring peace. In his speech he referred to the lack of mutual understanding and
respect for the traditions, beliefs, and faiths of others, and the initiative of creating the
Alliance of Civilizations to promote genuine understanding. New Zealand, as others
have said, can be proud today of our success in winning a Security Council seat, but
there is also the courage and the foresight of this Government in overturning the
previous Labour Government’s bizarre decision in 2007 to oppose the Declaration on
the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. So I count myself pretty lucky and privileged to have
been at the United Nations when Dr Pita Sharples presented the case and righted the
wrong. That was indeed a great privilege of my political career.
Although we congratulate all of those involved in supporting the bid for a seat on the
United Nations Security Council, as others have said, we must also recognise the
challenges ahead. New Zealand must use our strength and our moral courage to now
focus on those goals of connectivity, particularly in light of the rights of indigenous
peoples. We must take advantage of our efforts to address the most pressing security
concerns for humanity: issues such as the negative impact of climate change and the
degradation of our environment, the desperate need to disarm nuclear weapons, and the
elimination of poverty. We in Aotearoa are clearly respected throughout the world and
have a solid reputation. We need to ensure that we continue to build on that. Ka nui te
mihi.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I want to join with others in
paying tribute and congratulating the successive generations of politicians, diplomats,
and officials who over the last 10 years have mounted this wonderful campaign that ha s
seen New Zealand succeed in winning election on to the Security Council for the 2-year
term 2015 to 2016.
Last week I reviewed the speech that Peter Fraser made in San Francisco in 1945,
when he described New Zealand as being a small country. He said that it was, indeed,
one of the smallest of the small but that that did not remove our right to be represented
on the international stage and to have a voice. As we take up this role on the Security
Council, those words are as appropriate today as they were then.
Reference has already been made to the role that New Zealand played in the Rwanda
situation, and that was a combination of our independence, our insight, and our moral
courage to be able to take a stand that was ultimately right and that stopped the absolute
slaughter that was occurring. There will be challenges of a similar type that will face us
during the 2-year term that lies ahead.
We were elected to the Security Council because of the virtues that we bring as a
small nation. During that term and as we approach those challenges, the expectation will
be upon us to act as the voice of small nations, to bring that balance, that distance, and
that perspective that people admire in us, and not to simply be a surrogate for the major
players round the Security Council table. If we can perform that role with dignity and
with élan, then, in fact, we will not only achieve the aspiration that Peter Fraser set out
way back in 1945 but also make a material contribution to improving the circumstances
of so many people around the world in addressing the major issues that have been raised
30 Motions 21 Oct 2014
even in this House this afternoon that people expect New Zealand to take a stand on

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I would like to add my congratulations to all
of the people who have worked over many years to secure New Zealand’s
representation on the Security Council for the 2015-16 term. That this effort has been
ongoing for almost a decade is a tribute to the perseverance of all involved and to New
Zealand’s reputation in the world as an honest broker.
Like all representative institutions, the United Nations is not perfect. It brings those
free and democratic countries that share a profound respect for liberty and property
rights together with many countries that for now have few, if any, of those attributes,
and it gives relatively equal standing to all —except, of course, for the permanent
members of the Security Council. One important rationale for securing this position is
that it offers some chance to improve the institutions of the United Nations.
We are indisputably a free and democratic country with an independent foreign
policy and an outward-looking view on trading relationships. We have much to offer.
Another reason for participation is that we, like everybody else, should make a
contribution. New Zealand’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations and
Ambassador in Washington through 1944 to 1952, Sir Carl Berendsen, expressed this
well when he said: “We in New Zealand are not of those who ask what we are not
prepared to give, we are not of those who demand help which we are not prepared to
accord, and we are not of those who are content to leave to others burdens which w e
ourselves should assume.” In short, he was arguing that we should play our part. I
commend this motion to the House.
Motion agreed to.
Hon (Edward) Gough Whitlam AC, QC

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without
notice to acknowledge the death of Gough Whitlam, the former Prime Minister of
Australia.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? There appears to be
none.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House express its sadness at the passing
today of former Australian Prime Minister the Hon Gough Whitlam AC, QC, aged 98 .
Mr Whitlam was Australia’s 21 st Prime Minister, in 1972, and served as Australian
political leader for 3 years until 1975. I acknowledge that leadership and on behalf of
New Zealanders I would like to express our condolences to his family and the people of
Australia.
People around the world will remember Mr Whitlam for leading Australia during a
dramatic period in Australian politics, but, equally, he should be remembered for his
leadership and his achievements. Although he was Prime Minister for a short period of
time, Mr Whitlam maintained a lifelong interest in public policy, including, I might add,
an abiding interest in Australia’s identity, its place in the world, and, I would note, he
was a very strong advocate for changing his nation’s flag. He understood the
importance of national identity and having a flag that was instantly recognisable and
meaningful to the people it sought to represent.
New Zealand and Australia have historically maintained a close relationship, and
Prime Ministers of all political hues have continued to work together for the betterment
of New Zealanders and Australians. Australia is a country whose fortunes, values, and
people are deeply entwined with our own. We share a similar path in history and our
21 Oct 2014 Obituaries 31
shared aspirations for prosperity and opportunity for our people, bound by common
values, lead us to a shared future. The trans-Tasman relationship has continued to
strengthen and today is in very good health, but it is important that we continue to work
on this relationship, and this Government does so as a priority.
I would like to acknowledge the efforts of former Australian Prime Minister Gough
Whitlam and the part he had to play in the history of the friendship of our two countries.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Labour joins the Prime
Minister in expressing our sympathy to the family of Gough Whitlam, former Labor
Prime Minister of Australia from 1972 to 1975, who died at the grand old age of 98
years. As we say here in New Zealand, “a mighty tōtara has fallen” across the Tasman.
He was born in 1916 in Kew, a suburb of Melbourne, and his real name was Edward
Gough Whitlam. He was called by his middle name Gough because his maternal
grandfather was called Edward. He married Margaret in 1942 and they had four
children. Although he was Prime Minister for only 3 years he became a defining
political figure in modern Australia. He came into Government following long periods
of Conservative Governments, and there were a lot of similarities between Gough
Whitlam’s time coming into Government and our own time led by “Big Norm” Kirk.
He was a Prime Minister who did institute sweeping changes, and the Prime Minister
has talked about one of them —changing the flag. But he actually transformed
Australian society in many ways. He brought in the national health insurance scheme,
Medibank. He abolished university fees. He returned traditional lands in the Northern
Territory to the Gurindji people. He formed relationships with China, he withdrew
troops from Viet Nam, he passed the Racial Discrimination Act, and so much more. His
commitment to Labor values aligned very much with the values of our own great tōtara,
Norman Kirk.
He was a towering figure, and I remember meeting him in the 1990s when I went to
a meeting in Sydney. He walked into the room; he was 1.94 metres tall, he had a
flowing mop of silver hair and a big booming voice, and his oratory was spellbinding.
He was accompanied by Margaret, who was only slightly shorter than him, who was
also a very strong personality and who had very forthright views indeed. Wherever they
went, people stopped and looked at them. There was a real warmth towards them,
particularly from the Labor Party in Australia, because he became an inspiration for
generations of progressive politicians. Like our own “Big Norm”, he was  referred to in
Australia by his first name, Gough. He was also a man with a great sense of humour and
many famous quotes. After the famous —or infamous—dismissal of his Government by
Sir John Kerr on 11 November 1975, he stood on the steps of the old Parliament House
and said: “Well may we say ‘God save the Queen’, because nothing will save the
Governor-General!”. On his 80th birthday, he said: “I do admit I seem eternal. Dying
will happen sometime. As you know, I plan for the ages, not just for this life.”  When he
was asked about what his plans were for the next age, his afterlife, he replied, of a
possible meeting with his maker: “You can be sure of one thing—I shall treat Him as an
equal.” I am told that Norm Kirk and Gough Whitlam had quite a testy relat ionship, but
the similarities between the two are very apparent. When Margaret died in 2012 he said
that the love of his life had died. He was a man of superb intellect, knowledge, and
literacy.
We mourn his passing, for the people of Australia but also, as the Prime Minister
said, because of the bonds and relationships that have been formed between our two
countries over many, many decades. We pass on our sympathy to his family today.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: The Green Party joins the
Government in remembering Gough Whitlam. Gough Whitlam was a hero to
generations of progressive political activists in Australia like me. In fact, this is my
32 Obituaries 21 Oct 2014
signed copy of the The Whitlam Government 1972-1975 , which I got Gough to sign
many, many years ago. He bequeathed a progressive legacy to Australia. Gough
Whitlam—and also I think we should remember Lionel Murphy, in particular, the
Attorney-General, then High Court judge —stood up for something. They stood up for
something real.
Gough had a passion for social justice, and he had a passion for education and for the
arts. In his short Government —only 3 years long— he achieved free university
education, universal health care, legal aid, he passed the Racial Discrimination Act, and
he changed the national anthem from God Save the Queen  to Advance Australia Fair ,
which is also something of a dirge, it has got to be said, but it is better than God Save
the Queen . He introduced land rights —in particular, in the Northern Territory, where
the Gurindji people received their land rights. He ended conscription. He ended the
death penalty. He ratified the human rights convention, the World Heritage Convention,
he established the national parks and wildlife service, he protected the Great Barrier
Reef, and he set up the department of urban development. He introduced no-fault
divorce to Australia. He gave independence to Papua New Guinea and he recognised
China, and so much more, in just 3 short years.
He was, in a word, Australia’s equivalent to “Big Norm” Kirk, although he did have
an Australian-sized ego. To repeat Annette King’s joke, and it was quite a great joke, he
said of an afterlife: “You can be sure of one thing”— referring to when he might meet
God—“I shall treat Him as an equal.”, which was Gough’s approach to many things.
Gough showed that what matters in politics is not how long you are here; it is what
you can achieve. His great many achievements were a victory for the optimists in
history, and he will be remembered for that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand First joins with
other parties in marking the death of Gough Whitlam, a former Australian Prime
Minister, and in acknowledging his contribution to Australian political life. He will
always have a special place in Australian history because of the constitutional crisis that
saw his dismissal from office whilst Prime Minister. That event still reverberates in
Australian political life today.
It cannot be denied, though, that he was a gifted and charismatic and courageous
politician, and he had real character. When visiting the Queen he was required to go to
the outfitter first and dress up in tails. He was asked by the outfitter: “What side do you
dress on?”, to which he said: “Both sides, comrade; both sides.”  On another occasion he
was asked to kick the ball off at the former Queensland versus New South Wales annual
state rugby league match, before it became what it is today, the State of Origin. He was
up there, and, of course, at that time Bjelke-Petersen was the premier, and Gough was
extremely, extremely hostilely received. There was booing from the time he walked out
on to the middle of the paddock and kicked the ball off, all the way back to the stand,
whereupon he turned round to the chairman of the rugby league union in Queensland
and said: “Don’t you ever ask me back again. You are so unpopular!”.
It also cannot be denied that he was seriously let down by a number of his
colleagues. People can remember the Khemlani Affair and the illegal loan offshore, and
he was also let down by one of his Ministers, whom I will not name because he went
AWOL and virtually went bush. But as other colleagues have said, he was extremely
far-sighted and made many progressive changes that still benefit the Australian people.
He was active in political life well into his 90s, so for some of you there is hope into the
future. [Interruption] You are only jealous. But it cannot be denied that Gough Whitlam
was truly a great Australian.
Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL (Leader —Māori Party: Tēnā koe Mr Speaker. I te
ata nei i kōrerohia te āhuatanga o te hunga mate e taku tuahine e te Hōnore Nanaia
21 Oct 2014 Obituaries 33
Māhuta. Nāna tonu i whakapā mai ngā mate katoa o te motu, ka mutu, nō nā tata nei
tātau i rongo ai mō te matenga o tēnei o ngā Pirimia o Ahitereiria. Nō reira, me pēnei
rawa te kōrero hai whaiwhai haere i tāna i whakatakoto ai ki mua i te aroaro o Te Whare
Pāremata. Koutou te kāhui mate haere koutou, haere koutou, haere koutou, e moe, e
moe, e moe.
[Thank you Mr Speaker. This morning my sister the Hon Nanaia Mahuta made
references to those who had passed away throughout the nation, and, furthermore, we
have just heard about the death of one of the Prime Ministers of Australia. Therefore, to
follow on to those she brought before the House of Parliament, I say to you the dead,
depart, journey on, farewell, sleep, rest and slumber.]
The Māori Party stands, along with our colleagues in the House, to acknowledge the
passing of Gough Whitlam. In particular, I refer to one of the elements that has already
been raised by colleagues, and that is around the reaching out to the indigenous people
of Australia. There is a particular photograph from 1975 of Gough Whitlam passing soil
to the traditional landowner from the Northern Territory, a Gurindji man named Vincent
Lingiari. I have a photo here of him —a fine man—and it was seen as a defining image
of the Whitlam era. Mr Lingiari was one of four signatories to the petition to the
Governor-General in 1967. That petition argued that “morally the land is ours and
should be returned to us.”
Mr Whitlam, in a time when it was considered controversial, paved the way for later
reform through his early recognition of Aboriginal land rights, and in that symbolic
action of passing the soil he sent a message to the world that indigenous Australians
share the same nation and the same hopes of those who arrived earlier from other lands.
In 1974 the Australian Cabinet accepted in principle the Woodward royal
commission on Aboriginal land rights in the Northern Territory, which later led to the
introduction of the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act of 1976. We think
of the bold actions of Gough Whitlam today, and that symbolic land hand-back
ceremony is part of his legacy and also a challenge for future administrations. Such a
legacy can inspire hope around the world that politicians can be open to working with
indigenous peoples to help set an agenda for change. We recognise his passing and
express our sympathies to his family and to the peoples of Australia. E ai ki t e kōrero,
ko koe te tōtara o te wao o Ahitereiria. E koro, e moe, haere. [ According to the
aphorism, you are the podocarpus of the forest of Australia. Rest old one, farewell.]

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I want to join with other
members in expressing sympathy to the people of Australia and to the family of the late
Gough Whitlam at his passing at the grand old age of 98 this morning. He was the most
outstanding Prime Minister, in terms of flair, in terms of dynamism, and in terms of
achievement, of the last couple of generations in the lucky country. He had the
advantage of coming at the end of the very staid Menzies period, when Australia was
ready to come into the latter half of the 20 th century and to take some positive and bold
steps.
We have heard the range of reforms that he unleashed over a 3-year period referred
to by so many speakers in the House this afternoon. But if you look at Australia during
that time, it was also the time of a remarkable cultural renaissance. Australian literature,
film, and the good things in life —food, wine—all flourished, and there seemed to be an
air that the confidence and the style that the Whitlams unleashed had let these things out
of the bottle in Australia, and Australia had truly come of age as a country.
Like all grand men, he was not without fault. He was imperious, he dominated his
Cabinet both physically and intellectually, and on one famous occasion during a very
frustrating debate he was heard to proclaim: “God protect me from short people!”,
which was a reference to the Ministers around him. During the 1974 campaign, his
34 Obituaries 21 Oct 2014
second campaign, he insisted on the electoral slogan: “Gough’s going great.”, only until
such time as the Liberals rephrased it as: “Gough’s going. Great!”.
He will always be remembered, as others have mentioned, for the circumstances of
his dismissal. But the fact that nearly 40 years after that event we still talk about it and
we still recall it vividly—we remember the scenes on the steps of Parliament House, we
remember the intricate movements around it —shows what a remarkable man Gough
Whitlam was. He continued to be active right until the middle of his 90s. I recall
speaking recently, in the last couple of years, to a publisher who was saying that she
was publishing some work for him and she could not keep up with the pace of sending
him drafts one evening and having the corrected drafts back the following morning from
this nonagenarian gentleman—a man of remarkable intellect and skill.
It is a huge loss to the people of Australia. He was a man who, I think, did a lot in his
time to bridge the gap in the relationship with New Zealand. The Canberra pact signed
in 1944 had long since ceased to be operative between our two countries. Whitlam and
Kirk renewed it. People have referred to “Big Norm”. I sat behind the two of them, by
about two rows, at the opening of the Christchurch Commonwealth Games, and I have
to say to the House that when they stood up, Gough Whitlam was bigger, taller, and
larger, and that was a considerable achievement. A great Australian, a great man —he
will be missed. His country, deservedly, is proud of his achievement.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I come to this debate with somewhat less
primary experience than earlier speakers. However, let me say that amongst almost 200
nations in this world, there is no better friend of New Zealand than Australia, and we are
bound together as nations by our common classical, liberal heritage. So it is with great
sorrow that I pay tribute to an Australian leader who was instrumental in expanding that
heritage across the ditch. His removal of the death penalty and military conscription
were important liberal achievements for any leader, and he was the one who made them
for Australia. That is how I will remember him. I commend this motion to the House.
Motion agreed to.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: I move, That a respectful Address be presented to His
Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency’s speech . Mr Speaker, can
I first congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker. I am sure you will continue to
discharge the responsibilities of this office with skill and care. Can I also congratulate
the Deputy Speaker, the Hon Chester Borrows, and the Assistant Speakers Lindsay
Tisch and my opponent in the Hutt, my friend the Hon Trevor Mallard. I will look
forward to him chairing the debates.
It is an honour and a privilege to have been elected a member of Parliament. I am
here because the National Party has placed its faith in me to be an effective list MP, and
I am here ultimately, of course, because over 1 million New Zealanders voted for
National in the recent election. I thank the party and I thank New Zealand for honouring
me with this important job.
I also thank the people of Hutt South. Lower Hutt was where I was born and raised,
and I am happy to be living there again. I am proud to say that I am from the Hutt, an
area with which I have a long family connection. On my mother’s side of the family I
am descended from seven Dixon siblings who arrived on ships at Pētone beach between
1838 and 1856. Edward Dixon is one of them, and every summer when I go to the Basin
Reserve I sit beneath his memorial clock in the old grandstand. My great-great-
grandfather Joe Dixon walked the Hutt Road before it even existed, and, as a lay
preacher, held services on Pētone beach, a stone’s throw from where I now live.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 35
From the days of Oswald Mazengarb QC’s famous report into delinquent youths at
milk bars in the 1950s, Lower Hutt has had a somewhat, I think it is fair to say, mixed
reputation. Stereotypes are hard to break, but let me say this to the House: the Hutt is a
wonderful place. We have fantastic high-tech businesses at the forefront of the new
economy. We have excellent community facilities and a wonderful natural environment
right on our doorstep. Most of all, we have innovative and spirited people. I believe that
the Hutt Valley’s best days are ahead of it, and I am looking forward to serving the
people of the Hutt, fr om Wainuiōmata to the Western Hills, as a list MP based in the
area.
While I am saying thanks, I would like to put on the record my thanks to everyone
who has helped me get to where I am today: my family, who have loved and supported
me in ways too numerous to detail; my friends; my Hutt South campaign committee,
which ran such a high-energy campaign; the National Party leadership, in particular
Malcolm Plimmer, Glenda Hughes, and Roger Bridge; and the Young Nats, who make
it so much easier to stand by the side of the road at 6.30 a.m. doing human hoardings in
the cold because of their infectious enthusiasm. Most important, I want to thank my
partner and campaign manager, Jenna, who has been the rock of my life for the past 6
years.
As some members know, I have been lucky enough to work in roles behind the
scenes for this Government. I have worked directly for two very different but
exceptional Ministers —the Hon Gerry Brownlee and the Hon Steven Joyce. It is a
privilege—although, I have to say, a little bit surreal—to be joining them in a caucus led
by a man I also greatly admire, the Rt Hon John Key. Thank you, Gerry and Steven, for
your friendship, guidance, and wisdom. If I achieve half as much in politics as you
have, I will be doing pretty well.
I come to this House as someone who has always, for as long as I can recall, been
interested in politics, history, public policy, and the law. My parents, John Bishop and
Rosemary Dixon, are to blame. From dad I got my love of politics. Dad was in the press
gallery from 1982 to 1987. He was chief parliamentary reporter for TVNZ during that
momentous year of 1984. The political bug was transferred to me, or so the family joke
goes, when he was told to talk to his new baby. Most people would choose to talk abou t
the weather, what is on TV, or something like that. His topic of choice was none other
than this man called Sir Robert Muldoon. I have had an enduring fascination with him
and his politics ever since.
Growing up I would pepper dad for stories about his time as a journalist —about the
night of the 1984 snap election, about the night of the Mount Erebus crash, about
travelling with Geoffrey Palmer to try to save the ANZUS alliance. I drank it all in, and
those stories and those lessons have shaped who I am today. From mum I got my love
of the law, particularly public law. From both my parents I gained an interest in ideas, in
current affairs, and in the world around me. Growing up, our household was one where
everyone was expected to have a view and not to be shy about expressing it. Indeed,
both my parents were champion debaters, and mum was instrumental in establishing the
New Zealand Schools’ Debating Council, which I was president of for 4 years much
later in life. Almost every year since 1988, the grand final of the Russell McVeagh
national championships have been held where we were this morning, the Legislative
Council Chamber. There are now four alumni of the championships who have become

items.speaker: MPs
items.text: Jacinda Ardern, Megan Woods, Holly Walker, and myself. I am pleased that our
side of the House is now represented on that list, and I am sure that there will be many
more in the years to come.
My dad’s side of the family— although, I should say, not necessarily my dad, whose
politics I do not know —is true blue. The Bishops were farmers at Hillend, outside
36 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Balclutha in South Otago. My Poppa Stuart joined Wright Stephenson in 1928 and
worked for it until he retired, interrupted only by World War II, where he fought at
Monte Cassino. Stewart and Cora Bishop almost certainly voted National their entire
lives. They referred to national superannuation as “Rob’s lolly”.
My mother’s side of the family could not be more different. They were Methodists in
the great reforming progressive tradition, and Labour voters to their toes. One great-
grandfather was a wharfie who won the honoured 151-day loyalty card during the 1951
strike. My grandfather Haddon Dixon was a Methodist minister, a social activist, a
director of CORSO Aotearoa New Zealand, and an inveterate follower of politics. He
was the sort of man for whom Parliament TV was made. My nana was a progressive
socialist. In 1981, as a 61-year-old, sickened by apartheid in South Africa, she joined
the “Stop the Tour” movement, helped organise a sit -down protest on the Hutt
motorway during the Wellington test, refused to move, and was duly arrested. She
happily did her 200 hours’ community service painting the Barnardos centre in
Waterloo Road in the Hutt, so I think I get my social liberalism and my reforming zeal
from my grandparents, although, it is fair to say, not my Labour Party politics.
I come to this House as a 31-year-old, a representative of Generation Y. Our
generation does not remember needing a doctor’s prescription to buy margarine or
needing permission from the Reserve Bank to subscribe to a foreign magazine or any of
the other absurdities of life in the Fortress New Zealand economy. It seems scarcely
believable to us that from 1982 to 1984 all wages and prices in New Zealand were
frozen by prime ministerial fiat. For our generation, inflation has always been low, we
have always been nuclear-free, homosexuality has always been legal, and the Treaty
settlement process has always been under way.
New Zealand is a completely different country from what it was when I was born,
and I have always been profoundly fascinated by that transformation and what its
effects have been. It intrigues me, for example, that although Bob Hawke and Paul
Keating are regarded by the Labor movement in Australia as heroes and receive
standing ov ations at Labor conferences to this day, New Zealand’s own Labour
reformers are essentially pariahs from their party. I think a significant portion of the left
in New Zealand has never made its peace with the economic reforms of the 1980s and
1990s, and in some ways the debate inside the Labour Party today is the most visible
manifestation of that lack of reconciliation. The battles of the 1980s continue to echo
today and are still being fought. I think that is a shame.
A maiden speech is traditionally the time to put on the record your principles,
philosophy, and beliefs. I will do so with the caveat that I am not so arrogant as to think
that my current views are immutable. Some of my political heroes said things in their
maiden speeches they almost certainly would not have agreed with later in their careers.
Roger Douglas’ maiden speech in 1969, for example, is extremely sceptical of the
benefits of foreign investment in New Zealand. In 1970 Paul Keating told the Australian
Parliament that the Commonwealth Government should set up a statutory authority to
fix the prices of all goods and services in the Australian economy, and he bemoaned the
number of young mothers who were entering the workforce. I think good politicians
listen, reflect, read, and think deeply about the world, and, if necessary, change their
minds. I hope to always be open to that in my time in this House.
I am an unashamed economic and social liberal. The classical enunciation of
liberalism within the National Party remains John Marshall’s maiden speech as the
member for Mount Victoria in 1947. I believe, as he did, that the conditions of a good
society are liberty, property, and security, and the greatest of these is liberty. I think
individuals make better decisions about their own lives than Governments do. A
fundamental belief in the primacy of the individual over the collective should be the
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 37
lodestar that guides all good Governments. I think we should trust individuals more than
we do, and be more sceptical about the ability of Governments to solve social problems.
I believe that the best way to deliver the prosperity New Zealanders deserve is
through a globally competitive market-based economy that rewards enterprise and
innovation. The reforms of the 1980s and 1990s were vitally important in transforming
New Zealand from a sclerotic economic basket case to a modern, functioning,
competitive economy, but there is more to be done.
I support a tolerant multicultural New Zealand that is confident, proud, and open to
the world. Our society is enriched greatly by migration. The periodic desire by some to
