scapegoat migrants I find deeply distasteful. I am proud of how far New Zealand has
come in only one generation —from an inward-looking, insular economy and society to
one that is increasingly internationally connected and confident on the world stage.
I believe we can responsibly develop our natural resources and improve our
environment at the same time. We are blessed with abundant natural resources in New
Zealand, both renewable and non-renewable, and we are not wealthy enough as a nation
to not take advantage of them. What we know from history is that the wealthier a
country is, the more able it is to take practical steps to improve the environment. Some
of the most polluted places on Earth were in the communist Soviet Union. Growing our
economy through the responsible development of our resources gives us the ability to
preserve things precious to New Zealand like our rivers, lakes, and national parks.
I come to this House with a long history in debating, at school and university. I have
a profound belief in free speech, the power of ideas, and the importance of persuasion
by those in public office. Fundamental sustainable change in public policy is only ever
achieved when the argument is won. That is how marriage equality was achieved. It is
how Treaty settlements were started and how they have continued. It is how we tore
down the walls of the Fortress New Zealand economy. Leaders in this Parliament made
the case for those things and won the argument. One of the proudest moments of my life
was to debate in the Oxford Union, standing at the same dispatch box that Lange stood
at when he delivered his famous speech on the moral indefensibility of nuclear
weapons. Lange was at his best when he was arguing. I believe Bill English had it right
in his maiden speech as the member for Wallace in 1991: “what I do bring to this job is
a willingness to get into the argument rather than to avoid it. I owe it to my voters to
present in Parliament what is best in them —a credible, constructive, and committed
argument. Power without persuasion has no lasting place in a democracy,”. As long as I
am an MP I will always try to present credible and constructive arguments, and I will
always be willing to have one.
I am proud to be joining a Government that is demonstrably making a difference to
New Zealanders. I agree with the Prime Minister. We are on the cusp of something
special as a nation. This National Government has a historic opportunity to be the kind
of long-term Government that does not just administer the status quo but one that can,
through incremental constant reform, deliver ever-growing living standards for New
Zealanders. We have the economic opportunities right in front of us: globalisation, a
rapidly growing Asian middle class, and technology ending the tyranny of distance. We
have the right leadership through John Key, Bill English, and the Cabinet team, and we
have the right policy framework in place: smaller Government through better
Government, openness to foreign capital and labour, a tax system that rewards hard
work and enterprise, a growing culture of innovation, and, most important, we have a
fundamental belief in the power of the New Zealand individual and civil society.
This is a Government that is governing with a hard head and a soft heart. We are the
first Government in a long time that has a resolute focus on tackling some of the
intractable social problems that have bedevilled New Zealand for too long, such as a
38 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
persistent underclass, wel fare dependency, Māori and Pasifika educational
underachievement, and poor-quality social housing. We are not doing this simply by
throwing more money at problems. Care for those most vulnerable in our community is
not, or should not be, measured by the amount of money spent, the number of
bureaucratic agencies set up, or the number of people employed to deal with the
problem. We should judge policy by results. Milton Friedman was right: “One of the
great mistakes is to judge policies and programmes by their intentions rather than their
results.”
This is a results-driven Government. Across the fields of welfare, housing, and
education we are driving through quite remarkable and transformative change that is
delivering results for the most needy in our society. There is still more important work
to do. One thing that I am personally passionate about is our plan to reward excellent
teachers and keep them in the classroom, doing what they do best —changing kids’
lives. Everyone remembers their amazing teachers, growing up. It is simply wrong that
the classic career pathway for teachers at the moment involves leaving the classroom to
move into administration. I am proud to be part of a Government that is changing that.
When people look back on this passage in New Zealand’s history, it is my fervent
hope that they will recognise that it was the fifth National Government that put in place
the reforms to raise the quality of teaching in our schools, that challenged the soft
bigotry of low expectations, that made progress on tackling child abuse and family
violence, that made social housing actually work for people, and that invested in people
to support their aspirations for independence from the State. This Government’s signal
economic achievements are important, but I think and hope this Government will be
known for much more than that.
In closing, let me just say finally that I come to this House with the desire to serve, to
represent the people of the Hutt Valley, to apply my mind to the challenges facing New
Zealand now and in the future, and to work hard each and every day for and on behalf
of New Zealanders. Much faith has been placed in me by many people. I intend to work
hard to repay that faith.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: I second the
motion that a respectful address be presented to His Excellency the Governor-General in
reply to His Excellency’s speech. Tēnā tātou  katoa Te Pāremata hou. E Te Kaikōr ero
tēnā koe. E Te Pirimia tēnā koe. Ko ngā mea nui ko ngā wai, ko te whenua me ngā
tāngata katoa o Aotearoa. Nā reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[Salutations to us all in the new Parliament; to you, Mr Speaker; and to you, Prime
Minister. The things of immense importance are water, land and all the people of New
Zealand. Therefore, acknowledgments to you, and you, and to us all collectively.]
Mr Speaker, Prime Minister, Ministers, members of Parliament and party president
Mr Peter Goodfellow, welcome, and welcome to my guests in the gallery. My husband,
Louis, you have been a fantastic support and friend to me. We will be celebrating our
35th wedding anniversary 12 days from now at an electorate event in Ōtorohanga, which
in itself indicates the level of support you have given me during the campaign. My
family—Craig, Rachel, and Tony —Dad and I are both very proud of you, and we
appreciate that you are all in support for this special occasion. Tony, I know you are
watching. To your partners Kenneth and Zoe at home, to our four special grandchildren
Zak, Max, Aislinn, and Theo, and to mum and dad —Leo and Leonie —thank you for
coming. I would also like to acknowledge my grandmother Joan Jeffries in Ōpunake
who recently turned 98. To Peter Goodfellow, Peter Osborne, Leveson Gower, National
headquarters staffers, Young Nats, and party members, from selection to election you
have all welcomed me and supported me in my quest to become a member of
Parliament. Together we asked lots of questions and took good advice, and here we are.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 39
I was brought up on a Taranaki dairy farm and I had one goal: never to marry a dairy
farmer. Louis, I am very pleased I did because I learnt the ropes, developed a passion,
and enjoyed my time on the farm raising our family and developing an award-winning
business that continues today. This led to my many industry roles, the longest of which I
completed last week at DairyNZ. I would like to especially acknowledge DairyNZ
chair, friend, and colleague John Luxton, who is in the House. John, you and I were
elected to the board on the same day in 2003. Over the past 11 years I have learnt a lot
from you, and I respect the wisdom and knowledge that you impart.
I have served on a range of boards over the past few years. The Primary Industry
Training Organisation, the Taratahi Agricultural Training Centre, and Dairy Training
have provided me with the skills needed for the training industry. I was a New Zealand
Young Farmers board member, where I suspect I own the honour of being the only
granny who has ever been a board member. As an industry partner to this group, I was
able to enjoy working with young people having their first board experience, who I
know will feature in many areas of leadership in New Zealand over the next 30 years. In
2006 I was fortunate to travel as an Agricultural and Marketing Research and
Development Trust scholar on a food and agribusiness market experience to China,
Japan, the US, and Europe, looking at supply chains and customers. This experience
really highlighted the fact that New Zealand is favoured for its exports, indicating New
Zealand’s stand-out place in the international trading arena.
In 2012 the Dairy Women’s Network awarded me the inaugural Dairy Woman of the
Year, which was one of my proudest moments to date. It was not a one-person accolade,
as it was the result of all of the experiences I have had to this point in my life and of all
the people I have met. The information learnt on the course and the friendships formed
emphasise the rural and regional woman that I am, always looking for future ways for
the primary industry sector to grow. I was also a board member of the Venture Taranaki
trust, and in recognition of my governance roles I was recently awarded a fellowship of
the Institute of Directors.
Taranaki - King Country is a large electorate that extends from Waingaro right down
to Tuakau on the border of Stratford, thus including Waipā and parts of the Waikato.
Upon selection, one of my new constituents offered to buy this “Naki” girl a Waikato
rugby jersey. I told him I would wear it with pride. The respective mascots for the local
teams—Mooloo the Cow and Ferdinand the Bull —always managed to create a great
herd, and best of all, when Taranaki play Waikato I can only win as the Taranaki - King
Country MP. Minister Smith, we are looking forward to the Taranaki versus Tasman
final this weekend.
Although I have an interest in rugby, it is not necessarily my favourite sport. The
excitement of V8 supercar racing is another passion that I have to thank Louis for
sharing with me. I have been a passenger at 260 kilometres per hour on a racetrack with
a professional driver, and I can categorically say that my own driving skills are not quite
up to that standard. I will be honest and say that I am happy to be a spectator,
supporting Louis as he drives his star car, much like he supports me in my campaigning.
In the large electorate that is Taranaki - King Country we have eight district councils,
about 17 towns, and many villages. Our largest town is Te Awamutu, and
Whangamomona is one of the smallest. I am the MP who will not forget about the
Forgotten World Highway. I encourage all of you to take the tour. It is an excellent
tourism business, set up on an old railway. I am the MP who will not forget the natural
beauty of our electorate, which can be seen in the Waitomo Caves and the huge number
of visitors who visit annually to experience the beauty of the glow worms and the
history hidden in these caves. I am the MP who probably does not have the willpower to
drive past our famous whitebait fritters in our towns, including Mōkau and Raglan,
40 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
without stopping for that quintessential Kiwi lunch. Ultimately I am the MP who is here
to serve every one of our towns to ensure that the future of Taranaki - King Country is
bright.
Economic development in the regions is a key interest of mine. Getting the right
incentives in place for businesses to thrive in rural locations is a must. Housing is not
expensive, and the community atmosphere is supportive and embracing. The call for
more skilled young people is coming from every community. Coming from Taranaki I
have been witness to the growth that comes from a region that has worked together over
many years to create a vibrant region. That comes from having an open mind, a
willingness to trust new ideas, and a will to work together. From this we can see that
when communities actively work together, success can be achieved. Trade and exports
lead our region’s income. The dairy and beef and lamb industries are predominant
throughout our electorate. Energy in itself is one of the integral parts of the Taranaki
export economy. In Taranaki - King Country we also have dairy goats, mānuka honey,
and a popcorn factory—something for everyone. But the young are not forgotten either,
with the long-established Fun Ho! Toys factory in Inglewood. Each of my
grandchildren, the boys and the girl, all received a Fun Ho! Toys tractor and trailer for
their first birthday.
Ultra-fast broadband will provide a huge boost to our region. The productivity that
comes with connectivity will help us attract people who want the benefits of working
regionally. I look forward to working with Minister Amy Adams to ensure this rolls out
across Taranaki - King Country.
Roading and infrastructure will continue to be a focus in Taranaki - King Country. I
particularly look forward to the new roundabout at the intersection of State Highway 3
and State Highway 37, and the business case for the Mount Messenger - Awakino
Gorge corridor. I also look forward to the development of various bridges across the
electorate, which will further strengthen relationships between communities, with
improved accessibility and safety.
Mr Speaker, you recently came to visit Waitomo and Piopio. Louis in particular was
extremely honoured by your visit, namely because it was his birthday. This day we saw
some great examples of fledgling regional businesses. The new King Country brewery
and a small business in Piopio fitting out dinghies are indicative of the success that
ensures when our regions work together, we thrive. We must be sure that red tape does
not get in the way of new and emerging businesses that will provide employment for
our people. I have already seen some exciting technology businesses in Raglan, and the
encouragement of more will be welcome.
Access to health, education, and community services is vitally important to remote
and rural areas of New Zealand. Under a National-led Government over 17,000 more
elective surgeries have been administered across our electorates to district health boards
and this shows that somewhat remote areas of New Zealand are still gaining access to
those vital services and that location is not a barrier.
Across our region more children will attend early childhood education before starting
primary school, which is impressive for rural communities, considering the distance,
which is often regarded as a barrier. In time we hope to improve these rates even more,
with a target of 98 percent by 2016.
Volunteers connect our communities, from the Fire Service to the Coastguard to
those working in the prevention of family violence. I would like to thank all the
volunteers who do a wonderful job. Those who give up their time to take a neighbour to
a doctor’s appointment or those busy mums and dads who arrange playdat es for the
entire street—your support and continual commitment to the groups and individuals in
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 41
our regions is to be commended. These actions take away the vulnerability of people,
knowing there is a volunteer support base to care for them.
Water will be a prominent topic, not just through the time that I spend in Parliament
but for years into the future. This is reflective of the fact that we have an abundance of
water in our beautiful country, and it is amongst my aspirations to ensure that we utilise
our water wisely for our people, for our tourism, and for our industries. As a dairy
industry leader I appreciate how much work has been done on fencing, nutrient
budgeting, and finding ways to improve water quality. It will be a pleasure to join my
first Bl uegreens caucus meeting. National’s blue -green approach has shown that
successful economic and environmental policy can and must go hand in hand. The
abundant forests, rivers, and marine reserves are of real value and importance to the
National Government, which is committed to the long-term sustainability of these areas
that New Zealand holds dear.
On completion of my time as Dairy Woman of the Year I set myself a target that by
the year 2020 in New Zealand we will no longer be talking about the disconnec t
between rural and urban. We have the collective knowledge, talent, and ability to work
together to find answers. It is a big call, but one that I am up for. I ask each and every
one of you to join me in this project. We have only 4.5 million people. We have to work
collaboratively to take on the world.
Thank you to my colleagues for the support that you have shown over the past few
months, and particularly over the past 4 weeks. Maureen Pugh, the class of 2014
enjoyed the 2 weeks we spent with you and we were sorry to see you go. Samantha,
Claire, Sharon, and Tracey—welcome to my team. With your help I know that Taranaki
- King Country will be well served. Penn and Doug, thanks for your help and
preparation. I am excited about joining the Primary Production Committee and Health
Committee, where I can bring some of my existing knowledge with me and embark on a
new learning curve where new knowledge is required. I commit to be a hard-working
and loyal member of Parliament. Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I move, That the
following words be added to the Address: “and expect s over the next 3 years,  to see
every child grow up in a warm, dry home; the number of affordable homes built
increased; every New Zealander have access to affordable health care; wages for all
rising faster than the cost of living; jobs created and unemployment back under 4
percent; exports increased as a percentage of GDP; the economy diversified towards
value-added goods and services; economic and social inequality reduced; targets to
measure and reduce child poverty; a cross-party approach to addressing domestic and
sexual violence; real measures to target climate change and improve our sustainability;
a plan for the recovery of Canterbury; and the Government to be guided in their work
by the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi; because without these commitments and
goals New Zealand will not grow or move forward to the future New Zealanders
deserve.”
Mr Speaker, can I begin by congratulating you on your re-election as Speaker. It
seems to me that you took on the role somewhat reluctantly initially, but you have
grown to enjoy the job, and perhaps it is the liberation from the interminable National
Party caucus meetings that has seen a spring in your step—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I could not possibly comment.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —and a twinkle in your eye. But the Opposition over the
next 3 years has one expectation from you: relentless fairness. As Victor Hugo wrote:
“Being good is easy, what is difficult is being just.” We want both— good and just. I
will be on hand to offer you unsolicited advice, whether you need it or not, and I am
sure I will receive your standard response. Congratulations to Chester Borrows, Deputy
42 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Speaker, and to his two assistants, Lindsay Tisch and Trevor Mallard. Trevor, I have no
doubt you will be just, but the challenge is to be good.
Congratulations to all the newly elected members of Parliament. It is a terrific
honour to represent New Zealanders in this House and a great responsibility as well.
And welcome back to all the returning members of Parliament from all sides of the
House. It was a long, hard-fought campaign, but the reward is the privilege of serving
our country as its elected representatives.
I would like to particularly recognise the new and returning Māori members of
Parliament. The silver lining for the Labour election was the return of six of the seven
Māori seats to Labour. There has been a significant vote of trust in Labour by
Māoridom, and we will ensure that that trust is not misplaced by doing all we can to
advance its aspirations. This is a good opportunity to acknowledge the National Party’s
change of heart on the retention of the Māori seats. In the end National usually comes
round to Labour’s policies. Nuclear -free New Zealand, Working for Families, interest-
free student loans, KiwiSaver, the Cullen fund—I could go on.
I would also like to congratulate the members of Parliament elected in Canterbury.
There is a lot of work ahead for you and for the people of the region, and I wish you the
very best for your endeavours on their behalf. Be assured of Labour’s support over the
years ahead.
Finally, congratulatio ns to the Prime Minister on your party’s fine victory at the
election. Securing a third term is not an easy feat but you have achieved it. Of course,
with it comes huge responsibility. In your seventh year in Government no longer when
things go wrong can i t be blamed on Helen Clark’s Government or even on poor old
Mickey Joseph Savage. It is time for the Government to step up, it is time to own its
decisions, and it is time to take responsibility.
The result of the election from a Labour perspective was not what we had hoped for.
Voters on board have given us a message, and the measure of our party will be how we
pick ourselves up, take the advice of New Zealanders, and return to represent them in a
manner that reflects their aspiration and needs.
We are pleased that we have won a seat on the United Nations Security Council. It is
a significant result and builds on the great reputation we have in international relations.
It reflects a decade of hard work started by Helen Clark and Phil Goff and concluded by
John Key and Murray McCully. International relations have always been an area of
policy that Labour strongly believes in. When the United Nations was first formed the
then New Zealand Labour Prime Minister, Peter Fraser, said in San Francisco in 1945
that members of the organisation should undertake “to preserve, protect and promote
human rights and fundamental freedoms, and in particular the rights of freedom from
want, freedom from fear, freedom of speech”, and I commend those words to this
Government because they are just as relevant today as they were in 1945. It is
significant to secure a seat on the Security Council, but at the end of the day that was
about numbers. Now it is about how we use that position, and we must stand firmly on
the commitment we gave when seeking that privilege, and that is to be the voice of
small nations.
Like many New Zealanders, we are concerned at the haste in which we are being led
into conflict where we do not know what our involvement will be, what the outcome
will be, and what the exit strategy is. Like many New Zealanders, we do not feel that the
case has yet been made to us to be involved in the conflict with the Islamic State of Iraq
and Syria (ISIS) . The Prime Minister’s response to serious questions from the public,
from the media, and from the Opposition is too casual, it is too evasive, and it feels like
we are being fitted out for a decision that is already made. Any decision must be
considered and debated thoroughly, not rushed through glibly in a climate of claims
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 43
about domestic beheadings or security titbits dropped by the Prime Minister at media
stand-ups. It is reprehensible to use fear as a weapon to persuade the public. It can lead
to seeds of doubt in the trust that is placed in the Prime Minister, unless that trust is
backed up. And trust is lacking at this point, and it is self-inflicted by the Prime
Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: His comment, Mr Brownlee, on the meeting in Washington
last week that it was just a regular, routine meeting was demonstrably untrue. It was at
odds with international reports. It was at odds with defence personnel. It was at odds
even with President Obama. In fact, the meeting has been described as a gathering of
coalition members to plan a strategy against ISIS in Iraq. And some of us do remember
the gung-ho approach of John Key in 2003 and his insistence that we send troops to
Iraq. That was something the Labour Government refused to do without a UN mandate,
which never came. The Prime Minister keeps hinting of action, including troops on the
ground, which is something he said before the election would not happen.
He has also stated that a decision on New Zealand’s involvement is weeks away. If a
decision is weeks away, Prime Minister, it gives us plenty of time for that decision to be
made by this Parliament and not by the executive. This House must be provided with
the same briefings that Cabinet receives. Any decision that involves New Zealanders
and puts them or this country in harm’s way must be done in an open and transparent
way, and Labour is determined to take the debate to the Government on this and all
other fronts. We have to do that because we believe that this Government has already
shown that it needs to be held to account.
Since being re-elected, John Key has made some big promises, and he made them
again today. He said that he will tackle child poverty, that he will address the housing
crisis, and that he will improve wages, create more jobs, and create more health services
and access to education. These are all laudable goals, they are admirable sentiments, and
they need to be backed up by a real plan of action.
Let us take housing. For almost 6 years the National Government ignored the
growing housing crisis —particularly in Auckland and somewhat in Christchurch —
denigrating those who raised the issue in this House and outside. A year out from the
election the Government’s polling told it  that housing was a real issue for New
Zealanders, and a series of sticking plaster solutions were slapped in place. To date the
result, Dr Smith, has been five new houses built in Auckland in the so-called Auckland
Housing Accord zones. We have heard plenty from the Government on addressing this
issue—plenty of talk and no action. And splitting responsibility for housing between
three portfolios and three Ministers is not doing something; it is spreading the blame for
doing nothing. It is a housing policy by committee.
The Kiwi dream of homeownership is fast disappearing under this Government. And
while the crisis creeps further and further into the housing market, driving up rents and
mortgages, what does this Government decide to do? It decides to sell off billions of
dollars of State houses with no guarantee that the resources will go back into social
housing. In many cases they will end up simply as expensive private rentals or be sold
to agencies that will struggle to meet the cost of managing them. The Salvation Army is
held up as an example of such an agency but it has already said that it is not ready to
take on a large number of State houses, so Bill English changed tack. He said they will
sell houses to anybody, not just to social agencies. They can sell them to banks, they can
sell them to investors, they can sell them to speculators. He said: “We can sell to
anybody.” That is the mantra of this Government. It is a recipe for doing more harm to
those who are at the bottom of the housing market. I have to tell the Government that its
latest announcement on housing to privatise tens of thousands of State homes has no
44 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
mandate. The Government members have no mandate. They never campaigned on it.
They never gave a hint they were going to do this.
But some things, like the well-being of our kids and the ability to afford a roof over
their heads, are not “nice -to-haves”; they are part of a decent and a compassionate
society. We will reach across this House and back policies that actually deal with these
issues properly, because it is time for real solutions. At the next election New
Zealanders will judge this Government on the result of these policies.
The hallmark of this Government’s response has been to shift the blame on everyone
else, the doozy of them all being Bill English claiming that local housing planning laws
are responsible for poverty. With a claim as stupid as this it is hard to take the Prime
Minister seriously when he says he wishes to address child poverty —something that he
and his Government denied existed for the last 6 years. Call it anything else; just do not
call it child poverty. But he knows that New Zealanders care about child poverty. In
July MMResearch found 80 percent of people agreed child poverty is a problem in New
Zealand and just 19 percent thought the Government was doing enough to address it.
None the less, I am an optimist on the well-being of our most vulnerable children —I
just have to be —so I am going to offer the Prime Minister some advice and I hope that
he takes it. If he is really serious about tackling child poverty, if he really believes that
making sure all of our children have the food they need to grow and learn, if he really
understands that it is not acceptable for families trying to raise three children on $5 a
week after their rent, if he truly wants to make sure that every single child growing up
in New Zealand has a chance to succeed like chances that he himself had —if he really
believes all that, he will walk the walk and he will talk the talk. He will take his
aspirational statements and he will commit them to a firm target and a firm measure,
and that means making reducing child poverty a public service target. Right now there
are 10 such targets. They are admirable targets like increasing participation in early
childhood education, increasing immunisation, and so on, but there is no target for
reducing child poverty. That needs to change because that is what a Government that
actually cares about our kids would do. It would set targets and it would take
responsibility for meeting them. Make no mistake: child poverty is a shame on thi s
Government and on this nation and Labour will hold John Key’s Government to
account for it.
We will vigorously oppose policies that make things worse for New Zealanders. We
will oppose the removal of New Zealanders’ rights at work. This legislation is a tragedy
for every single worker who is treated unjustly and who has no legal recourse. It is a
pathway to making employment even more precarious for thousands of men and
women, especially our young people in our communities. It is a tragedy for the tens of
thousands who will find their incomes dropping further and further behind the cost of
living and society becoming less and less fair.
New Zealanders have been told that wage increases need to come from productivity
gains. I have heard Mr Joyce say this many times. I have got a question for him today
that I would like him to answer: how do we get more productivity out of 45,000 home-
care workers who earn close to the minimum wage? Do they hang out only half the
washing of the old people when they call in? Do they clean only the toilet bowl and not
the seat when they go to clean their houses? How do you get more productivity out of
them? Why does the Government not face the fact that pay increases are needed now for
people carrying out work that most of us would not want to do?
We will oppose the weakening of environmental protections in New Zealand. Last
term we offered to come to an agreement on the more benign parts of the proposed
Resource Management Act changes, but the Government made it clear that it wants
wholesale change. We will not support wholesale change. The Resource Management
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 45
Act is the way in which New Zealanders have a say in what happens where they live,
how their environment is treated—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What about some houses?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —and what the future of their communities will look like,
Dr Smith. I am told that the Prime Minister has instructed his Ministers to put a green
tinge over their portfolios. I have to say that that has to be seen as a cynical political
ploy rather than a genuine commitment to our environment.
“Undemocratic” is a word that I think we are going to hear a lot about over the next 3
years. Certainly we will hear that word as the Government continues to pervert the use
of the Official Information Act. I have to say that I was astounded to hear the Prime
Minister admit just last week to gaming the system. I was not astounded that it
happened—you have only to look at how many complaints are now being made to the
Ombudsman—but by how many are as a result of Ministers and departments not
complying with the law. I am astounded that Mr Key —the Houdini when it comes to
avoiding taking blame —should admit to it. Compare that with his claim when he first
came into Government. Maybe he has forgotten it, so I will remind him. He said: “My
style is to be open and transparent and take people with me.” I have to say that open and
transparent is not how I would describe his Government’s response to Official
Information Act requests.
A good example was a report on child poverty, Prime Minister. Did the Prime
Minister know that that report was held back for 17 months —17 months? It took
multiple complaints to the Ombudsman, and it got released —finally got released—after
the election. It was withheld not because there were top secrets in it but because it was
politically embarrassing. When the Chief Ombudsman herself says that she is very
concerned then this abuse of the Official Information Act has to stop and this House has
to censure such behaviour.
I think we will hear the word “undemocratic” again and again as more dirty politics
are unravelled over the coming months and the attacks of institutions and individuals
who act in the public good are revealed.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Oh, stop talking about your leadership campaign.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I look forward, Gerry, to seeing what comes out in the dirty
washing. I am sure there are going to be some rather large items there. I think political
motives are going to be laid bare. The worst of it is not about politicians being
attacked—after all, we are a pretty tough breed in here —but, as Rod Oram noted in the
Sunday Star-Times recently—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I hear the old grunter up the back there, Maurice
Williamson, laughing at the name of Rod Oram. Can I say that he said something that
so many New Zealanders believe, and maybe —just maybe —if you listen, you might
actually agree.

items.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
items.text: Who cares what he said?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Well, I believe it, and I care. He said that many people —
scientists, academics, health professionals, concerned citizens —have been smeared and
abused by people working on behalf of the National Party. That is reprehensible. It is
reprehensible, and some of it has come out of Ministers’ offices and, unbelievably,
some of it even out o f the Prime Minister’s own office. As Rod Oram says, they are
destroying some good people and good society. They are harming our good name as
New Zealanders and our reputation and undermining our values and our principles.
In this term of Parliament the c onsequences of this Government’s past actions will
come home to roost, and that includes the young Minister now sitting in the front row,
Simon Bridges. Some of his decisions will come home to roost, particularly the
46 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
decisions about the much-heralded economic boom, because that economic boom is
turning into an endless stream of bad news about dairy prices and manufacturing lay-
offs. You know, the National Party members always laugh when we talk about
manufacturing lay-offs and job losses. You see, they do not believe it.
I have to say that the years of health cuts are starting to show through. When you
have senior doctors and senior members of the medical community upping and leaving
because there is not enough money in health, you have got a problem. I have to say to
the new Minister of Health —and congratulations, new Minister —you have got to
smarten up your attire. It is really not up to scratch. You need some brighter ties and so
on. But can I say to the new Minister of Health that I want an assurance from him that
this country is ready for Ebola. I want this Minister to assure New Zealanders that we
are ready for Ebola. We have made huge cuts in public health funding, Minister. You
will find that is correct. We have made cuts in hospital funding. As the Minister will
know better than most, disease does not honour country borders, and just saying that we
can hide behind the fact that Africa is many miles away will not protect New
Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: Ring up. I’ll give you a briefing on it.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Minister, do not interject —take a call and assure New
Zealanders of the readiness to deal with this potentially deadly disease. It is not a
laughing issue. I was the Minister of Health who had to deal with bird flu and with
severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars), and I know we have a ministry that is capable
of putting together extremely good processes. So I am saying, Minister, that you should
inform this country of exactly what is in place. The Prime Minister said this week:
“Ebola is hard to contract. You have to get it.” Well, I am not sure exactly what that
means. But I have to say that it is an issue that is going to face the world. As the
Secretary-General of the World Health Organization has said, it is a problem across the
world, not just in Africa.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Open up nominations again.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Well, now I will get on to you, Hekia —do not worry. We
are told that the expansion of charter schools is about to proceed at a pace. National has
given a party that got fewer than 17,000 votes the role of driving through its charter
school programme. This programme is costing five times as much per student as public
schooling, and it is not delivering to our children. So here is the challenge, Minister:
fund every other school child to that level. Instead of cutting funding in real terms, see
how our fine public education system will run when it gets equal treatment. So,
Minister, that is the challenge to you. That is what we want to see over the next 3 years.
I have said that this Government will have to account for its actions. It has got a
mandate from the public to carry out some of its policies —as we know, some of them
they did not know about—but it will be held accountable for its actions. We will lead an
Opposition that will not allow this Government to slide out from under the problems
that it creates, we will hold the Government accountable, and we will fight for the right
of New Zealanders to have a fair go. We ran our election campaign on three themes: on
work, on home, and on family.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How did it go?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Well, of course, that is very interesting, because we have
just heard from the Government that it sneers and scoffs at issues of work, home, and
family. Are we surprised? Are we surprised? We will now review our policies. That is
the only sensible thing to do. But I can assure this House that we will not lose sight of
our values or our vision, because that is why we are Labour. This country needs a strong
Opposition, and we are determined to rebuild this party and to provide opposition to this
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 47
Government. I am sure, as Bill English sits there today with his head buried in his
hands, that he will recall so well 2002. In 2002—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: And you’re doing it all wrong.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —the National Party got 20 percent of the vote. And look
where Bill English is now—he has got the limo, he has got the big salary, he has got the
allowance for the house—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Jealous.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: No, not at all —I have had it before. What I am saying is
that this party on this side of the House can look across at the 2002 election result and
say that ours is 25 percent and we can build on that because that is a good base for this
party to build on. We remain committed to working alongside all New Zealanders to
ensure that everyone who wants a job can have one and that work is secure, safe, and
pays fairly, and we will continue to champion the living wage, which this Government
scorns. We will take seriously the concerns of New Zealanders and be ready to lead an
alternative Government in 2017. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Annette King deserves some
congratulations, because I tell you what —that speech lasted longer than the average
tenure of a Labour leader these days. “No fish” was my favourite part of the speech.
Can I take this moment to congratulate all members of the House on their election and,
in some cases, re-election. For those who are here for the first time, can I wish them the
best for the next 3 years. I hope that they enjoy it. I hope they enjoy the excitement of
making a difference. Can I offer them the same advice that I offer members of my own
caucus who are new: avoid making the mistake of walking over broken glass to come to
this Parliament, moaning and complaining the whole time you are here, and then, when
you leave, doing everything you can to come back. Enjoy your time, make a difference,
and make sure you look after your families.
It is my pleasure to lead the Government of the 51 st Parliament. It has, I have got to
say, a certain déjà vu about it. We seem to be returning where we left off, although the
composition of the National caucus is slightly different, and it is slightly larger. But
once again it is full of unity, passion, determination, and a commitment to continue to
work for New Zealand. We return to the 51 st Parliament with very much the same
partners we had in the 49 th and the 50 th Parliaments. One partner is the ACT Party, and
we thank it and David Seymour for the relationship I am sure we will have together.
One is United Future and Peter Dunne, and we thank Mr Dunne for the strong working
relationship. We look forward to that in the years ahead. We wish the Māori Party and
its newly elected leader Te Ururoa Flavell the very best. Together we will work hard to
provide a strong and stable Government. Together we will work hard to deliver even
better results when it comes to economic growth in terms of lifting more children out of
poverty and ensuring that more families move into work, in terms of continuing to
improve the quality of our critical services of health and education, and in terms of
continuing to see the crime rate fall. That is the National caucus and the members who
support it.
That is not the sorry state of the Labour Party. Labour members started the election
with a leader whom —let us be blunt —none of them liked, and they ended the election
with a leader whom none of them can name, and that is because they do not have one.
They do have wannabe leaders. Yep, there is some risk, actually, that they will have
more wannabe leaders than people who actually voted for them in 2014. It is, I have got
to say, and, has been over the last 3 weeks or so, the gift that keeps on giving. It is a sort
of soap opera playing out on TV every night —a cross between The Blacklist and House
of Cards set in Wellington.
48 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Of those wannabe leaders, first out of the blocks, of course, was Grant Robertson,
freshly minted, may I say, in the pages of Woman’s Weekly with his loyal —a word not
often used in the Labour Party —deputy leader, Jacinda Ardern. The next contestant, of
course, is Andrew Little, a man who singlehandedly managed to turn the marginal seat
of New Plymouth into a National stronghold that is now brilliantly represented by
Jonathan Young. Then, of course, there is David Parker, who apparently has worked out
in some sort of epiphany that no one likes Labour’s policies. Well, hello! I could have
told Labour that 6 years ago. But he has come up with a brilliant idea. He is going to
copy Colin Craig. I kid you not. He is going to have a referendum. It will go like this:
do you want to pay more taxes? I do not think so. Do you want pay more for your
electricity? I do not think so. Do you want to lose your job? I do not think so. Do you
want to lose your inheritance? I definitely do not think so. Or do you want all of the
above? And the final contestant they have, of course, is Nanaia Mahuta. Let us be blunt:
the affiliates will not vote for her, the party will not vote for her, and the caucus will not
vote for her.
So, sadly, the batch of wannabe leaders is not the future leader of the Labour Party,
and we know that. It is the next batch because —do not fret —there is another batch
sitting behind them. There is David Shearer, who was white-anted by David Cunliffe —
OK. There was Phil Goff, who was also white-anted by David Cunliffe. There was
David Cunliffe, who was white-anted by everyone other than David Cunliffe. But my
favourite, the dark horse of all of them —and let us be honest, it is spoken of quietly in
circles around the Labour Party —is Stuart Nash. It is Stuart Nash, and you will know
when the leadership bid is on —I thought it was actually on for David Clark yesterday
with that jacket, very nice —for Stuart Nash when you go on to TradeMe and you see
one thing, and that is when he stops riding around in his fire engine and replaces it with
an ambulance, which he knows he needs to take to the Labour Party caucus because it is
a train wreck going on over there.
This is a Government that is very, very firmly focused on the issues that matter to
New Zealanders. That is why this Government was re-elected for a third time. It was a
Government that brought to the people of New Zealand credible, sound policies that are
working and delivering for the people of New Zealand. The policies start with the
economy. This is a Government that will return the books to surplus and this is a
Government that will continue to work hard to meet the Crown objective of getting debt
down to 20 percent of GDP by 2020. This is a Government that will ensure that we
spend taxpayers’ money wisely, because we know how hard they work for those
taxpayer dollars. This is a Government that in 2015 and 2016 will reduce ACC levies
for New Zealanders so that they can have their money returned to them.
This is an economy that is growing strongly at 3.9 percent to June and has created
83,000 jobs in the last 12 months. It is an economy where wages are rising faster than
inflation, an economy that is the envy of so many countries around the world, and one
that is underpinned by good, solid economic policy. It has a Business Growth Agenda
with 350-odd initiatives, which are transforming our economy into a modern, outward-
facing, competitive economy that is not only competing but succeeding on the world
stage. Part of that integration with the world comes with our free-trade agreements, and
this is a Government that is working hard to finalise a free-trade agreement with Korea
and one that will work hard to see a conclusion to the Trans-Pacific Partnership. It is
also a Government that will work hard to get the Gulf States agreement over the line. As
part of working hard with New Zealand businesses we will continue to expand the
activities of New Zealand Trade and Enterprise so that our companies —large and
small—can have access to the international markets and the huge consumer base that is
supporting them.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 49
If you want to have an economy that delivers results and opportunities for all New
Zealanders, you need flexibility in the labour markets. This is a Government that will
pass the employment relations legislation to increase flexibility and fairness in the
labour market, and it is long overdue.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: It’ll drive down the wages.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, that is exactly right. Andrew Little is the man who
wants to lead the Labour Party and who wants to rob young New Zealanders of
opportunities by taking away the 90-day probation period, by having national awards,
by jacking up the minimum wage to a rate that is unaffordable —it is a step backward
not forward for the young people of New Zealand. We will continue, as a Government,
to work hard in the areas of health and safety and the environment, and we will make
sure that parents have more time to spend with their youngsters by extending paid
parental leave from 14 weeks to 18 weeks and by increasing the parental tax credit for
families that do not get paid parental leave.
Across the country we see businesses doing better. We see businesses strongly
investing, and we will continue to fund more in the way of science and innovation, and
research and development grants. We will be establishing a food and safety science and
research centre as well as four additional centres of research excellence. One of the
saddest things that I had to confront on the election campaign was the rhetoric from
David Cunliffe trying to tell New Zealanders that this was a country that only sold milk
powder and logs. It was a complete disservice to those companies right across New
Zealand that are innovating in so many different facets, are proud to be New Zealanders,
and are taking their great businesses to the world, and we will continue to grow more of
them.
Speaking of taking New Zealand to the world, what we are going to take to the
world, or at least to Australia, is job fairs in Sydney, in Melbourne, and in Brisbane just
in case there are a few New Zealanders who deserted ship under the previous Labour
Government and have not recognised how strong New Zealand is under a National-led
Government and want to come back. I say to them with open arms: “Come home. Come
home to New Zealand. Come home to New Zealand.” There is a shortage of skills in so
many areas and we would like to have those New Zealanders return.
I am the Minister of Tourism and I am proud to see tourism continuing to grow here
in New Zealand. There were 2.8 million international visitors who came to our shores
for the year ending 2014 —an increase of 4.9 percent. We are seeing an increase in a
range of different areas from business to high end to those who come for sporting
interests and those who come for cultural experiences. We are seeing a significant
increase—30-odd percent—year on year from China. By the end of the third term of
this National-led Government, I am pretty confident that we will see those international
business tourists going off to the Skycity convention centre, paid for not by the
taxpayer, creating thousands of jobs and millions of opportunities for New Zealanders.
And just like the Christchurch Convention Centre, that will also be a piece of
infrastructure that is taking place.
This is a Government that one day will be remembered for building infrastructure in
so many different forms, and one of them is certainly roading. Unlike so many political
parties that do not seem to understand that you need to move both cars and public
transport on roads, we do. This will be a Government, under the leadership of Simon
Bridges as the Minister of Transport, that will continue to see important roads built in
this country, including the Pūhoi to Wellsford road. We will start to see the construction
on Pūhoi to Warkworth. I did not see a single Labour member during the election
campaign get up and say that they were going to be the ones to stop Transmission
Gully. They did not want to say that.
50 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: They were silent.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: They were silent like little lamb chops on that particular issue,
but do not worry. The people of Wellington and the Hutt understood that and they voted
National, and yes, Transmission Gully will be beginning, as will be the completion of
MacKays to Peka Peka. The Waikato Expressway —we will see a completion of the
Cambridge bypass and we will start to see the construction on the Huntly and Hamilton
bypass. When I first kicked off in 2008 the ambitious plans we had for the Waikato
Expressway, I could only dream that I would be there when it finished, but the way
things are going, I may well be, and it may well be extended all the way through to
Whangarei and maybe even Cape Reinga. I do not really know, but it will be four lanes
each way, I am absolutely sure, by that point. And, of course there are those regional
roading projects that I announced. So many of them will be happening. There is $100
million for urban cycleways. We will be working hard with the transport authority to
make sure there is more money spent on urban cycleways and we are doing well there.
Connectivity is important to a small and growing economy, whether you are bringing
educational services, health services, or business to the world. I am proud to be leading
a Government that had the courage to stand up and roll out ultra-fast broadband. I was
proud to be the leader of the National Party as we campaigned across the country to
extend ultra-fast broadband to 80 percent of New Zealanders and to extend the rural
broadband initiative. That extension of ultra-fast broadband will see towns like Te Puke,
Motueka, Morrinsville, Kaitāia, Ōtaki, Dannevirke, Alexandra, Stratford, Carterton,
Westport, Te Kūiti, and Wairoa all getting ultra-fast broadband. We will see more
money spent on black spots for phones.
When it comes to the environment, this Government has a good record, but, yes, we
will be introducing legislation to amend the Resource Management Act. I just heard, I
think, Annette King, the “Acting Acting Leader of the Labour Party”, saying that—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yes, but it’s the “Acting Acting Deputy Deputy Leader”.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, the “Acting Acting Deputy Leader”, I am sorry—I stand
corrected. The “Acting Acting Deputy Leader” of the Labour Party said in her extended
tenure address that she would stand opposed to reform of the Resource Management
Act. That is the reason why house prices doubled under Labour. So Labour members
can scream from their lungs when they go out there, as they did during the campaign
trail, but not a single New Zealander watching TV really believed that they were going
to produce 100,000 homes built by the Government on mythical bits of land for
unbelievable amounts of money. No one believed it. If you want houses to be built
faster, as we all do, reform of the Resource Management Act is critically important. We
need to balance our environmental responsibilities with our economic opportunities.
This is a Government with a good record when it comes to the environment. There is
$350 million committed to cleaning up iconic waterways. We have seen 23,000
kilometres of waterways fenced to exclude stock so far, and we will see all of that
completed by 2017. Again, on the campaign trail, I was proud to announce the $100
million that we are going to invest to buy and retire areas of selected farmland next to
important waterways. My particular favourite, actually, in this area came one Sunday
afternoon when I had the privilege of going down to the harbour in Auckland t o
announce that we would be establishing recreational fishing parks in the Hauraki Gulf. I
heard Winston Peters cheering all the way from Herne Bay when I announced that. He
is a man who loves to catch a snapper. He loves to catch a snapper. He said to himself:
“That John Key, I tell you— I don’t agree with everything, but Johnny boy’s on to it
there. I’m going to catch a few snapper.” In fairness, he did not know he was going to
have quite so much time on his hands between 2014 and 2017 to catch his snapper, but
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 51
he will, and if he wants to go down south, he can go to the Marlborough Sounds
because there will be a recreational fishing park there as well.
When it comes to health, this is a Government spending more money on health than
ever in the history of this country. But it is not just about spending money; it is about
getting a good result, and we have got great results. Again, one of the things we
announced on the campaign trail was what we are doing for New Zealanders who are
diagnosed with cancer. I think there is not a New Zealand family that has not been
touched by someone who has passed away from cancer. At the moment the average
time from the doctor’s diagnosis to the first treatment is 62 days. Under this
Government, we are going to work hard to make sure that 90 percent of patients receive
their first cancer treatment within 62 days. That is something that New Zealand families
will welcome. We are going to extend free GP visits and prescriptions for children
under the age of 13. We are also going to continue to expand the number of elective
surgical operations that are undertaken. The last point I would make is that we are going
to continue to increase funding for hospices by $20 million a year.
We hear a lot of nonsense spoken in this House by Opposition parties. One of the
things that I am sure we will hear a lot of over the course of the next few months is
when they stand up and say that they do not support professional development of our
teachers. They will not say for one moment that a good teacher should actually get paid
more to stay in the classroom than to go through the only career path they can, which is
to leave the classroom to get more money. They will not support more money going to
those principals who will leave high-performing schools and take their skills to low-
performing schools. If those members of Parliament believe that they want New
Zealand to be a true egalitarian society, then they have got to stop the nonsense of
stopping the current situation of great principals not transferring to those schools. We
have to deliver change in our education system and we will.
This is a Government that will stand up for those families who have a child with
special needs by funding up to 800,000 more teacher aide hours at $18 million a year.
There will be more funding to support deaf and hearing-impaired children. There will be
more money spent on Māori and Pacific trades training. There will be more money
spent on training our engineers. There will be more money spent on new schools and
classrooms right across our country, particularly in Christchurch and Auckland.
When it comes to welfare reform, I want to acknowledge the achievements of the
previous Minister for Social Development, the Hon Paula Bennett, and say that we have
now got to a situation where I think the settings in our welfare system are set in broadly
the right place. We are seeing tremendous results. Benefit numbers are falling. We now
have the lowest number of sole parents on a benefit in this country since 1988 —the
lowest number since 1988. We have 30,000 fewer children living in benefit-dependent
households compared with 2 years ago. One of the things that worked tremendously
over the last 3 years was when we extended the Youth Service approach to 16, 17, and
18-year-old mothers. We put in a wraparound service for those young mums. We made
sure there was someone to walk that journey with them. We made sure that they were
enrolled in education, that they had support for budgeting, and that they had advice
about parenting. There were incentive payments made to those young mums. Do you
know what happened as a result of that? We have seen a 40 percent reduction of young
mums who are now on that extended Youth Service approach —a 40 percent reduction.
This was the single approach that came out of that —a plea by those young mums for us
to extend that programme to 19-year-olds, and that is exactly what we are doing.
I remember when we got up and talked about the 3K to Christchurch —giving people
$3,000 to move to Christchurch if they came off a welfare benefit. That has been an
overwhelming success and it may well be something that we try to do in other parts.
52 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
When it comes to children who live in poverty, I say this: we are deadly serious about
continuing our work there, but the fastest way out of poverty is into work. Make no
mistakes—the fastest way out of poverty is into work. Yes, we will spend some time
defining the group that we are talking about, but that has been the problem of the
Labour Party of the past. Far too much time was spent on definitions; not enough time
was spent on actually doing something. This Government is going to get out there and
continue to work hard for those who are the most vulnerable and most at risk in our
community.
When it comes to housing, that is an issue that worries New Zealanders, and I accept
that issue, but that has been a very longstanding issue in our major cities for quite some
time, particularly in Auckland, but it is this Government that has had the courage to
actually stand up and have the special housing areas. There are eighty of those special
housing areas. There will be thousands and thousands and thousands of homes
established within those special housing areas. Young New Zealanders will get the
chance to get into those homes through the Homestart loans programme, where a couple
who put their money into their KiwiSaver account will be able to withdraw their
employer co ntribution, their own contribution, and the Government’s contribution.
They will have up to $50,000-odd as a deposit, which will be wrapped around a
Welcome Home Loan. It will present more than enough for them to buy a house in
many locations around the country, including Auckland, I believe. We will see builders
starting to build for that demand that is there.
We will be looking to extend the social housing area and there will be some changes
in the mix of ownership between Housing New Zealand homes and social housing that
is provided by other providers like Presbyterian Support and others. That is a very
credible policy that is working extremely well in a place like Australia. I say this to
those who will oppose it —like those in the Labour Party, because we have already
heard it in the “Deputy Deputy Leader’s” speech— what do those people want? Do they
actually want a house or do they want to know whether it is owned by Presbyterian
Support or the Government? It is pretty simple —they want a home. This will be a
Government that will be working hard through the work we have already done around
income-related rents to ensure that more at-risk families do get the opportunity to live in
a home. We will be working hard to make sure that interest rates remain low and that
we challenge all the areas of the building and construction sector. But one of those
important parts of ensuring the housing affordability is under control is to reform the
Resource Management Act and make sure we deliver those houses.
Law and order is an issue that matters to a great many New Zealanders, and with
very good reason. I am proud to lead a Government that has got a crime rate at a 35-
year low. That has been a lot of hard work from a huge number of Ministers, our
caucus, and those who work in the sector. Again, this has been a Government that has
recognised what those drivers of crime are, whether it has been drug or alcohol abuse.
This has been a Government that has made sure that those prisoners who go into a
corrections facility do get access to a drug and alcohol programme. This is a
Government that has turned three of our prisons into working prisons. Again, during the
campaign trail I had the opportunity to go out to the Wiri Prison to see that public-
private partnership in action and see the magnificent facilities they are building out
there—a huge big trade training facility is being built out there. We will make sure that
every prison is a working prison because we know that when a prisoner gets the drug
and alcohol treatment and when they get the skills, then there is a much lower chance
that they will be recidivist and go back to prison. We know that there is a great chance
that they will turn their lives around and make something of their lives by ensuring that
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 53
they stay in the workforce and not in prison. So that is going to be part of what we will
do around law and order.
When it comes to Māori development, I look to my left and see Mr Finlayson, who,
as I have said on numerous occasions, will go down as the greatest Minister for Treaty
of Waitangi Negotiations in the history of New Zealand. He has undertaken more
claims. He has signed 46 deeds of settlement. The Labour Government managed 25 in
its entire 9 years. If the Labour Government had still carried on at that rate, it would
have taken until 2060 to see those claims completed. The other great work that Chris
Finlayson is undertaking is in relation to the Ture Whenua Maori Act, where we will
see an opportunity to unlock some of that land that can be used for the development of
the iwi, for job development, and for the enrichment of the communities. Eighty percent
of the 1.5 million hectares is in that position. We will see more young Māori getting
opportunities. We are already seeing more achieving with National Certificate of
Educational Achievement (NCEA) level 2 and bachelor’s degrees and above. We will
see a continued commitment to Whānau Ora.
I just want to finish briefly, if I may, on a couple of issues. The first is in relation to
the United Nations Security Council and the obligations that New Zealand has in 2015-
16 to discharge its responsibilities wisely. We will be doing that. I congratulate, as I
already have, the team that made that possible. But the second big issue that is worthy
of some discussion is what is happening in Iraq and Syria at the moment in relation to
the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS). We can turn our eyes away from that situation
if we want to, but I tell New Zealanders with great honesty that we face international
risks, we face regional risks, and there is a very real risk that we may one day face a
domestic risk. We have to play our part in some form. We have not made a decision
what that part might be like. There is a very wide range. We will continue to engage
with the other political parties, including the Labour Party. We are more than happy to
share as much information as we practically can when we have it. There is a wide range
of options available to New Zealand. But I really believe that when the Opposition
parties have the benefit of understanding all of the information that the Government
understands, I will be absolutely amazed if they actually stand back and say that we are
going to leave all of that not just to our traditional friends like Australia, the United
States, the United Kingdom, and Canada but to so many other countries, whether they
be countries like the Netherlands or others like France or Germany. New Zealand has to
play its part, but it needs to think through that very wisely.
Finally, over the course of the next few years there will be an opportunity for the
New Zealand public to decide on whether they want to change the flag. I personally
believe that the flag should be a visual representation of modern New Zealand. I believe
that if New Zealanders choose wisely and decide to change their flag, it will be like
Canada the week after it changed its flag from what was a flag that used to look a lot
like the New Zealand flag, except it was red. Canada changed it to the maple leaf. I
think you will struggle to find a Canadian who seriously wants to go back to the old
flag. Young New Zealanders with pride —like all New Zealanders, actually —want to
have overt signs of patriotism for this great country. We do that when we put on a piece
of clothing that has a silver fern on it. I am pretty indifferent about the background that
that silver fern might have, but I do think New Zealanders should think wisely and
carefully about it. If that debate is not won over the next few years, then it will be a
good 50 years or so before it is decided again. This debate has been going around for 25
years. I want to achieve something that the Hon Gough Whitlam could not, and that is
to change our flag. I hope New Zealanders will support that view.
54 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
We are a National Government working very hard for New Zealand. There is a very
big agenda over the next 3 years, but we are a Government that is working for New
Zealand while we face an Opposition that is in disarray.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te
Whare. The other day I had a moment of genuine inspiration while watching The Paul
Henry Show , actually —I know, it was a unique moment. Paul and I get along, but I
have to say that the most inspiring thing about his show is usually the urge I get to turn
it off. At the time Paul was interviewing Dr Kirk Smith, an expert on climate change
from Berkeley. Waxing lyrical about his humungous salary, his gas-guzzling boat, and
his enormous carbon footprint, Paul posed a question: what could one man like him do
that would actually make a difference? Paul plaintively suggested: “I could sell my
massive boat, but no one else is going to, so what difference could it make?”. To this
the ever-patient scientist replied: “Well, Paul, you’ve got your own television show.
You are a leader. If you say that you drive an electric car, people will take notice, and,
who knows, they might even buy one too.” So yes, Paul, even a little guy on the telly
can do his bit to help save the world, because that is what leading is. That is what the
role of the Green Party is in this place. We will continue in the 51 st Parliament to lead—
to lead through our ideas, lead through our campaigns, and lead through our
commitment to addressing the big issues of our time.
An emboldened National will now be able to pass any laws it wants with the help of
the sole ACT marionette, to whom it gifted the seat of Epsom. Look, all of the puppet-
masters are here today in the Chamber. First on the Gov ernment’s hit list will be our
workers’ rights, followed by our world -leading environmental protection law, the
Resource Management Act, and further asset sales in the form of our State homes.
National has nothing but destruction on its mind.
For 6 years the Green Party has filled the National Government’s vision vacuum with
our ideas—with new thinking like school hubs, nurses in schools, the climate tax cut,
the urban cycleways, and the Green Investment Bank. In the process we have shifted the
debate and we have set a new political agenda. Just 2 years ago National denied child
poverty even existed, and now apparently it is on the top of the Prime Minister’s to -do
list—not that you could tell from his speech today. The Greens have been a key part of
a network that has relentlessly worked to expose New Zealand’s child poverty crisis and
that stirred the nation to care so much about child poverty that it has now become
politically untenable for National not to listen. That is victory, that is leading, and that is
what we do.
And yet there are those —even those who did not vote for us —who say that that is
not enough and who would like us to have more influence at the table. Since the
election I have received a number of letters, even from some National Party members,
pleading with us to form some other kind of arrangement with National because they
feel guilty about voting for a party with such a poor record on the environment. The
idea apparently is that the Greens could act as some kind of foil to National’s ant i-
environment agenda, if only we just focused on environmental issues. So let me respond
to that directly.
The Green Party is now established as the third-largest party in New Zealand and one
of the most successful Green parties in the world. We are part of an internationally
established movement that is on the ascendancy around the globe. Ours is a movement
based not just on environmental principles but on the principles of social justice and
democracy, and, of course, here in Aotearoa, that is enabled through Te Tiriti o
Waitangi. This is who we are. We could not stop caring about the environment or the
people—or our economic direction, for that matter —just because it might be politically
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 55
expedient to do so. It is not our job to move to the centre; it is our job to move the
centre.
We have often led the agenda and achieved practical change by working across
issues and across the political divides. We remain open to working with National on
select projects during this term of Parliament. In 2008 we drew up a successful
memorandum of understanding with National that saw 320,000 homes insulated across
our country. This was a massive success —a win for New Zealanders. We kept that
going as long as we could until National radically cut the programme. More
Government funding —over $400 million —was committed to the Green Party’s
memorandum of understanding with National than was provided to projects with its
coalition partners. That is leadership from Opposition.
Prior to the election we drew the line at propping up a conservative Government at
the expense of a progressive one, but in the event that National won, we always said
that we would work with it to create good, Green change. It is John Key, however, who
has indicated that he is not so keen to work with us. Since then, we have heard it said
that our social policies stand in the way of us working with National on the
environment. No. In reality, it is on environmental policy where we are the furthest
apart. National’s policies include its plans to gut our environ mental protection law, the
Resource Management Act, to remove the principle of sustainability from the Act, and
this will accelerate environmental destruction. We, the Greens, are about increasing
environmental protection.
Crucially, National has completely failed to grasp the challenge and the opportunities
presented by climate change. Such a failure could not be more evident than in the fact
that the most significant global environmental issue of our time and of our generation
went barely without a mention in the Speech from the Throne this morning, other than
some oblique reference to managing our emissions, but this is no surprise. Under
National’s management New Zealand’s net emissions have increased 20 percent and are
set to rise by another 50 percent in the next decade. New Zealanders have the fifth-
highest per-person emissions in the developed world. For a country that prides itself on
“100% Pure New Zealand”, that is 100 percent failure. National has rejected the Green
Party’s idea for a meaningful p rice on carbon and has instead chosen to stick with the
failed and discredited emissions trading scheme, which has driven up emissions and
accelerated deforestation.
If we were to believe the Minister for Climate Change Issues, Tim Groser, it is
because National Party voters apparently do not care. He told hundreds of New
Zealanders at a pre-election climate voter event that to many National Party supporters,
climate change is nothing more than a United Nations conspiracy —a non-issue. “Those
are the people we are carrying.”, he said. Well, I refuse to believe his generalisation
about New Zealanders. I think Groser wildly underestimates how important our
environment is to us all, and in doing so abdicates responsibility for actually doing
something about the single most important challenge facing humanity. I know that lots
of New Zealanders care about the environment. I know that a love for our rivers and our
mountains and a desire to protect our clean and pure brand is not the domain solely of
the Greens or those on the left. If anything, the clamour for the Greens to go blue should
be a wake-up call for National. People want real political action on climate change.
Here is the thing about the 21 st century, a century into which the National Party has
completely failed to transport itself: a shift to a smarter, cleaner economy is the single
biggest opportunity of our time. Being Green is not about doing the right thing
anymore; it is about doing the bright thing. It is about leadership. We will continue the
push for New Zealand to make the transition to a smarter, low-carbon economy. We
56 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
relish the opportunity to work across Parliament to make this happen. Like we have
done with child poverty and inequality, we will now move National on climate change.
For this reason, we have decided to elevate the climate change portfolio to my co-
leader, Russel Norman. This will mean that both Green co-leaders, Russel and myself,
will have responsibility and lead campaigns for change on the two key crises facing our
nation and our world: inequality and climate change. How we respond to these distinct
yet often intertwined challenges will define us as a nation and will define the shape of
our children’s lives. Russel w ill lead a team of MPs focused on setting the
environmental agenda and driving the bold, innovative, smart Green policy ideas that
can have New Zealand leading the world while playing our part in helping to save it.
Already these talented MPs have produced a comprehensive set of solutions that will
address the immediate climate and environmental challenges that we face. Gareth
Hughes will retain the energy portfolio and also take on innovation. Gareth is an ideas
factory, seeking out the exciting innovation s of New Zealand’s business and bringing
them to public attention, and driving an energy policy that will see New Zealand 100
percent renewable by 2030. Kennedy Graham will continue his global affairs work with
a particular focus on international climate negotiations. It is our view that New Zealand
can be a key player and a leader in achieving a global climate accord. Eugenie Sage will
continue in conservation and Steffan Browning in primary production. They will
continue to fight to protect our environment, our previous species, our fragile
ecosystems, and the primary industries that rely on them all and depend on the
environment from National’s 20 th century pollution economy that places it all at risk.
Julie Anne Genter will continue to make the case for smarter investment in transport
while also picking up the environment portfolio, leading the campaign against the
Government’s Resource Management Act reforms, which will cause so much
environmental and community damage. James Shaw, the Greens’ newest MP, will put
his many years of experience supporting New Zealand’s small and medium sized
businesses and leading on sustainable business to good effect in the economic
development portfolio, so that even where the Government drags its heels on a smart
Green future, New Zealand business will know that they have an ally and an advocate in
the Greens. Climate change and environmental protection must occupy an essential
