place at the top of the political agenda. It is not an optional luxury but essential to the
New Zealand way of life and our national identity. The Green Party will lead on the
environment.
Although we know that the climate change trajectory is frightening in its enormity,
we do have a very clear picture of inequality. We can see the damage here and now. We
can calculate its fall-out in the future. The Prime Minister’s address on this issue was
startling in its lack of compassion for the 265,000 children he is actually talking about.
We know, for example, how much poverty costs —around $8 billion a year. We know
how many kids will stay below the bread line if we maintain the same 30-year economic
plan that has left 265,000 kids in poverty —about a quarter of all New Zealand children.
We know what those poor kids look like. They are mostly Māori or Pasifik a and they
often come from single-parent homes. We know where they live. We can estimate how
many of them will get sick and how many babies will die of preventable illnesses.
Around one baby a week in this country dies from an illness that is related to poverty.
How many will drop out of education —we know that. How many will grow up poor
and go on to have babies who will repeat the cycle —we have got some idea of that as
well. As brutal and cruel as it sounds and as brutal and cruel as it is, New Zealanders
over the past 30 years have been slowly encouraged into accepting that sick, poor,
hungry, and undereducated kids simply go with the territory. They are the price of the
rock-star economy. Child poverty rates are double what they were 30 years ago, and yet
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 57
National claims as a success the fact that it has maintained that 30-year high. Success to
me is a radical reduction in child poverty.
We have at least had in the speech this morning recognition of the importance of
child poverty if not its urgency, but there was, however, absolutely no mention of the
fact that poverty is largely a question of inadequate income. The question for National
remains: does it care enough about these children —the children in poverty —to change
the economic drivers that have perpetuated that poverty? The Green Party says it is
unacceptable to have kids who are hungry because their parents have to survive on a
benefit. National’s excuse that it needs to maintain a gap between work and benefits
does not pan out when 40 percent of the kids in poverty live in working homes. Their
parents—beneficiaries and workers—need to be paid more. That is blindingly obvious,
and yet this Government is pathologically allergic to taking the action that it can to fix
this problem.
Over the next 3 years I will make it my business to generate an even bigger appetite
for change in New Zealand in order to end child poverty, and I am joined by an
incredible team of Green MPs who believe the same. Call us “Team Kids”, if you will.
Kevin Hague, while holding the health portfolio, will also now take on the crucial
housing portfolio. The Greens have made incredible progress in improving New
Zealand’s housing stock through the home insulation programme, working with
National to insulate more than 300,000 homes and significantly improving the health of
the children and families who live in those houses. But that is not enough. We need
more affordable housing and improved quality. National offers none of that; the Greens
do. Catherine Delahunty will continue in educ ation, promoting our school hubs’ unique
plan to alleviate poverty and build stronger communities in schools. School is so much
more than just achievement in the three Rs. Imagine if schools were great places not just
for kids to learn but where parents could upskill as well, and the whole place is run on
solar power, like so many schools already do. These are the connected solutions in
education that the Greens will lead on. Jan Logie will take on the whole of the social
development portfolio and employment, and Denise Roche will tackle industrial
relations and immigration. Between them, they will lead the charge to raise incomes for
the families who call New Zealand home —beneficiaries and workers alike —incomes
that National now directly threatens with the reforms in industrial relations and welfare.
Mojo Mathers will continue her incredible advocacy for those hundreds of thousands of
New Zealanders with disabilities, and will protect the rights of all New Zealanders to
decent, affordable food through the food portfolio. Dave Clendon will continue to build
a safer community by improving our criminal justice system and reducing offending,
and will stand up for civil rights within the criminal justice system, including the rights
of the children and families of prisoners.
For a little country, New Zealand has a proud history of leading on the solutions. We
were once the global leaders in women’s rights. We gave women the vote 52 years
before France, which is celebrating its 69 th anniversary of suffrage today, incidentally.
We stood up to the mighty US in the 1980s and said no to nuclear power. Other nations
noticed, in part because of how small we were and how brave we were to take that
stand. We are the little country that can.
So there is all the more reason to think twice before leaping in when the US says:
“Let us go to war.” John Key says it is odd not to follow the US into military conflict
against Sunni militants in Iraq and Syria. What we say is what is odder for our brave
little nation than to follow the US into yet another military incursion when all the
evidence points to it being the wrong move. The overwhelming outcome of half a
century of US military intervention in the Middle East is that life is worse for the people
in that region and for those of us in the rest of the world. There is no doubt that the
58 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Islamic State threat is a very real one, but there is too much doubt that the way to
respond is by committing New Zealand to war. Military incursions so far have
radicalised many of the most radical groups. The endless bombing of the Middle East
will not solve the problems there.
The Green Party does not have all the answers on this issue —none of us in this
House do—but we do think that New Zealand should examine its non-military options.
We are prepared to be the lone voice in this Parliament against the notion of involving
our country in another war. New Zealand should and could take a more constructive
approach. There is an urgent need for humanitarian assistance in the region. We have
the skills and the experience as a nation to respond to that. There is far more good to be
done by providing shelter to those displaced by conflict than by going to war. War is by
nature self-destructive.
So are the economic strategies that perpetuate climate inaction and inequality. New
Zealand can and must lead with smart, modern responses to all these challenges, and the
world will notice. By meeting the challenge of climate change and inequality, we can
transform our economy and our society for the better, and in doing so lead the world,
because New Zealand is uniquely placed to seize the opportunities arising from the
global shift to clean energy. We have the best cards in the pack —the natural resources,
the people, the intellect, and the know-how. We just need the leadership. Our
competitive edge is not cheap labour, more cows, and dirty oil; it is environmental
stewardship, a fair and tolerant society, and smarter, cleaner economics.
Over the next 3 years the Greens will honour the one in 10 New Zealanders who
gave us our seats in this House. Last Parliament we led the Opposition, and we return
with the same number of MPs to set the political agenda again. We will hold the
Government to account and be a voice in this place for those who are too little or
disenfranchised to have a voice of their own. I note with some dismay that I am the only
woman political party leader in this House. I am proud though to be helping to lead the
most diverse and the most representative of parties in Parliament, because, like New
Zealand, the Green Party caucus is half women and a quarter Māori. We are a collection
of passionate people who have spent our lives fighting the good fight, leading in pursuit
of not money or prestige but the values that we stand here to represent —a fairer,
cleaner, smarter New Zealand playing its responsible role in the world.
I genuinely wish my colleagues across the House well, especially those new entrants
who arrived after the last election. My enduring hope is that we can reach across our
political barriers and make real progress for our people and our country over the next 3
years, and that in doing that this nation of journeyers and pioneers will lead the world
yet again. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Could I, first of all,
congratulate David Carter on resuming his office as Speaker of this House, also the new
Deputy Speaker, the returning Assistant Speaker, and the new Assistant Speaker in the
person of yourself, Mr Mallard, and say what a surprise it is that this event has
happened. I want to congratulate all the MPs who have been elected to this House—new
and old—especially those from New Zealand First.
We are deeply appreciative of the support we received from the electorate in 2014. In
an early election campaign that was deliberately held over the stark, inclement winter
months, our campaign clearly connected with the New Zealand public. That is because
we argued for a comprehensive set of common-sense policies to improve life for all
New Zealanders. The National Party, with all its money and untold resources, managed
to grow its vote by only 72,000. In contrast, New Zealand First, starved of all the
privileges of Government incumbency and the millions being thrown behind National
and the “Moon Party”, increased its vote by about 61,000. Had the election been held in
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 59
November, when it should have been held —and not around the bogus APEC agenda —
then we would have done far better.
In this Parliament, as always, we will demand of the Government clear and forthright
answers to matters of public concern. We will do our duty and hold the Government to
account. We are not going to tolerate the kind of obfuscation and straight-out deceit that
the Government mounted, for example, over the Oravida scandal.
Surely every parliamentarian understands now how Parliament was short-changed in
endeavours to get to the truth in this matter. It was in the heat of the campaign that the
Prime Minister was forced to act against one of his Ministers, and not in the heat of
Parliament seeking full disclosure. In short, that is a shame on this Parliament and it
goes to the heart of—or lack of substance in—our democracy. We are going to hold the
Government to account because this is not a Government that truly represents the New
Zealand people. Remember that over 800,000 people did not vote. Although a million
voted for the Government, another million voted for other parties.
This Government is deeply compromised by some very sordid political
arrangements—for example, propping up the ACT Party in Epsom; an unbelievable
arrangement. Why, we even got more votes in Epsom, on the party vote, than ACT did.
Then National propped up United Future here in Wellington and brought back someone
who was caught leaking State secrets. Remember what the Prime Minister said? He
said: “I’d like to believe them, but I can’t.” Well, what has changed now? The
Government propped him up, put him back in as a Minister —in other words, having
absolute contempt for accountability in this Parliament, including ministerial
responsibility. Then, to compound that, National organised a fund- raiser for the Māori
Party at an Auckland men’s club, at $5,000 a plate, and said they were just trying to
spread democracy—just trying to spread democracy. I can tell you that the Māori Party
will not survive the next election. It showed in this last campaign how damaged they
were by this association.
Although the new swag of National MPs might pretend to be relaxed across there, we
wager that many of them will be having the jitters already. It is not because they are
new but because they know how many exited the “blue” benches for a multitude of
reasons in the last 3 years. MPs have been dropping like flies whilst John Key has been
at the helm. In the last 3 years there were 17 alone —17 MPs alone. Some jumped,
others were nudged, and some were given a big shove with tea party - like tactics within
their electorate organisations like, for example, the seat of Kaikōura, and like our p oor
friend Dr Hutchison, one of the finest doctors to ever visit this House, who was tea
party - taped all the way out of Parliament. Why? Because there is a certain outcome
that is expected of them.

items.speaker: Hon Nicky Wagner
items.text: What happened to Andrew?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: What did we do to Andrew? We fired him. When
you step out of line, in New Zealand First, and you make statements against the
organisation that are totally untrue, we do something about it. That is why we are back,
with a huge increase. I just want to say again that 17 MPs alone —the clean-out at the
end of the 50th Parliament was delivered by the Prime Minister as “refreshing the team”.
The media duly reported that he was doing the right thing —that one-third of the
National caucus had gone. Noticeably absent from the commentary, however, was that
the Prime Minister was shoring up his power base. Think of it. All the newbies nodding
and agreeing—music to the Prime Minister’s ears. He makes a pretty ordinary s peech
and they all jump up and clap. Not one person thought it was an ordinary speech, but
they all got up and clapped. Amongst those falling on their swords—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: What’s going to happen at the end of this speech?
60 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Now, now, Mr Brownlee. What is going to happen at
the end of this speech is that you are going to hear a series of very good speeches, 10 of
them—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Running out of time.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: No, I am not running out of time; that member is.
And he is running out of credibility. He is running out of credibility. He ran out of
credibility a long time ago. Bluster will not cut it any longer. Bluster and bumpf will not
cut it, Mr Brownlee. What we want here is substance. What we want here is analysis.
Among those falling on their swords or retiring gracefully were King, Wilkinson,
Hayes, Auchinvole, Calder, Heatley, Henare, Roy, Ryall, Tremain, and Hutchison.
Those who tripped up along the way and just had to go included the man who wanted to
know: “Don’t you know who I am?”.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: No one remembers who he is.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Aaron Gilmore. And there was the one, Claudette
Hauiti, who went out of here because she allowed the National Party to use another
member over here to attack New Zealand First, and we turned the attack back on them.
Within a matter of weeks she was gone. So my advice to Mr Brownlee and his
colleagues is: do not try it again in this term of Parliament, 2014 to 2016. It might have
some very damaging effects.
We have 14 novices in the Government ranks, and today we get told that they are
going to be made deputy chairpeople of select committees. Got any experience? No.
Got any ability? Not known about yet. But straight away—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Got buckets of it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, buckets, have they? Well, when are we going to
see some of it? Because I have never seen it in the past. In fact, when I was
campaigning in Whangarei, that member was not there. Oh, he knew I was coming, and
they could not see him for dust and small pebbles. He was gone.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Just a set-up.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: He was gone. No, it was not a set-up.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: It was.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, it was a set-up? Well, I went all the way from
Auckland to go to the Whangarei meeting. The people of Northland were coming out in
their droves. The place was packed. Where was the local National Party candidate? He
was not there. Unbelievable. For goodness’ sake. If you are going to have deputy
chairpeople like that, then we have got a recipe for a circus at the select committees.
Now to the Speech from the Throne that we heard today: “As has been well
signalled, the Government will put a possible change of New Zealand’s flag to a public
vote this term.” A public vote? What happened to the two referenda? The fir st was for
an option, and the second for the option of going against the existing flag. Well, what
happened to the two referenda, if you are going to have a vote?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, that’s what’s going to happen.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, you see, a referendum is a vote. A referendum
is people speaking. A referendum is a public expression of what people think.
[Interruption] I know Gerry is going to find it very difficult to get his head around this
concept of expanded democracy. I know Gerry is going to find that very difficult, but it
is two referenda that the Prime Minister promised.
Compounding this confusion is the fact that this Government, in its needless
compromise with the Māori Party, has already  admitted a second flag, Hone’s flag. Has
everybody forgotten that? Well, Hone might have gone but the flag is not —the so-
called Māori flag that flies on the Auckland Harbour Bridge and Government buildings
on Waitangi Day and national days. This flag was the result of Hone, at the taxpayers’
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 61
expense, holding 21 hui around the country at which the total attendance of Māori,
those are the indigenous people, was fewer than 1,000—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Your people.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —no, not my people —fewer than 1,000. Māori
supporters of New Zealand First are legion. In fact, we got far more votes than the
Māori Party. We got far more votes than the Māori Party, and we are still the only party
that ever took all the seats off the Labour Party. It will be 20 years before they can
rectify that. So be very careful —that new member. I am pleased to see her here.
Congratulations. But do not be led up the garden path. The smartest thing she did the
other day was to vote for the New Zealand First member. That was a very smart
move—a very smart move.
How many flags do we need? Well, apparently it is about branding for what National
likes to call “New Zealand Inc.” There is no spark firing out there amongst the public
for a new flag. Talking of Spark, branding soaks up money. Telecom doled out $20
million to try to change its brand. How much will it cost for all the Government
paraphernalia, every soldier’s uniform, every police uniform, everything we have got, to
be changed because the Prime Minister wants to have —what? A legacy —of economic
improvement? No. Of social change? No. Just a new flag. How barren is that? He even
finished his speech on that today. He wants a new flag. Mind you, it is not looking too
flash because his original idea looks a bit like the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria. He is
not too keen on that any more.
Then, of course, in the Speech from the Throne I read this: “… will complete the
implementation of the Financial Markets Conduct Act, and will progress legislation to
strengthen competition laws”. Really? What happened to South Canterbury Finance?
What happened in the trial just concluded last week? What happened when South
Canterbury Finance went bust, with $1.58 billion of payouts, $800 million of which was
never recovered, from the taxpayer? Today the Government is talking about financial
markets conduct, and right under its nose, in the last 3 years and in a trial that finished
last week, was this rip-off of the taxpayer.
Mr Brownlee can perhaps explain what he was doing, when he was asleep on the job,
behind the wheel. This is the man with all the financial knowledge of how markets
work. But then again, of course, Gerry was a former director, for a brief time, of the
Christchurch casino alternative. [ Interruption] Oh yes, he was. He did not last very
long. The guy who set it up, of course, is in prison at Pāremoremo at the moment. Gerry
was associating with crooks, and they even put him on the job.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh yes, it is true. I have got the prospectus with your
name all over it, Mr Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, it is true, all right. And then today we had this
extraordinary circumstance of your announcing that you are going to fix up financial
markets conduct. Right under our noses people are screaming out: what happened to the
Secretary to the Treasury, who should have been in front of the court at the time —the
man to whom the proposal was put? And, whilst we are at it, what was Bill English
doing? Or that genius from Merrill Lynch, the Prime Minister? How did we get ripped
off for $800 million? And worse still, of course, when we sought an inquiry on that, the
Government stopped it because it knew, like the old saying, that all roads led back to
the Government.
It is going to be a long 3 years unless the Government can be persuaded to lead in the
interests of all our people. We waited throughout the election —and, indeed, today —to
hear of a vision, a plan, or an idea to restore our country’s former economic and social
62 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
greatness, and we recall just what happened back in July of 1984 with the change of
Government.
The new, wet-behind-the-ears member for Epsom might think it is funny, but he is
there only because somebody else pulled down his own hoardings to give him a chance.
Where is the man’s integrity? How can you be possibly talking about negotiating with
the Government when you are a puppet, when you are in its pocket, and when it is
actually finding the money to finance your operation here in this Parliament? Most of us
could not stand such a consequence, when it is—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Oh, come on.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, no, Gerry could —Gerry could. Oh, I know that
Gerry could, but not one of my colleagues could stand such a fraudulent set-up. None of
my colleagues could stand such hypocrisy and cant, but I know that that member can,
because he went on TV and the only thing he made sense about when he went on his
advertisements was to say the word “Hi”, and after that, everything was drivel. After
that everything was drivel. In fact, it was most amusing. I almost felt like going along to
some of the Epsom meetings myself. They said it was the biggest joke you have ever
seen. Unbelievable that someone could be in Parliament that way, but it is no worse
than, say for example, the member for Ōhariu. It is just a disgrace that MMP, which is a
very expanded form of democracy, has been allowed to be abused and misused in this
way. It is going to be a long 3 years.
There is always a lot of talk from the Prime Minister. He reminds me of that fellow
in that moss ad. You know, the guy who comes on and say s: “I just spray and walk
away.”—“I just spray and walk away.” The Prime Minister was on about the Kiwi
dollar. Do you remember what he said? “It should be US65c.”, he said. That is a pretty
serious thing to say when you believe in the independence of the Reserve Bank, is it
not? He said that it should be US65c. Where is it? Well, it is close to US80c. Is he going
to do anything about it? No. And out there in provincial New Zealand there are dairy
farmers in their hundreds who are going to be heading off to their banks for some
mercy. And the milk price is not going to stop where it has got to now; it is going to fall
a whole lot further.
Now then, Mr Brownlee, what does the Government intend to do?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Devalue, and you get less for it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, then, why would you say that the dollar should
be at US65c? Why would you agree with the World Bank, the IMF, and everybody else
that it is massively overvalued? And why would you say that it should be at US65c and
then do nothing about it? It is “Mr Spray and Walk Away”. And what happened to the
Budget surplus? Remember what we were told? At the last Budget in May we had a
Budget surplus. What do you reckon it is now, with the billions that are being lost in the
dairy price? And the beef farmers should not get too cocky, because it will not last long.
It is cyclical.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Never does.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It never does, and they will be back pleading for
mercy very, very shortly.
There is never any real action to make a difference, and all we have now is the
stuttering start-up of the National Government’s third term propaganda machine. After a
glimpse of the agenda released today for public consumption, our first reaction is:
“Well, what is on their secret agenda?”, because there was nothing there today—nothing
for scrutiny, for us to look at. What is really happening on the ninth floor? Who is
plotting what with whom? Something is certainly happening out of sight because that,
today, could not have been what the plan is for the next 3 years, and we need to know
what and why and how and when.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 63
Let us be clear about what leadership now means in our country. More than any other
person in public life, a Prime Minister should set the ethical climate of our politics.
Rather than follow the dirty tricks of the wreckers who lurk on the dark fringes of
politics, he needs to lead through personal example a Government that protects the
rights of all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister has already revealed
that he dealt regularly with a blogger called “Whale Blubber”, or some phrase like that.
This blogger ran a dirty tricks campaign with like-minded National Party members,
National Party staff, and a certain Minister he no longer calls “Hon”. What sort of
inspirational leadership mixes with people who specialise in character assassination,
deception, defamation, and spreading malicious propaganda? Obviously the current
leadership does and, as someone once said, you can judge people by the company they
keep.
With this in mind, looking at this 3-year term fills us with foreboding. Why? Because
what does this Government actually intend to do? In June, before the election, we were
not going into a Middle East war. Within days after the election, we now are. Foreign
policy is becoming increasingly murky. Sure, there is a safe seat on the UN Security
Council, but how can New Zealand help solve world problems with a Prime Minister
who makes up foreign policy as he goes along? He claimed that the last meeting at
which Tim Keating was at was not official —it was not official. The only person who
thought that was the Prime Minister. Every international correspondent and everybody
in Washington did, but the Prime Minister did not. How can there be substance in our
democracy if Parliament is used to rubber-stamp a decision to go to war?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, I know it is rubbish—I know what the member’s
specialty is. I know that rubbish is his speciality, but let me say this. If it is good enough
for the British and it is good enough for the Canadians to trust their parliaments, why
will this Government not trust this Parliament?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: The Government said it will.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: What insightful things does Gerry Brownlee know
that the rest of us do not? I mean, you have to spend more time on a woodwork lathe to
gain more of an understanding of international affairs than he has currently got. Why
will the member not trust Parliament? The British did, with a conservative
administration. The Canadians did, with a conservative administration. Why can this
National Government not? We are off to war.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, we’re not.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, yes, we are. How can there be any substance
when Parliament is not trusted? How can there be any depth in our democracy if
Parliament is asked to give a blank cheque to law changes on the Security Intelligence
Service and the Government Communications Security Bureau?
Even before the special votes were counted post the election, the Prime Minister
started raising the spectre of people being beheaded —straight after the election, before
the special votes were even counted. These are the tactics of fear. They are used by
dictators all over the world. And if people think that that is a harsh comment, then why
was this not urgent before the last Parliament ended? What did we not know in June that
we know now? Well, the answer is nothing new, Mr Brownlee, so why was the
assurance given pre-election by the Prime Minister that we were not going to the
Middle East? New Zealanders do not want a State run by the secret service. New
Zealanders do not want the lousy excuse that if you are not doing anything wrong, you
have got nothing to worry about. What sort of democracy and system of laws puts that
sort of argument up?
Denis O’Rourke: The National Party does.
64 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The National Party. You would never have heard of
Holyoake or, I dare say, even Muldoon trying that trick on, but that is the new National
Party—no principles, power at any price, power for power’s sake. But when it comes to
the substance of the quality of the democracy those members live in, they do not give a
damn.
Take, for example, the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement. Why would we trust
international corporates with this co untry’s sovereignty or, indeed, with the rights of
Parliament? And why are congressmen in the United States entitled to know the terms
but people in New Zealand are not? Why are members of Parliament in this country
shut out? Indeed, why is most of Cabinet shut out, so that a little cabal within the
Government is out there negotiating on behalf of this country, deeming that it has the
power to tie up Governments for decades against the rights of New Zealand’s
Parliament to examine whether it is right or wrong? The interests of New Zealand
people should come before such agreements are signed. And to say that you are going to
bring it back to Parliament after you have signed off the document and that Parliament
will rubber-stamp it with people like “Mr See-less” from Epsom is hardly any assurance
at all.
Is Peter Dunne going to make a stand for democracy? Of course not. Is the Māori

items.speaker: Party going to step up and say
items.text: “This is not acceptable.” because the people who will be
hammered worst are the Māori at the bott om of the economic and social heap? Are the
Māori in the National Party themselves, like the new member for Whangarei— or those
other ones who have recently discovered their heritage just the other day. They have
recently discovered their heritage just the other day. [ Interruption] Oh, yes, I have
known that. I read about those fellow members in that Government who did that. They
came here not even knowing who their iwi was and went on a long genealogical search
to try to give themselves further value. I kno w he is the head of the Maōri Party now. I
congratulated him on winning. I am glad he won. I am glad he won, because his
opponent was even worse. His opponent was even more radical. I am glad he won, but
my point is: when is somebody over there, put in there because of their genealogical
background, going to stand up for it? The member for Whangarei? Or the one from
Tauranga? He discovered his genealogy after he got here. Or the one from out in
Howick way—you know, the friend with a double-barrelled name—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Jami-Lee Ross.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: That is right. You have got to commend people who
do that, but surely if you are going to say we have got all these people in our Parliament
and therefore we have got a multi-ethnic background, we would want to know when
they are going to do something about it, because going along with this neo-liberal, far-
right nonsense is not going to help the mass majority of New Zealanders, and not the
Māori people in particular. You can be sure of that.
Go up to Whangarei and Moerewa —all around the North—and tell me how they are
going on there, because at the moment, as an economist recently said, Whangarei is
dead. That is what he said. I saw it in the Northern Advocate. I did not see any protest
from the new member of Parliament —not a word, not a syllable, not a sound, not a
murmur. When you get elected for a place like Whangarei, you are not going to last
long unless you start standing up for the people up north. But that is what the economist
said—a leading economist from one of the banks. He said that the north is zombie town.
Those are his very words. If I was the local member would you not be barrelling up and
saying: “If there’s some truth in that, I’m going to do something about it. I’m going to
ensure that I go down and shake the place up. I’m going to put my rubber stamp away
and I’m going to get out my microscope and start examining policy to see how
Whangarei is going to be advantaged.” But no, not a syllable, not a sound.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 65
But back to the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Let me tell you that American
corporations have gained tremendous control over the American political system and
any assurances from that Government about our interests have to be taken with the
greatest of suspicion. And my real question is how this will help heartland New
Zealand, where the people are continually being hit by businesses cutting back or
closing down. Go down Port Road, Whangarei, or Wanganui, or all around Hawke’s
Bay, or Gisborne and see how many businesses are closing down and so how little
prospects lie there now for provincial New Zealand. It used to be, and will be again, the
powerhouse of this economy, but not with the policies this Government has been
pursuing for the last 30 years.
And remember this. When the Government started these policies it said that there
would be so many jobs we would not have enough people —so many jobs we would not
have enough people. Well, just today we found out that we have hit new record levels of
immigration: 45,000 over the last 12 months. Where are they going to? Auckland, and
Auckland has got no chance now of solving its infrastructural problems or its housing
crisis, or anything else. But meanwhile the good people of Whangarei and Invercargill
are going to pay with higher deposits and higher interest rates—four increases this year.
So I want to hear from these new members over there what they are going to do in
the next 3 years, because they are not here just to keep the seats warm. That is a very
fateful future if that is what you prospect for yourselves, because in the last 3 years 17
went down that way. My advice to you, ladies and gentlemen, is not to waste your time
here. When you go to caucus, keep your ears open. Ask a few questions —not “Where’s
Bellamy’s?” but “Where’s it all taking us as a country?”.
We learn back home after the election that we have got a housing crisis. There was
not one before the election, but the election is hardly over and the Government has got
such a housing crisis that the Prime Minister appointed not one but three housing
Ministers—not one but three housing Ministers. What did you see on morning TV?
Their special project in Auckland has built the magnificent figure of five —not a
thousand, or a hundred, but just five—homes. The Prime Minister’s defence on morning
TV on TV3 was: “Well, it’s the Labour Party’s fault, because they wouldn’t let us
change the Resource Management Act.” Sorry, the Government has had a majority for 6
years. Stop blaming everybody else for their fiscal incompetence.
As for the issue of selling State houses, did not Prime Minister Key say that after the
Genesis Energy sale that was it? Did he not tell Bill English? And last week Mr English
said that the money the Government had made from the selling of the housing stock was
not going back into State houses. So there is $18.7 billion of housing potentially going
to go into some other market.
And as for the question of productivity, what did the Productivity Commission say in
2012? Well, it questioned the transparency and accountability of the allocation of
hundreds of millions of dollars to community groups, charitable trusts, NGOs, and
Māori social housing providers. So it cannot be for that reason, can it, and yet that is
what the Prime Minister is saying today.
I think that the National Government is going to be in serious trouble on the question
of housing, because it has got a tiger by the tail and, just to make sure it cannot win, it is
bringing in massive numbers of people —45,000 alone in the last 12 months —most of
whom are going to Auckland. Many have gone to Epsom already —many have gone to
Epsom already.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: They’ll learn.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: They will learn all right, sooner or later. There is
going to be a housing bubble that is going to burst and when that happens there will be
an amazing change in how voters think.
66 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Mr Assistant Speaker Mallard, congratulations yourself, brother, on your position
and I give our assurance that whenever we can be cooperative we will be, that we will
be here to be proposing and opposing —opposing bad ideas and proposing and
supporting good ideas.
New Zealand First is on the cusp of something great. We know after the last
campaign that in 2017 we intend to be utterly ready in every respect —we know that if
we had had greater resources and the election had not been in the wintertime we would
have done so much better. In fact, the Government would look different from the way it
looks now. So count yourself lucky. Congratulations, but it is not going to happen one
more time. In fact, in 2017, with the work that we are going to do, New Zealanders will
have a chance to have a better economy and a better social future. After 30 years of this
experiment, it is surely time to fly the white flag and say: “It does not work.” We need a
better economic and social strategy than that.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker Mallard. Firstly, can I say congratulations on your appointment. Even if you
have not made too many decisions yet, I am threatening to recall the Speaker to give
you something to think about and test out your facing the things that you used to put in
front of the House. But I do join with others in congratulating you on your appointment
and I think that you are going to do a fine job. I feel sorry for Mr Tau Henare, who is no
longer with us, because actually I think you are a cut of the same cloth that brings a
certain edge to the House. I wish you well. Ka nui te mihi.
Sixteen days ago the Māori Party signed a historic r elationship accord called Te
Tatau ki te Paerangi, implying a doorway to the horizons —a doorway that leads to
development in cultural, economic, social, and environmental terms, to opportunities
that every New Zealander should be entitled to but opportunities that, unfortunately,
many do not actually see and are denied. The Māori Party has always been of the view
that the most important goal for any public servant, any political party, is to kick in that
door and to let the people come in. That is how we have always operated. Our single
focus is the doorway to whānau well -being—the ultimate expression of tino
rangatiratanga, which is to be self-determining for yourself and for your whānau, and
that you can aspire to be all that you want to be.
We as politicians are often influenced by our childhood memories and the things that
happened when we were young. I think about my upbringing in Ngongotahā— and
shame on those people who do not know where Ngongotahā is— in Rotorua, watching
my grandmother as a 90-year-old carrying her own firewood. She still cooked her own
food. Life seemed so simple to her and, I am sure, to that generation. My job was to go
and get her smokes and her milk and bread. What I learnt from her example was a
number of things. It was to be feis ty when the good of the whānau was at stake, to
provide for my children no matter what, to be resourceful, to love our land, to love our
language, and to love our identity.
So these are powerful drivers of motivation —motivation that the Māori Party has
always located in the future prospects of whānau. It matters to us that one in seven
people in Aotearoa is Māori. It matters to us that one -third of people of Māori descent
are aged under 15 years. In sheer numbers, 669,000 New Zealanders —17.5 percent—
whakapapa to a thriving, living culture, a culture infused with the value of kaupapa such
as manaakitanga, generosity of spirit of one person towards another; kotahitanga, a
sense of unity, of purpose, of togetherness; and kaitiakitanga, careful regard for our
environment and to be guardians of our planet. Māori matter to the greater well -being
and prosperity of this nation.
So when the Prime Minister invited the Māori Party into the relationship with the
Government, we jumped at it. I take this moment to mihi to him for the opportunity that
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 67
is afforded the Māori Party. It was with the greatest humility that I accepted the role as
the new Minister for Māori Development, Minister for Whānau Ora, and Associate
Minister for Economic Development. In doing so I am forever mindful of the legacy
that is left behind by those who went ahead of me, the likes of whom I will always
aspire to be —the likes of Sir Apirana Ngata, Matiu Rata , Iriaka Rātana, Pita Sharples,
Tariana Turia, the Rt Hon Winston Peters —now and again —Parekura Horomia, and
Tau Henare. They are honourable gentlemen and ladies who have graced this
Parliament. I will endeavour to meet their standard, if not to go higher.
These are triple bottom lines that I have set myself in the future: Māori development
running alongside a dedicated policy approach to supporting families through Whānau
Ora, while at the same time focusing on an economic platform. These things provide a
strong base for moving through that doorway to our horizons.
The Productivity Commission has just released an inquiry called Cut to the Chase ,
which focuses on the challenge of moving and achieving more effective and efficient
social services. Currently, a large amount of public money —around $34 billion —goes
into social services. So it is vital that we do well with it.
Whānau Ora is premised on the expectation that with the appropriate support in place
whānau can be self-managing and take responsibility for their own development. They
can be the all-powerful drivers towards their own destiny. It is an admirable ideal and
one that I am determined to do the utmost to uphold, not just for better governance and
for the most effective use of the taxpayer spend but, most important of all, for the
security, stability, and success of all generations to come. As politicians we are the
guardians of this time. We must take seriously our responsibility to build on the
progress spearheaded by Tariana Turia in enabling whānau to achieve outcomes for
themselves. We must work collaboratively to support those who are struggling, to create
a meaningful living wage, and to enact the recommendations of the Expert Advisory
Group on Solutions to Child Poverty. I am delighted to be joined by my colleague
Marama Fox, who has enormous energy in making progress on poverty reduction and
well-being. She is going to be a huge asset for the Māori Party and, indeed, to this
Parliament. Nau mai e te tuahine. [Welcome sister, colleague.]
The formalities of the Commission Opening and the State Opening of Parliament
have enforced the standing of tangata whenua and the status of the Treaty of Waitangi
as central to New Zealand’s understanding of itself. The Māori Party is proud of two
particular ceremonies that have been able to be added to the rich traditions that form the
fabric of the modern Parliament. The karakia that we had yesterday morning, which
established the Tiriti o Waitangi as our foundation document again, and supported that
notion, was attended by representatives of all parties of the Parliament, and the formal
mihi, of course, today, expressed by my tuahine Nanaia Mahuta. It is a welcome sign
that culture is evolving, that the traditions made in this Parliament can truly be
representative of our indigenous people, and that unity of vision is possible across the
political realm. I believe that this Parliament can be proud that 18 members across the
House delivered their oaths in Te Reo Māori. Later this week I will be attending the
Minister for Women’s blessing in her office. All of these events are an indication of
goodwill, which augurs well for this term.
I have a clear vision for a Māori development agenda, which is to cast the net wide in
focusing on outcomes. The strategic imperative that we all face in investing in our long-
term health and well-being is to actually ensure that we give robust consideration to
families, to whānau, and in particular to our tamariki and mokopuna, by bringing
together a much tighter pipeline through to the role of innovation and economic
development. I am determined to build on the leadership of Pita Sharples in making sure
that He Kai Kei Aku Ringa makes substantial differences to our communities. I have a
68 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
particular regard for regional economic development and the role that community hubs
can play in accelerating opportunities both in Māori business and global markets. We
must boost the productivity of Māori families, of Māori assets and enterprises, and of
New Zealand, through harnessing economic and employment opportunities in a way
that will advance Māori development. While I will bring a strong focus on innovation to
my ministerial work, I am equally determined that we must always balance any changes
with responsibilities that come from kaitiakitanga.
A key priority for me will be determining our approach to the Māori Language (Te
Reo Māori) Bill. I intend to reopen submis sions on the legislation and to work
constructively on consolidating our pathway forward. The capacity to be fluent in Te
Reo Māori has a significant impact on a person’s mauri, on their well -being, and
wairua. I am also very keen to develop greater priority for a cultural revitalisation
strategy. As part of our new approach to Māori development we specifically negotiated
a priority for a Māori engagement strategy as a part of our relationship accord. We look
forward to working with the Prime Minister to achieve that.
I want to work with Māori members of the Māori electorate seats, the wider
Parliament, Māori organisations, iwi leaders and chairs, and businesses and corporations
to create a more useful dialogue, worthy of the Crown’s relationship with iwi, hapū, and
whānau. I will be convening an annual ministerial summit on the Māori economy to
advance the Māori economic strategy.
I am also determined that we uphold the momentum and the priority of some key
strategic statements established by my predecessors, including a whole-of-Government
approach towards addressing family violence —He Whare Āhuru He Ōranga Tāngata,
the Māori housi ng strategy, and He Korowai Oranga , the Māori health strategy. This
year is going to be positive, I am looking forward to working with you and other
members of Parliament, and I look forward to the many times that we will have
interaction in the best interests of Te Ao Māori. Tēnā koe.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker, may I at
the outset congratulate you and your fellow presiding officers on your election to your
respective roles for this Parliament. You are a rather unique breed. I think yours are the
only positions in Parliament that are elected by the entire Parliament and that enjoy the
support of the entire Parliament. As a consequence there are certain expectations that
members have of you, which I am sure will not be disappointed over the next 3 years.
Can I also extend a welcome to all of the new members who have joined us for this
51st Parliament. I know that many of you will be still in that state of excitement about
what lies ahead —and the more immediate panic of preparing for your maiden speech,
and I can understand why, given the two fine examples we have already heard today —
and also that broader sense of purpose and commitment to the people on whose behalf
you were elected. I wish you all well. I look forward to hearing your contributions and
to working with you during the term of this Parliament.
Earlier today we witnessed the formal State Opening conducted by His Excellency
the Rt Hon Lieutenant General Sir Jerry Mateparae, our Governor-General. I think that
he and Lady Mateparae serve us particularly well in the viceregal role. I am very proud
to be able to refer to them as our de facto heads of State. I look forward to the day when
we can have a genuinely New Zealand head of State and when the oath of allegiance
that we take at the start of Parliament is one to New Zealand and its people, not the
antiquated form that we have at the moment.
I think the process that the Prime Minister has initiated regarding a debate around the
flag is perhaps the start of a wider discussion about the future structure and
constitutional direction of this country. Frankly, I think that New Zealanders are ready
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 69
for that discussion. It is long overdue. It is a mark of our reflection and our maturity and
I believe that it is one that we are well capable of conducting in a measured, responsible,
and ultimately successful way for our future. It will be a determinant of the type of
nation that we want to become. Our diversity has grown dramatically in the last quarter
of a century. The old norms are being challenged constantly, and to keep our country
relevant to the generations now and in the future we need to be prepared to consider
change, and that change will be significant.
United Future has entered into its third confidence and supply agreement with a
National-led Government, following on from two earlier confidence and supply
agreements with Labour when it was in office. During each of those processes there has
been the opportunity to support some Government measures and to oppose those that
are seen as inappropriate. That will be the pattern during the 3 years ahead. Although I
would expect to vote for a significant part of the Government’s legislative programme,
there will be matters that will draw some criticism from time to time and a contrary
vote.
If I can refer to the speech delivered earlier today, there were a couple of matters
raised there that I want to comment upon a little further this afternoon. The first relates
to changes to the Resource Management Act. Ever since its introduction in 1990 the
Resource Management Act has been a talisman for opposition from a range of quarters
who do not understand its fundamental purpose. They do not recall that prior to the
passage of that Act planning legislation in New Zealand was found in some 54 different
pieces of often contradictory legislation. What the Resource Management Act sought to
do was bring all of those provisions together in one place and set an environmental
baseline upon which decisions could be made regarding development opportunities for
the future.
I think that one of the grave tragedies with the Resource Management Act was that
the great New Zealand tradition prevailed and it was launched in a vacuum. A change of
Government had occurred and the new Government was not as committed to the
legislation as the previous Government. As a consequence, a lot of the preparatory work
in terms of the preparation of national policy statements, etc., did not take place. But
that is not an excuse to now come and say that to make the Act more relevant to today’s
situation we will gut its principles altogether. No one argues that there is not a case for
streamlining the procedures of the legislation, and no one argues that there is not a need
to address issues such as the provision of housing, but they can be accommodated
without amending Part 2 of the legislation—clauses 6 and 7 in particular.
If the Government wants to proceed on the basis of making those necessary process
changes, it will have my full and loyal support. But I will not support legislation that
weakens or significantly changes the provisions of Part 2 because they fundamentally
remove the whole basis on which the legislation has been founded and operated. They
remove 20 years of case law. They set us back to the days prior to 1990 and 1991 when
we had a convoluted, difficult, confusing planning environment that was driven largely
out of the old Town and Country Planning Act 1928. Anyone who sits and rationally
looks at the situation says one thing: we do not want to go back there.
We have the chance with this legislation to actually ensure that we address the issues
that need to be addressed. After all, a quarter of a century later many of the processes
will have changed simply because of the change in technological procedure, and it is
appropriate to tidy those up. But it is not appropriate to throw out the principles on
which the legislation, hailed as groundbreaking at the time, was founded. I hope that the
Prime Minister’s announcement a couple of weeks ago that indicated a little bit of
movement, perhaps, is carried through, and I am looking forward to discussions with
the Minister for the Environment on those matters. I think there is a reasonable
70 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
compromise available that will allow the Government to maintain its objectives but also
keeps in place the principles under which the Resource Management Act operates.
The second issue that the Speech from the Throne referred to today was the
international situation regarding terrorism and the need for a review of New Zealand’s
privacy legislation. The two are not immediately related, although there is a tangential
connection. Like everyone else in this House, I am not in any way impressed by,
tolerant of, or supportive of the activities of the Islamic State. I cannot believe the
barbarism, the cruelty, and the crudity of a lot of its actions. I think that the world does
need to take positive steps to ensure that the spread of that virus, if you like, i s
contained. But we need to be careful as we do so that we do not compromise
unreasonably the privacy of our own citizens and that we do not use the opportunity as
one to strengthen other intelligence-sharing relationships that we might have amongst
international partners. This is a very specific and very serious situation, but it occurs
against a backdrop around the world where the whole issue of the protection of personal
privacy and communication is becoming far more pronounced. When you see details
emerging about the type of information that telecommunications companies have, for
instance, and that large entities like major companies have and are sharing, often
without protection, day by day, then the issue becomes more pressing.
This Parliament was elected to work our way steadily through those issues with a
measure of good judgment and balance. I think, on reflection, that the speech we heard
this morning delivers that in large measure, but the challenge for this Parliament as it
starts to come to grips with the issues will be to ensure that we do not get carried away
by the immediacy of a crisis and end up doing things or restraining people’s activities in
ways that we will regret later on. That is a fundamental principle on which a liberal
democracy is founded —the protection of the rights of the individual, the upholding of
the prerogatives of the State, and ensuring the maintenance of balance between them. I
look forward to working in this Parliament as we seek to achieve those goals.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party in reply to
His Excellency’s speech. I never knew I was smart until I came here. For the avoidance
of doubt, I am not referring to meeting the Opposition but, rather, to quoting a student I
met at the Vanguard Military School, a partnership school, a kura hourua, just last
week. There could not have been a better entrée to my first speech in this House than
meeting that student, and before I return to that quote, allow me to visit some of the
journey to that meeting and to this House today.
I represent the communities of Epsom, Mt Eden, Parnell, and Remuera. A look at our
electorate might explain why we collectively made this choice. Epsom is typecast a s
wealthy, and that may well be true in many cases but it is certainly not universal. The
largest industry in our electorate is education. Our 30 schools include many of the
largest in the country. We also host one large tertiary campus and are adjacent to three
more. Education is aspiration. You can tell everything you need to know about a
person’s politics by acquiring their sincere answer to a simple question: “Is wealth a
zero-sum game or not?”. Unfortunately, the sincere answer of many in this House
would be yes. They lay a litany of elaborate excuses and set about constructing an even
more elaborate web of rules to reallocate finite wealth to the most deserving. In practice,
the most deserving means those whose special pleadings resonate loudest in the theatre
of politics. My answer to the question is no. My fellow Epsom voters elected me if not
in full support of my philosophy then certainly with knowledge of it.
I will tell you something else about the Epsom electorate. Not only is it the most
educated electorate in this country but it is also the one that had the lowest party vote
for New Zealand First. Voters elected me because they understand the danger that the
zero-sum brigade present to us. Our communities are leafy and our schools prestigious,
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 71
so if people want more Epsom, then the answer is to create more Epsom, more good
schools, and more good suburbs. But the Opposition would cram more people into
smaller, denser dwellings, changing the character of our communities and putting
intolerable pressure on burgeoning school zones.
When it comes to wealth, for too many the answer is higher tax rates and taxing the
same dollars one more time with an envy-fuelled capital gains tax. When many of us
voluntarily invest our time and talents in helping others, those who think there is only so
much to go around want to crowd out even those efforts for their tax-funded coercive
schemes. Small wonder, then, that we voted the way we did.
The people of Epsom did not vote for a mere abstraction or even a political strategy,
though. Not many, if any, of those who say that I am here due to the latter can say that
they came to this House by way of 13,000 doorsteps, and delivered personally 85,000
personally addressed direct mail letters, had nearly 1,000 attendees at private house
meetings, and waved signs at traffic for 300 hours. Actually, most of that was done by
my extraordinary team who accompanied me, delivered, hosted, and waved. I
acknowledge many of you who are here on the floor of the House and in the galle ry—
the people who have filled the gallery today —and those of you who could not be in
Wellington. I thank you all.
Those people supported me because their answer to that great political dividing
question is: yes, wealth is a positive-sum game. Those of us who believe that are
interested in a different question: under what conditions can individuals best create
wealth? The answer lies in the use of knowledge in society. Since the total inventory of
that knowledge is never given in its totality to any single mind or small group of them,
it must be grown and applied through a widespread process of conjecture and refutation.
That is the creative power of a free society; the power to try new things and find what
works. This power is greatest when the role of Government is not whatever the
Government defines it to be, as one former Prime Minister put it, but when it is clearly
defined to maximise individual freedom. That definition relies heavily on an
understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of government as an institution.
Governments have extraordinary power to coerce legally. In some cases this power
brings great goods, and chief among them is an environment where we can safely go
about our business in our various communities. That, in turn, requires the rule of law
rather than the arbitrary rule of man. We meet today at the pinnacle of several centuries
of progress towards that goal. We have moved towards the light of liberty by removing
distinctions in law that once treated people differently depending on their religious
conviction, their gender, or their race, and most recently this House decided to remove
gender from the marriage laws. Many countries have never achieved that, but it is
extraordinary that as if engaged in some form of historical shuttle run, we who were
first to touch the cone are now rushing back to create new distinctions in law. I refer to
those who claim that the only way to achieve a material equality between the Māori side
and the British side of my ancestry is to create more legal inequality. No doubt they
have noble intentions, but public policy should be measured only by results.
Beyond the rule of law there are other public goods that a good Government might
employ extraordinary powers to provide. Believe it or not, the outcome of private action
is sometimes inefficient and Government regulation can improve matters. We see this in
our fisheries and our atmosphere, where well-crafted regulations protect us from the
ruin to which all men would otherwise rush. Insurance against genuine misfortune of
birth or catastrophic events is another role that a good Government might cautiously
assume. Funding but not providing education, regardless of parental wealth, is an
example of such insurance.
72 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
When used beyond these limited roles as protector, regulator, and insurer, however, a
Government’s extraordinary powers corrode the powers of a free society. The problem
is one of knowledge and politics. It is a fatal conceit to believe that one mind or group
of minds can know enough to plan the myriad activities of the very society that they
themselves are a product of. To quote Bastiat, there is: “Ce qu’on voit et ce qu’on ne
voit pas”, but politics has a tendency to narrow human endeavour to what is visible to
only a few actors. The alternative is spontaneous activity coordinated by only a few
general rules and simple laws.
Perhaps the most literal examples of new wealth from finite means are found in the
field of engineering. I am one of two engineers in this House and I come from a family
of engineers, several of whom are here today. Although a generous person could barely
call my own engineering achievements modest, what my profession has achieved is
anything but modest. Suffice it to say that when the member seated to my right gave his
maiden speech, phoning a person when they were not at home must have been rarer than
a bow tie.
The challenge is to create the conditions wherein this kind of wealth creation is likely
to flourish. Thankfully, nearly 200 nations have unwittingly carried out a vast natural
experiment on this question. We now have several decades of data showing which
public policies work and which do not. They are an adherence to low Government
expenditure funded by low-rate broad-based taxes, monetary policy targeted at price
stability, a liberal approach to trade and investment abroad, flexible labour markets, and
secure predictable property rights. Countries that adopt these principles do not just
achieve greater wealth; they also make for better environmental custodians. They also
achieve greater civil liberties. Interestingly, when countries are ranked according to
these five measures, New Zealand is consistently in the top five and often in the top
three of nearly 200 countries on earth.
I returned to New Zealand because it is my home and it is easily among the most
prosperous, pristine, diverse, and yet harmonious societies the world has ever seen. The
desire to go back to the monocultural, isolationist, intolerant, and interventionist New
Zealand of the 1970s is forgivable only to those who were not actually there. In any
case, we ain’t going back.
When confronted with an Opposition promising to unpick years of consensus on
monetary policy, tax, trade, and even electricity markets, the people of New Zealand
have said a resounding no. New Zealand today is a country that has adopted since the
mid-1980s more of ACT’s market liberal policies than all but a couple of other
countries in the world. To paraphrase another former member: “We won, you lost.” But

items.speaker: I am able to heartily say
items.text: enjoy this great country that has been created.
Much of the credit must go to Sir Roger Douglas, who is here on the floor of the
House today. Roger’s reforms occurred at a unique time in our demographic history. Sir
Robert Muldoon’s World War II generation gave way to the much larger generation
they produced in what must have been a rather ravenous reunification after that war. In
their entry to public life, the boomers created a society in their image, and symmetry
demands that their exit will be similarly disruptive.
My generation, which I share with a growing number of recent entrants to this
House—and I note that my speech echoes very closely the very fine speech made by
Chris Bishop earlier —also faces a number of acute challenges in the wake of our
parents’ reign. In the news this week and for the p ast decade has been housing
affordability, an entirely supply side, entirely regulatory problem. For the first time in
our egalitarian society, parental assistance—not in my case, I might add—has become a
prominent factor in homeownership and there is a hereditary element to property. I look
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 73
forward to supporting this Government’s efforts to increase the supply elasticity of
housing.
Fiscal sustainability should interest our generation. Treasury predicts that on
historical trends Government debt will reach double GDP by the time we might think of
retiring circa 2060. We can only lament the advanced auctions in stolen goods that pass
for elections every 3 years and wonder how the various promises would add to this
burden. With the demographic headwinds we face, fiscal discipline must be a mantra of
our generation.
The best thing about New Zealand is our pristine natural environment. Sadly, our
history as environmental custodians is far from perfect, but again we must think
carefully about the role of Government. It is no coincidence that the countries that have
been farthest down the path of Government intervention also produced the worst
environmental catastrophes. Modern environmentalists should practise the four Ps:
pricing, property rights, prosperity, and private initiative. We pride ourselves on being
an egalitarian society. However, we must be honest with ourselves about the success of
the 80-year-old promise to look after our most vulnerable citizens from the cradle to the
grave. Welfare and education reform are essential to maintaining an egalitarian New
Zealand for my generation.
I began by quoting a student I met last week at a partnership school: “I didn’t know I
was smart until I came here.”, she said. Her story matters because in a global and
increasingly technologically sophisticated economy the value of skills is ever
increasing. We cannot afford to have smart people wasting their potential. The school
she now attends does things differently from the ones she previously attended. The
principal leads the school differently from the one he used to teach at. It is not pedagogy
for every student, but such universality does not and cannot exist in a country of nearly
one million students. What matters is that it works for her. The school draws together all
the strands I have spoken of today. Like all human endeavour it is imperfect, but by
conjecture and reputation it grows and applies the store of knowledge about educating
children. The Government plays a role, but a limited one. It brings the creative powers
of a free society to bear upon one of our most urgent challenges as a nation.
I am honoured to represent my fellow Epsom electors and to lead the ACT Party in
this House. It is my hope that I will contribute here to improving public policy for al l
New Zealanders so that prosperous and free individuals may flourish in this green and
pleasant land. Thank you.
Can I begin my comments this afternoon by congratulating you, Mr Speaker, on your
return to the Speaker’s Chair with the overwhelming endorsement of members of this

items.speaker: House. I want to congratulate your assistants
items.text: the Deputy Speaker, the Hon Chester
Borrows; Lindsay Tisch, who has been a long-serving and very loyal member of this
Parliament and who continues his work as your assistant; and also the new man in the
team, the Hon Trevor Mallard, who I know will bring his own style to the work. I want
to also congratulate the Clerk’s Office, the Governor -General’s office, and the
Parliamentary Counsel Office for the work that they have done to organise the
ceremonies of the past 2 days, which remind us of the deep ties we have to longstanding
democracy in this country.
I also need to acknowledge our mover and seconder of the Address in Reply debate
today, Chris Bishop and Barbara Kuriger. My colleague Tim Groser was remarking
before—and I think he was absolutely right —that it showed why the National Party is
so strong. Firstly, the urban liberal Chris Bishop gave a great speech to reflect on his
views about where this country might go in the time that he is in Parliament, and then
Barbara came in to speak as the quintessential rural person who is very, very connected
74 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
to the needs of those rural communities. I think that when you put those two together,
you start to see some of the breadth of the National Party, and I know that other maiden
speeches will expand that in the days ahead.
I also want to congratulate David Seymour on that last speech. I think that what you
demonstrated to us all was the reason why the National Party sits so comfortably in a
governance arrangement with the ACT Party. I am sure that your contribution to this
House will be considerable over the years to come.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: It’s a jack-up.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I did not want to go on to discussing the New Zealand
First contribution quite so quickly in my limited time today, but the member over there
invites me to do it. He sits there saying: “It’s a jack-up. It’s a jack-up.” He is saying that
only because he is saying: “I did so well but I’ve got nothing.” Then there was the issue
of him saying: “Well, look what happened—the Prime Minister is shoring himself up by
14 new members and a whole lot of other people exiting.” This is a guy who has exited
his entire caucus on three occasions during his time here in Parliament. It is so bad that
one of his returning members, Mr Ron Mark, was not even known to the deputy leader,
who yesterday described him as Don Clarke. Well, Don Clarke is not available for the
All Blacks, and he is certainly not in this Parliament.
I want to turn now to the substance of what I want to say, which is support for the
Prime Minister’s motion put before the House in this Address in Reply debate. I was
disappointed by the contribution from the Labour Party but not surprised —not
surprised—because if it is boiled down and analysed, it is more of what we have had for
the last 6 years. If only the ungrateful voter had voted for Labour members, everything
would be OK! If only the ungrateful voter had recognised that everything they said was
good and everything we did was bad, then everything would be OK! If only the
ungrateful voters would stop thinking about what is best for them in their lives and start
thinking about what the Labour Party thinks is best for them in their lives, then
everything would be OK! I have got to say that although this Government going into a
third term is very, very conscious of showing any signs of arrogance whatsoever, there
is a fundamental arrogance in that Labour Party position that will not change with a
change of leader. It needs a deep change of the culture of that party. It would be easy to
spend a lot of time today talking about the leadership challenge, but it does not matter.
It does not matter at all. As long as that attitude prevails, Labour will not connect with
New Zealanders.
What connects with New Zealanders are the sorts of things that the Government has
set out in the Speech from the Throne today, like the idea that we should constantly
strive to improve New Zealanders’ incomes. In that regard, we have heard a lot of
comment from other parties about how, for example, you should perhaps devalue the
dollar, because that might somehow make things easier for people. Well, the question
there is: where on earth is there a place where the purchasing power of one economy is
enhanced by another economy deciding to reduce its own purchasing power? That is the
problem that we have got inside other parties here trying to comment on that.
The reality is that in the next couple of years, the average wage in New Zealand will
climb to $62,000. It is climbing at a rate that is ahead of inflation in this country. There
is a reason for that. It is because the Government has policies that do not of themselves
create work, do not of themselves create export opportunities, but that facilitate the
people out there who take risks on a daily basis to build businesses, to seek out markets,
and to sell their products, and along the way they provide opportunities for other New
Zealanders to enjoy that success through higher incomes. That is a pretty simple thing.
Then there is the issue of child poverty, which we have said we want to do a lot more
about. I think it is only fair to look at some relativities in that regard. If you listen to the
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 75
Green Party, then everything is all bad and there is no hope for anybody in this country
in that regard. If you listen to the Labour Party members, they are going to hold us to
account. Well, all they need to do is watch what is going to happen as we see more
people exiting benefits and going into work. There can be no denying that life for a
working family is a lot easier than for a family that lives on a benefit. If the only answer
you have got is to say: “We’ll make it all easier for those people on a benefit by lifting
them up.”, then you start to persecute the people who work. So there will be some v ery
interesting debates in this House over that particular issue.
The other thing that has come up constantly over the last 6 months has been housing
in New Zealand. It is staggering that we have had the Labour Party members come out
today and say that they will not support change to the Resource Management Act.
Green Party members came out today and said they will not support change to the
Resource Management Act. Well, it is very simple. If there is not more land available
for subdivision, if there is not better use of existing land, and if the artificial costs that
are put into the cost of using that land are not removed by taking away laws that put
those costs in place, then there is no attack on the issue of low-cost housing. So I
challenge the Labour Party members to think for themselves, beyond the rhetoric that
has been their mantra for the last 6 years, and to start to think seriously about the issue
of housing costs.
This Government will do it, and no one should underestimate, either, the need for a
Government to get its own finances in shape to be able to show a picture that says we
do not have rampant runaway expenditure by the Government, we do not have
expenditure plans that go beyond the means of the Government, because that reflects
directly in interest rates. It is an easy calculation. Every time an interest rate goes up one
whole point, then that is an extra $1,000 a year on whatever your mortgage amount is
that has to be found. If we are looking at $300,000 and $400,000 mortgages or bigger —
which are, in many cases, the norm —then that is a large amount of money that can be
altered or taken out of a person’s income each week by virtue of bad Government
policy. The Homestart loans programme will see a change in the way that developers
put product into the market. Couple that with some Resource Management Act changes
and a desire by the Government to see more of this housing built, and I think we will
see some real movement in that regard.
I should speak a little bit about the other issue that has come up repeatedly this
afternoon—that of what New Zealand might do in response to the Islamic State
activities in the Middle East. I can repeat only what the Prime Minister has said over
and over. There will be a discussion among the political parties. There will be a debate
in the House. There will be a considered position that represents New Zealand’s
position. I want to say that I watched the Q+A programme last week and those four
Labour leader aspirants were all appalling on this subject because they were
scaremongering where they need not scaremonger. The New Zealand defence forces are
extremely capable, and they are capable across a range of activities that might be useful
in the suppression of this appalling organisation that is so barbaric and repulsive to us.
But it needs to be something that is well considered, and it will be. Thank you.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: Tēnā koe Mr Speaker. E Te
Kaiwhakahaere o tēnei Whare, tēnei te mihi atu ki a koe me ngā kaiwhakahaere tuarua o
tēnei Whare, a Lindsay Tisch, te Hōnore Trevor Mallard me te Hōnore Chester
Borrows, ā, me koe tō tātau Kaiwhakahaere Matua, a te Hōnore David Carter. Tēnei te
mihi ki a koutou kua riro atu i wēnei tūranga ō koutou. E ngā mema huri rauna i tō tātou
Whare, tēnei te mihi ki a koutou ahakoa he mema hou, he mema e hoki mai ana. Tēnei
te mihi ki a koutou i runga i te tūmanako, ko tō koutou whāinga i roto i tēnei Whare, he
hāpai i ngā āhuatanga e pā ana ki te oranga o ō tātou whānau, hapū, iwi, hapori puta noa
i Aotearoa. Tēnā koutou.
76 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. My acknowledgments to you, the Speaker of this House and
the Assistant Speakers, Lindsay Tisch, the Hon Trevor Mallard, the Hon Chester
Borrows, and, of course, yourself, our principal Speaker, the Rt Hon David Carter. To
you who have acquired these position of yours, congratulations. Also to you members
