throughout our House, whether new or returning, my salutations to you collectively. I
greet you in the hope that your aim in this House is to lift up aspects pertaining to the
welfare of our families, subtribes, tribes and communities throughout New Zealand.
Thank you.]
Mr Assistant Speaker, first let me just congratulate you again on your return to the
Assistant Speaker’s position, as well as the Hon Chester Borrows and the Hon Trevor
Mallard, as well as the Rt Hon David Carter in the Speaker’s position.
This is not my maiden speech but it is my first speech as the elected member for Te
Tai Tokerau. I am extremely honoured at the faith that the people of Te Tai Tokerau
have placed in me to work on their behalf. When I became the principal of Kaitāia
Intermediate School I said to my chairperson and my board of trustees that they would
never have to worry about a personal grievance from me to them because if the day ever
came when I was not doing the work, the core business that I was employed to do —that
is, raise achievement —then they just needed to tell me and I would resign and allow
somebody else to come into the position to do the job that I could not do. My pledge to
the people of Te Tai Tokerau here and now is exactly the same. If ever I am not doing
the job that I was elected to do —give me a few years, I must admit —talk to my
electorate people, who will tell me, and then I will resign. I am not a member of
Parliament just to sit here and fill up space; I intend to make a difference for the people
in the north.

items.speaker: I campaigned on four priorities
items.text: education, the economy of Te Tai Tokerau, to raise
outcomes in Te Reo Māori, and also the elimination of sexual and domestic violence
throughout New Zealand. I make no apologies for the elimination of sexual and
domestic violence from New Zealand being my priority of priorities. When I listened to
the Speech from the Throne today, I heard the Governor-General talk about eliminating
poverty, reducing health disparity, and improving educational outcomes and housing. I
say now that if we can eliminate sexual and domestic violence from New Zealand, we
will go a very, very long way to improving outcomes in all of those social areas.
The No. 1 cause of youth suicide is sexual abuse. We do not need to sit here navel
gazing and wonder why it is that our youth are killing themselves at an alarming rate.
Sexual abuse is the No. 1 cause of youth suicide. The second most prevalent cause is
domestic violence. Watching your mother get beaten up a couple of times a week is
likely to lead you down that path. Mental health issues are often the result of unresolved
sexual violence issues from a person’s past. As I am told by someone from the Mason
Clinic, 75 percent of inmates are not the nasty, evil, horrible people that we are led to
believe. Most of them have done things that have got them into prison, but those crimes
are the manifestation of unresolved issues from sexual violence or domestic violence.
Domestic violence and sexual violence are both major drivers of poverty. We talk
about poverty and eliminating poverty and reducing poverty. Domestic violence and
sexual violence reduce a survivor’s— in most cases, a woman’s— sense of agency,
which is a term used to describe her ability to lift herself above her circumstances.
Survivors of sexual and domestic violence have difficulty concentrating at school and
learning. They have difficulty getting a decent job. They therefore have difficulty
providing financially to their whānau’s situation, so often kids go to school without
shoes, without food. I say here and now that if we want to feed our kids, the first thing
we should do is love their mothers.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 77
The funding of services to help people who have suffered from sexual and domestic
violence is woefully inadequate. This is something that I ask the Government to
improve. Two weeks ago I was talking to an agency in Kaitāia that works wit h the
survivors of domestic violence. It said that it is funded to work with 2½ whānau a
week—2½ whānau a week is what the agency is funded in its contract to work with. It
actually has 52 whānau on its books that it is working with. That is the extent of the
issue that we are talking about in terms of sexual violence and domestic violence being
rampant throughout all strata of society. We say now that it is not an ethnic issue. It
goes across all ethnicities, it goes through all communities and through all socio-
economic areas; it is just that wealthy people tend to have lawyers who can hide the
problem a lot more.
Between 23,000 and 28,000 young people under the age of 24 in west Auckland,
central Auckland, and on the North Shore alone —we are not talking about Te Tai
Tokerau, we are not talking about the south of Auckland; we are talking about just those
three areas within Auckland —have experienced sexual abuse. I ask how those young
people can sit there and learn and concentrate on what the teacher is saying or what their
lecturer in university is saying when their heads are filled up with the nonsense that
went on and occurred to them, probably the night before, probably in the safety of their
home, usually done by somebody they know, they love, and they should be able to trust.
I said in my maiden speech that it is one thing to be born a male; it is another thing to
become a man. This is predominantly a male issue —90 percent of offenders are male.
Obviously, 10 percent of offenders are female, but we as men need to step up and
address this issue. The greatest enabler of sexual violence and domestic violence is
silence. An example was last night on Television One news where a political party on
election night had a man who is facing charges of the rape of a young girl, standing
there at the election night function and mihi-ing.
Just to wind up, I implore the Government to address these issues of sexual and
domestic violence so that we have improved outcomes for reducing poverty and
improving health, education, and housing. I just would like to finish with this poem. I
have been working with a group of women in the Hokianga to address domestic
violence. This poem, I believe, sums up the whole situation. I am sorry, I do not know
the author, but it starts:
We turn away, and she goes back,
We judge her life, and she goes back,
We deny her rights, and she goes back,
We fail to protect, and she goes back,
We offer scraps from our table, and she goes back,
We doubt her truth, and she goes back,
We look at her and thank God that we are strong,
We stand powerful in the love of a good relationship,
We are blessed because we did it right,
We would not go back.
She goes back to what she knows because she does not know anything else,
She goes back to what is safe because he will hurt them if she leaves,
She goes back to what is home because she worked so hard to make it a home,
She goes back to fix it because she believes she broke it,
She goes back for the kids because children need a father,
She goes back for the dream because she wants to be in love,
She goes back to heal him because she has seen the wounds,
78 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
She goes back to hide because he will keep it hidden,
But I wonder what would happen if we did not turn away,
If we did not judge her life,
If we did not deny her rights,
If we did not fail to protect,
If we offered her the best instead of scraps,
If we listened to the truth instead of doubting it, could we make a difference?
Could we make a difference for the wounded children, the broken hearts, and the
shattered lives?
Could we make a difference if we did not turn away?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Can I begin my first contribution in this
the 51 st Parliament by just once more adding my congratulations to the speakers who
have gone before me; to you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, on your own reappointment,
as well as to our presiding officers —obviously to Speaker David Carter, to Deputy
Speaker Chester Borrows, and, of course, your new presiding officer colleague, the Hon
Trevor Mallard. We welcome the group of you leading us in this Parliament and I have
no doubt that you will do that to your usual high professional standard, Mr Assistant
Speaker. I look forward to working with you.
Can I also just take a moment to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the
motion we are now debating, Chris Bishop and Barbara Kuriger, who gave us their
maiden speeches this afternoon and, I think, set a very high tone and standard for those
who will follow. Can I pass my congratulations to all the members of National and all
parties who have been elected to this Parliament for the first time. Being sworn in as a
member of Parliament for the first time is a tremendous moment. It is a significant
accomplishment that most New Zealanders will never get to experience. What the Prime
Minister said this afternoon at the function is absolutely right. Getting here, of course, is
a tremendous accomplishment but New Zealand will judge you and look to you in terms
of what you do in your time here. I know that you will all be dedicated in that mission.
Just by way of introductory comments, I also want to acknowledge the incredible
achievement of New Zealand being elected in the fir st-round ballot to the United
Nations Security Council. It is something that we should all be incredibly proud of,
because it is the international community recognising and reflecting the very high
regard in which this country is held. That is a product of everyone in this House,
everyone in New Zealand, and many people who have come before us, and I think it
does deserve to be recognised just once more.
For me, it is a great privilege to be back, as it always is. I do not think any member of
Parliament ever goes into an election —or should ever go into an election —with an
assumption that they will be back. We put ourselves before the voters. We ask them for
their support. Actually, it is probably the only time in 3 years that we really get a
performance review from our employers. I like to think that I have about 65,000
employers in Selwyn and I am sure each of them has a view. Once every 3 years they
get to turn up and express their view on how I have gone in supporting them. I am
incredibly grateful to the people of Selwyn for once again being willing to support me
to be here as their representative. I will certainly renew my pledge that I made on my
first day to work very hard in their interests and in the interests of all New Zealand.
This afternoon, as the leaders kicked off the substantive part of this debate, I could
not help but reflect on Annette King, the “Acting Acting Deputy Deputy Leader of
Labour”, saying: “Oh, well, this is just our 2002.” Well, there is one significant
difference, of course, that I just want to reflect on. National certainly went through a
period of rebuilding in 2002, but that was 3 years after we had been removed from
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 79
office. The next election, 6 years out, we were not only well on the way to coming back
in but we ran a very, very close-run thing in the 2005 election. Here we are now, 6 years
after Labour was removed from office, and not only are the members still rebuilding but
it is getting worse. The dysfunction, the disharmony, the disjointedness, and the
disconnection I think are stronger than they have ever been. There is certainly a much
longer road ahead than I think they themselves are yet acknowledging.
In the meantime, the National-led Government is very clear that we are here, as the
Prime Minister said on election night, to run a Government for all New Zealand. I know
that my colleagues both in Cabinet and across our caucus are focused on exactly that:
how we can work to improve the lives of all New Zealanders now and into the future.
We have a team so ably led by the Prime Minister. We have 59 other members of our
caucus who are dedicated to that very thing.
I have to say that when we come back into the House and we take up our new
positions, there is always a sense of both regret in terms of what you have not got don e
and looking forward to getting done what you will get done in your new portfolios. For
me, it marks the ends of my time as the Minister for the Environment. I can tell you that
I look back on the 3 years that I served as the Minister for the Environment with an
immense sense of pride. There are still some jobs unfinished and that is always the case,
but I can look back and know that we have done more as a National-led Government to
really improve environmental management in this country than I think any other party
in this House. There is a lot of rhetoric in that space, but it is the National-led
Government that for the first time put in place national standards for freshwater
management, that set up and gave effect to the recommendations of the Land and Water
Forum, and that had the courage to tackle setting up independent, arms-length
environmental reporting after the disgrace of the Labour Government in 2007 simply
removing chapters that it did not like. It is National that put in place the exclusive
economic zone legislation to protect our oceans and to make sure that drilling permits
offshore were not simply the rubber stamp that they had been. This is a Government
that has delivered for the environment and I have no doubt whatsoever that under
Minister Nick Smith he will not only continue that work but take it even further.
In that vein, one of the challenges, of course, that we still have to complete is our
work to reform the Resource Management Act. This is an Act that has been tinkered
with almost every 18 months during its 23-year history. It is not working for New
Zealanders. Almost every New Zealander you speak to acknowledges that it needs to be
fixed. The difference is that the National-led Government has the courage to say that if
we want different results from the system, we have to be prepared to look quite
differently at how the Act works. We are going to do that. We are not going to continue
to see New Zealanders pushed out of the housing market and face higher costs in their
food, fewer job opportunities, and worse transport infrastructure outcomes across all of
our planning decisions because as a Government we do not have the courage and the
drive to stand up and make the reforms that need to be made. I am very much looking
forward to supporting my colleague the Hon Dr Nick Smith in achieving that.
As I say goodbye to the environment portfolio I am delighted to take on the role of
the Minister of Justice. I want to reflect and acknowledge the very thoughtful, deeply
held, and clearly passionately held comments of the previous speaker, Kelvin Davis,
who spoke very eloquently about the issues of family violence. I can tell the House that
that is an issue that as the Minister of Justice I certainly want to focus on. I am not naive
to think that these are easy problems to solve, but I do not think they will best be solved
by a very partisan, divided, antagonistic approach within this House. The problems have
to be solved through working together. None of us have all the answers, and I certainly
want to extend a hand to Mr Davis and his colleagues to work with us on tackling what
80 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
is an incredibly difficult issue and one of the most important issues, I think, facing us in
the justice system today.
I think we can reflect, though, on the justice system and the work that is going on in
it again with an incredibly good heart. We have, as you have heard this afternoon, the
lowest crime rates in 35 years. We set ourselves a target of having crime reduce by 20
percent from 2011 levels. It is already down 16 percent. We wanted to see violent crime

crime, we set ourselves a target of a 25 percent reduction. We have already surpassed
that. We have seen a 30 percent reduction already and the reoffending rate that we want
to drop by a quarter has already reduced by 12 percent. So there is lots to be proud of in
the work that has happened, but we still do have much more to achieve.
A big part of that, I believe, is continuing to have all-of-Government agencies and
those in the NGO sector working consistently across justice. The Ministry of Justice on
its own cannot solve the problems, but we can work very closely with our colleagues in
social development, in police, in corrections, in education, and in health, because, as we
have heard, these issues are not only desperately interwoven in their causes but the
effects of them and their ramifications are felt throughout society and throughout
generations. They are very difficult challenges, but we are not going to shy away from
at least trying to work better on them. We have to do better. We have to make a
difference for those New Zealanders who suffer serious sexual and domestic violence. I
believe we can do better.
Let me just finish with a word briefly on the communications and broadcasting
portfolios. I am so excited to be now in a position where we will be taking ultra-fast
broadband out to at least 80 percent of New Zealand. We will be extending the rural
broadband programme by another $100 million and providing a $50 million fund to
address mobile phone black spot coverage across New Zealand. Connectivity is not the
only thing that matters in information and communications technology but without it,
nothing else works. It underpins the exciting economic future for New Zealand using
the digital economy and digital transformation. We had a poor communications
infrastructure in 2008. We are turning that round. New Zealanders are clever, innovative
people. They show us that day in and day out. This National-led Government will
ensure that we are supporting them every step of the way.
Can I close by once more congratulating all of my colleagues on being back in the
51st Parliament and restating my commitment to work as we can across the House and
with all New Zealand for a better New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I do not know what happened. I was rudely
interrupted about 3 years ago, and I come back and there is a little bit of dust on the
paper. I look across the other side of the House and the same faces are looking out, 5
years older, but not much has changed.
First and foremost I must congratulate you, Mr Deputy Speaker. This is the first time
that you are in the Chair? Congratulations. Wonderful. Well done.
I congratulate all the new members and the returning members. It is great to be
sitting beside Carmel Sepuloni and it is fantastic to have Kelvin Davis here as well. We
know what it is like. We know what it like to lose —well, not lose your seat, but to miss
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 81
out in 2011, and then work incredibly hard to get back here. The reason we worked so
hard is that we know there is work to be done. We know that the Labour Party is the
only party that can drive the sort of change that New Zealand needs.
It is good to be back—there is no doubt about that—and I must admit I am very, very
proud to stand here as the elected representative for the wonderful electorate of Napier.
My promise to the people of Napier is that I will work incredibly hard to repay the faith
of those who voted for me and I will work even harder to earn the respect of those who
did not. But if you will just allow me 2 seconds, what I must do is just thank a team that
really went hard for 2½ years: Rob Johnson, my campaign manager, Pete Findlay, Sue
Simone, Pauline Elliott, Keith, Raewyn, Mike, and many, many others who worked
incredibly hard because they believed that change was necessary, and we did it.
I must also thank Paula Bennett as well. You may ask why I would thank Paula
Bennett. I will tell you what Paula Bennett did. She came down to Napier and she called
the deputy mayor naive, she called her petty, and she called her immature, and I reckon
that was worth about 1,000 votes. I remember seeing Mr Tremain and Wayne Walford
in the meeting and they heard Paula Bennett call the deputy mayor that. The deputy
mayor stood up and said: “I am actually a National voter.” Paula Bennett said: “You’re
immature, you’re naive. The people of Napier don’t know what they’re talking
about.”—fantastic. We want Paula Bennett back more in the Napier electorate.
As mentioned, we ran a 2½ year campaign, with 125 street-corner meetings, over
10,000 telephone calls, hundreds of doors, and one red fire engine, which was
everywhere. But I will tell you what else we did. More important, we came up with a
plan for a strategy to win back the provinces. So what I would like to do is put every
National Party MP who holds a provincial seat on notice. There are going to be a whole
lot of very, very hungry —very hungry—Labour Party candidates, who are going to be
running the same sort of campaign that I ran. They are going to be raising the money,
they are going to be out there for 2½ years, and they are going to be concentrating on
the issues that are important to their electorates and the people who determine elections.
One thing that really, really shone through for me was that at all the street-corner
meetings, what the thousands of Napier people I met were really concerned about was
the lack of opportunity and the lack of jobs. They wanted to know where the strategy
was for the regions. In fact, Lawrence Yule, the Mayor of Hastings, who is also chair of
Local Government New Zealand, is actually on record saying that this Government has
no plan for the regions. You have left us behind. You cannot have an economy that is
based on Auckland house prices and a Christchurch rebuild because that does not take
New Zealanders along with it.
Mr Deputy Speaker, you know how hard the Labour candidate worked in
Whanganui. I expect the deputy mayor, Hamish McDouall, to be in this House in 2017.
He is an incredibly good man.
Another thing that this Government did is it stripped away local democracy, and that
was an absolute disgrace. It took away the ability for communities to determine their
own future when it changed the Local Government Act 2002. I am going to put a
member’s bill into the ballot and I challenge any one of those provincial MPs to vote
against it if it is drawn out. They know that, in fact, if amalgamation proposals were put
to their regions, then their constituents would want a say in the future of their loca l
communities. So we need to take that back. We need to take it back —of that there is no
doubt.
But the most important thing we need to do is we need to change the nature of this
economy. We need to move away from a commodity economy, where all we do is send
products offshore without a cent of value being added. Let me give you just one
example, and that is the forestry industry. Last year there were 28 million tonnes of logs
82 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
harvested, and 16 million tonnes of those logs were sent offshore, without 1 cent of
value being added. Of those, 70 percent went to China. That is an absolute disgrace —
not 1 cent of value being added. In fact, I will tell you what has happened in the local
industry—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Outrageous!

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: If that member spoke to his sister, he would know what is going
on in the regions. Over 40 sawmills have closed —40 sawmills have closed. Over 4,000
men and women have lost their jobs in the regions because that Government has no
strategy. In fact, this is an industry that is worth $5 billion, and the New Zealand Forest
Owners Association actually came out and said in the media about a week ago: “What is
wrong with the Government? It has no strategy for the forest industry.” It said how
disappointed it was that this industry has the third-largest export earnings and the
Government did not even give it to a Minister inside Cabinet. It gave it to a Minister
who does not know even how to spell “strategy” let alone how to write one. That is how

hard-working Kiwis in the provinces, when all they want to do is work hard, go back to
their families, and live a life.
The Prime Minister said that crime had fallen. In Hawke’s Bay, crim e has risen. In
the provinces it is a different story from the speech the Prime Minister gave. The
provinces are being hollowed out. There are jobs going. People are leaving. This is not a
rock star economy. Real change needs to happen, and this Government is not doing it.
There are massive issues. More voters are becoming disillusioned with the whole
parliamentary system and they are not voting. Twenty percent of Kiwis could not even
be bothered voting this time because they did not see a future and they did not feel
engaged.
The other thing I would like to make a comment on is that Amy Adams stood up and
made all these random statements about the Labour Party. I will tell you what I see in
our caucus. I see a whole lot of really good MPs, who are now very, very hungry and
who want to go out there and win. I see opportunities. I see one new guy here, Peeni
Henare, who is going to make a real difference. We now hold six of the seven Māori
seats and, I tell you what, in 3 years’ time these guys are going to be sitting on that side
of the House because we have the caucus that is going to make a difference. We have
the caucus that is going to go out there and create a real mood for change. Do you know
what we are going to do? We are going to go out there and we are going to engage with
the people of New Zealand like we know how to and like that Government has forgotten
how to do—like that Government has forgotten how to do.
I see only opportunities—I really do. I see only opportunities in the Labour caucus at
the moment. I see a lazy, arrogant Government on that side. You know exactly what I
am talking about, Mr Deputy Speaker. You are from a provincial electorate. The people
of Whanganui are really worried about the opportunities for their children.
Well, Labour has solutions. Labour will have the policies and Labour will create that
mood for change where in 3 years’ time they will determine who and how our
Government will drive the future of this country. There will be a vision for this
country—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: —and I know that we are going to get out there and we are going
show Kiwis that we have the policies to take us there. We have the people to lead New
Zealand.
I tell you what, the future is not fracking —the future is not fracking. Imagine an

green image that we have. The irony we have is that the Minister of Tourism is the

not—it is not. It is not the way forward.
The Government says this in Hawke’s Bay: “Fracking oil, and gas is the future.”
Well, that is a future that I can tell you the vast majority of Kiwis are going to reject.

Labour is back, Stuart Nash is back, Carmel Sepuloni is back, Kelvin Davis is back, and
we are here to take it to the National Government and present an alternative vision.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, I
want to begin by congratulating you on your elevation to the deputy speakership. You
have been a great member of our caucus over many years, a good mate, and we know
that you will preside over this House with fairness and applying your intricate
knowledge of Speakers’ rulings and Standing Orders.
I also want to congratulate all the new members. There are plenty of them here
behind me, on the National side of the House tonight. You guys are in for a rewarding
and interesting career. It is great to come in while the National Party is in Government
because we have set out a very detailed and ambitious programme for New Zealand
over the last 6 years, and there is plenty to build on. But I want to congratulate the new
members from all parties. This is a great place to come and exercise your skills, but
also, of course, to represent your electorates and the people of New Zealand.
It was interesting to listen to that speech by Napier retread Mr Nash. I do want to
congratulate him on winning his seat, but if that is what we are in for over the next 3
years, it is going to be a very long 3 years. There was nothing in that speech that was
any different from what we heard on the campaign trail from David Cunliffe. Of course,
we all know what happened there. Mr Nash threatened us a bit. He said that there will
be a vision. He said that stuff is coming, but he was very short on the detail. It was very
threatening, of course, to anyone holding a seat in the regions. I am sure, Mr Deputy
Speaker, you are absolutely terrified by what you have just heard from Mr Nash. But we
know the reality is that we have just had an election, the result was decisive, and the
people of New Zealand have spoken.
When looking across to the other side of the House today, I just could not help but
think that that is an Opposition that is really going through the five stages of loss and
grief. I think we have seen that quite decisively over the past few weeks. The first stage
happened on election night, and that was denial and isolation. You saw a Labour leader
up there giving a speech that would make you think they had actually won the election.
Of course, the isolation bit —well, we know what happened next. Then the anger
followed—the angry recriminations. By Monday morning the Labour Party was telling
us that the guy they had been backing for the past year as the putative, likely Prime
Minister of New Zealand was actually no good after all. Someone had got something
wrong. The guy they were trying to sell to the electorate on Friday, 19 September was
the guy who was absolutely useless by Monday, 22 September. The anger had started.
Then you got into the bargaining phase. You got all the horse trading and people
saying this candidate and that candidate. At one stage we had more chiefs than people to
boss over. You are looking now at a line-up of about four people in that camp, looking
for the leadership. So the bargaining has been on. Then I think they have been in the
depressive phase. But finally, today, phase five hit. It was acceptance. You saw when
they were sitting there how they had just rolled over completely. When the Labour Party
84 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
members are nodding benignly, agreeing with the Prime Minister, wanting to be really
friendly, you know that they know they have completely lost it. It is a long, long road
back for Stuart Nash and Co.
It is going to be an interesting 3 years. We took a very detailed programme to the
electorate. We have been very clear about our priorities, with balancing the books being
No. 1. We are going to be back in surplus this year. Economic growth —Steven Joyce is
an excellent Minister for Economic Development. He has led that Business Growth
Agenda. There are 350 different initiatives there, which we have been ticking off, one
by one. We have got a very good programme ahead. Our economic growth is now the
envy of the Western World. Countries around the world are just longing to have the
books that New Zealand has. We are in a very, very good position. The people of New
Zealand fully understood that, going into the election. Of course, rebuilding
Christchurch—Labour was telling us that that was going to be the graveyard for the
National Party. Well, we even won the party vote out in Christchurch East. That is how
much our party impacted in Christchurch. We decisively won that argument there. It
was not on the basis of rhetoric; it was on the basis of solid progress over a long time, in
many different areas.
Of course, Better Public Services is the fourth thing we have committed to. We have
said: “Look, we are going to set very specific targets in hard-to-achieve areas.” We have
got those five areas, those 10 targets. We have said it is not about the money, although
more money has gone in under this Government to a whole range of difficult areas; it is
actually about how the money is spent. It is about making Government relevant to the
people in places like Glenfield, the area I represent within the Northcote electorate, and
the people out in the suburbs all around New Zealand. We have made Government
relevant to New Zealanders, because, in the end, people vote on the basis of how their
family is doing. Is there enough money in the pocket at the end of the week to do
something a bit extra? Does the local area feel safe? Can you get the kids to the accident
and emergency department at the hospital when they need something there? Are they
happy with the local school? Those are the sorts of things we have focused on, the
things that really count for New Zealanders.
I can tell you that my electorate of Northcote is always a place that is a barometer for
how the Government is doing. That was once a seat that Labour held. It had been a seat
that moved back and forward over the years. It is an excellent seat, and it is where I live.
I can tell you that it is now a seat where we hold both a party record and electorate
majority. It has a bigger margin than any other party has ever held in that electorate. I
want to thank the voters of Northcote for the faith they have shown in me, but, more
specifically, the faith they have shown in the National Party. That seat reflects what has
changed over time in Auckland and in New Zealand. Seats where once the Labour Party
had a change, they have not got a hope in the proverbial now—absolutely no hope at all.
So you can see that there has been a fundamental recalibration in the political climate.
We have moved into the centre, to where people’s concerns are being addressed, and it
is those basics such as education, health, law and order, and the economy.
I feel very honoured now to hold the health portfolio in this Government. It is a huge
portfolio. There are many challenges ahead. But we have got a solid 6-year record,
which we are going to build on over the next 3 years. My predecessor did an excellent
job in that role. He has been the most successful Minister of Health in the history of
New Zealand. He pulled off some stunning successes, when you look at what he
inherited—a health system in disarray. What he did there was he focused very
specifically on the things that matter to New Zealand. Look at the progress there —an
extra 40,000 elective procedures over the last 6 years, and hundreds and hundreds more
doctors and nurses in our district health boards. He focused very specifically on a set of
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 85
six health targets, and he said to the district health boards: “These are the expectations.
This is what I expect you to achieve.”, and he did that. There is more elective surgery,
more cancer care for sufferers of one of the biggest diseases in New Zealand, a more
effective cardiovascular disease and diabetes screening service, and he has done great
work on preventative medicine.
But now with this new set of manifesto promises we have, we are going to take it
even further. We are rolling out free GP visits for under-13s. That is going to have a
massive effect on the health of young New Zealanders. It is very widely accepted as a
great idea. We have got a new cancer care target. Every New Zealander who goes to
their general practitioner and is thought to have a serious diagnosis needing
investigation will start their first treatment within 62 days. That is the international gold
standard, which is that 90 percent of Kiwis will be getting that level of care by June
2017. So that is going to be fantastic.
An extra $50 million is going into bone and joint pain, so we are actually looking at
more elective surgery. We are looking at multidisciplinary pain teams to address that
specific issue, and that is going to make a big difference. We are also putting an extra
$20 million into hospice, so we are going to be funding multidisciplinary teams. There
will be 60 new nurse educators across the system to actually help patients, their
families, and those providing care out in the public system and the community.
My first task has been to get around the 20 district health boards, and we will have
done that by Christmas. I can tell you that this is fundamentally a different health
system than the one we inherited 6 years ago. We have got an enthused workforce.
There are challenges, but we have got people who realise that despite the fact that we
have got a record amount of money going into health, we have got to continue to rejig
the system, to reconfigure the services, and to deliver the services that New Zealanders
need.
So I have got to tell you that it is great to be back in Parliament. We have set a great
pace during the election and over the last 6 years. New Zealanders have shown fantastic
faith in, frankly, the best Prime Minister I think this country has ever seen. There is a
great path ahead, but it is all bad for Labour. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Mr Deputy Speaker, it
is an honour to stand in this Parliament and speak in one of your first turns in your role
as Deputy Speaker. May I say that you look so comfortable in that Chair. I also want to
offer my congratulations to the Rt Hon David Carter on his reappointment as Speaker
and to Lindsay Tisch as Assistant Speaker, and I welcome and look forward to my time
in the House while the Hon Trevor Mallard occupies the Chair as well.
In the Speech from the Throne this morning there was a lot of pomp and ceremony
that, quite rightly, goes with the House of Representatives, but the Rt Hon John Key had
an important message. It was that this National-led Government will work in the
interests of every New Zealander. It really is both a privilege and an honour to be in a
Government that New Zealanders have so decisively given support to. Sixty National
MPs. It was 61 for a couple of weeks, but we now have 60 National MPs. That is a
resounding vote of support for the policies that we took into the election in 2014.
One of the things that is just so fantastic is that I am just thrilled at the 14 new MPs
our caucus has brought in. You will see that I am surrounded by several of them this
evening, and this afternoon we heard in the Address in Reply debate the mover and
seconder, two incredibly impressive speakers who are new members of Parliament in
this House. You will know that one of my roles as a former chief whip was to help get
new members settled into this place, but I can tell by the calibre, the depth, and the
breadth of our MPs that it will take no time at all.
86 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
I do also want to say that I have handed over the reins —or, should I say, the whip —
to Tim Macindoe. I know he will do a wonderful job as the senior Government whip,
ably supported by Jami-Lee Ross as the junior whip and Joanne Hayes as the third
whip. I want to just echo the comment that the Hon Chris Tremain made about the
whip’s role. It is a cross between being a sergeant major and a parish priest, and those in
this Chamber who have been a whip will understand that role only too well.
I do also want to welcome new MPs —and returning MPs, for that matter —from
across Parliament. I only wish that on days like today more people actually watched this
House in action, because this is probably the day of the year when there is more
generosity, more friendliness, and more cooperation. You know, actually, for new MPs,
there would be one thing I would say: your reputation is in your hands, and your
reputation as a member of Parliament is not just with your own caucus colleagues. It is
with parliamentary colleagues across the Chamber, it is with the many hundreds of staff
in the Office of the Clerk and the Parliamentary Service who support us in our role as
parliamentarians, and it is with those who work incredibly hard in your electorate
offices, who become the face of you in your electorate while you are here representing
your constituents in Parliament. So I encourage you to think about the opportunity for
you to form your reputation here.
It is also an honour to have been named as the Minister for Women and the Ministe r
for Land Information, and to be given associate responsibilities in both tertiary
education and local government. I did just want to touch briefly on those four areas.
Firstly, in the portfolio of women, I am incredibly excited about working with a very
able, dedicated, and committed team of professionals in the Ministry of Women’s
Affairs. I am a real firm believer that women should have every opportunity made
available to them to realise their potential, and I am thrilled to work alongside some
incredibly able and competent women in our caucus.
It is actually the responsibility of all of us —men and women —to support women to
do better, and to encourage, to inspire, and to support women to take the next step
forward. I, for one, am really incredibly committed to making sure that we have more
women in leadership roles and on our boards, so part of that means actually getting
them into the funnel early on. There are some women out there who do not see that
there are opportunities, so as the Minister for Women I see that it will be my
responsibility to make sure that we provide those opportunities and encourage more
women to step into those opportunities and to realise their potential.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You could start with Parliament —the number of women you have in
your caucus.

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Our economy is growing, our economy is thriving, and
women have a critical role to play in that. You know, I was not going to go there, but I
will. One of the Opposition members is piping up and chipping away to say that women
in Parliament are not well represented. Well, I suggest you look at your own
constitution. I understand that you are now in breach of your own constitution, so sort
out your own side before criticising this side.
In the spirit of cooperation, I do want to acknowledge the comments that Kelvin
Davis made in his speech earlier today and talk about his commitment as a local MP
and his stand on reducing sexual and domestic violence. He is a great example of an MP
who can stand up and say that no matter which political party he is part of, he can
constructively and actively make a difference for his community, and I applaud him for
that. I echo the comments of Minister Amy Adams, who is the Minister of Justice, and I
am looking forward to working with Minister Anne Tolley, the Minister for Social
Development, because this is a problem that exists for New Zealand, not just for the
Government of the day. I challenge every member in this House to look at what you can
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 87
do for your community to protect women and children from violence. As the Minister
for Women, I promise you that my door will be open to hear your practical solutions on
how we as a Parliament can serve our country by protecting women and children in
their own homes.
Land information was a portfolio that was an interesting surprise, and it has been
really interesting to get a better understanding of just how valuable our property
information is. I think that what Land Information New Zealand has is an absolutely
incredible piece of potential. If we can use its data and its information —it is location-
based—in greater ways, then it will have a significant impact on the sorts of decisions
that we make in central government, in local government, in businesses, and in all sorts
of areas, whether it is emergency response, whether it is national defence, or whether it
is businesses making decisions about where they go next, how they grow, and how they
develop. So it is really exciting to see Land Information and how we can unlock the
potential of the information it holds. And it is great to see the important work it is doing
in the Canterbury recovery. I am looking forward to working with the Hon Paula
Bennett in local government and the Minster for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment, the Hon Steven Joyce.
Before I finish I want to come back to the comments that Stuart Nash made about
National forgetting rural or provincial New Zealand. Mr Nash, I suggest you look at the
electorate results up and down New Zealand and look at rural and provincial New
Zealand election data, which will prove to you that in 99.9 percent of cases —yours
being the 0.1 percent —rural and provincial New Zealand supports National. I want to
take a moment to thank those of the Taupō electorate who supported me in this recent
election, because MPs who are returning to this place know that every 3 years you have
a performance review and your community decides how you are doing at your job of
representing them in Parliament. I am clear that that is my priority first and foremost —
to represent the constituents in Taupō.
I want to thank two of my team who have worked incredibly hard for me in my
electorate office: Lisa Mackinnon and Vivian Rikona, who are finishing up with me in
this term. I really acknowledge the incredible work they do serving constituents in need.
It is an exciting time to be a New Zealander and I am incredibly proud to be a part of the
John Key - National-led Government, because we are delivering results for New
Zealanders and each and every day over the next 3 years we will continue to show New
Zealanders how hard we are working for them.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker, and I
start by congratulating you on your new position. Having worked with you on the
Justice and Electoral Committee, I know that you will be fair. I also congratulate the Rt
Hon David Carter on his appointment, and Lindsay Tisch and Trevor Mallard on their
appointments to the position of Assistant Speaker.
I, like Stuart Nash, have got some dust to blow off these papers, having taken a 3-
year sabbatical, but on reflection, actually, some of the best MPs that we have have had
a 3-year sabbatical, so I hope that I, Stuart Nash, and Kelvin Davis will go on to have as
efficient and effective and productive careers as people like Trevor Mallard, Phil Goff,
and Annette King. We are back. We have all been productive over the last 3 years —so
productive, actually, that I went on to have a baby while I was gone, and Stuart was
even more productive because he had two while he was away.
I listened closely this morning to the Speech from the Throne and the speech ticked
all the boxes and told us many of the things New Zealand wanted to hear. But the reality
is that the rhetoric does not match the reality. I was fortunate at this election to be
elected by the people of Kelston—the new electorate of Kelston—as their MP. Over the
past 3 years I have spent much time trying to be involved in the local community, to
88 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
find out what is going on, to get involved at every level —as a representative on the
board of trustees for my son’s high school and a member of the Thrive Teen Parent
Support Trust board of trustees. I have seen firsthand that, actually, despite what the
National Government says, a lot of people are actually struggling out there. I am
speaking here tonight on behalf of the 25 percent who did vote for us, the 25 percent
who do know that this National Government has not served the majority of New
Zealand well.
The contradictions that we saw throughout the speech that was provided this morning
were many, and I want to talk about some of those contradictions. The first
contradiction I want to point out is the contradiction around one of the points that was
raised by the Prime Minister. We heard: “in response to the Government delivering
high-quality public services focused on getting results.” So the Government was saying
that it wants to focus on getting results, seek new and better ways to deliver public
services, and contain and reduce costs. It talked about continuing to deliver high-quality
public services but, actually, over the last 3 years —in fact, over the last 6 years —we
have seen anything but high-quality public services.
Let me just point out Novopay, which I know my colleague Chris Hipkins has done a
lot of work on. I think that would be considered anything but a high-quality public
service. We have seen ACC and the many instances of it leaking its own documents
under Minister Judith Collins’ watch—e.g. in 2012 involving Bronwyn Pullar, who was
sent nearly 7,000 files. That does not sound to me like a high-quality public service. We
have seen privacy breaches at the Inland Revenue Department. In 2012 there were 32
separate privacy breaches at the Inland Revenue Department. That shot up to 151
incidences in 2013 —again, anything but high-quality public service from this National
Government. In 2012 blogger Keith Ng walked up to a kiosk in a Work and Income site
and was able to access thousands of confidential files. So if John Key when talking
about continuing to deliver high-quality public services is talking about examples like
that, then I think as a country we should be very concerned.
We heard the Government talking about its commitment to tertiary education. We
heard the Government saying that it wants to continue providing high-quality tertiary
education, but when we think about the tertiary education system that we have at the
moment, then again we have to be concerned. Just recently we heard Sharn Riggs on
behalf of the Tertiary Education Union talking about the job cuts at the Manukau
Institute of Technology, one of our polytechnics. So at a time when people are being
pushed off benefits —pushed off benefits —into work and study and at a time when
people need to upskill to get good paying jobs in the workforce, we see proposed
redundancies at the place that they can go to do that, their local polytech, because those
polytechnics are under the crunch by that National Government.
What we saw today, or I think it was in a media release that came out today, was that
Manukau Institute of Technology staff in the faculties of engineering and trades —
engineering, the very area that that Government said it would be investing in —and of
education and social sciences found out this week that that they face a massive
restructuring. The Manukau Institute of Technology has proposed 64 full-time
equivalent job losses in two faculties. The polytechnic is also proposing 18 new
positions, and union organisers are working to ensure existing staff can redeploy into
those new positions. The impact on staff and students will still be devastating.
The Tertiary Education Union National Secretary, Sharn Riggs, says those impacts
include halving the staff in early childhood education, English, and foundation studies
as well as losses in sport, social services, manufacturing, automotive construction,
engineering, and administrative positions across both faculties. So early childhood
education, another area that that Government purports to be investing in, is going to see
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 89
cuts. Engineering, an area that that Government purports to be investing in, is going to
be cut. In a number of other areas that we would deem important moving forward as a
country, we are seeing cuts at one of our major polytechnics in this country.
We heard today that the Government is committed to ensuring that we have quality
housing in this country. We heard today that this Government is committed to ensuring
that everyone has access to quality housing in this country. And yet I think all of us as
members of Parliament have recently been contacted by our local Work and Income
offices to let us know that there are some major changes coming up with regard to
social housing. I got a phone call from Work and Income New Zealand telling me that it
would brief me during that phone conversation. I said: “Actually, this is not the time to
do it.” I said that I want to meet face to face, I want to meet with our social services, and
I want to know what real impact this is going to have on our community.
When the Government says it will be investing in quality housing and making sure
that everyone has access to it, we find it a little bit difficult to believe when we see then
that it is planning on selling off a significant chunk of New Zealand State housing. This
is something that I do not recall National actually campaigning on. Even now, having
been elected only 3 or 4 weeks ago, whatever it was, the No. 1 thing we are already
getting phone calls about in the Kelston electorate is housing, and I do not think that is
too dissimilar to the rest of the country. Already we have people ringing us distraught
because they do not know where they will be living. The other day I had someone —this
is a good example—ringing me to say they are living with their mother-in-law in a State
house. It has only two bedrooms. They are a couple with two children and they were
given 2 weeks to go and find another place. He is on ACC. She is working part time.
How on earth could they get a bond together and find a place in 2 weeks?
But, actually, those Government departments are only reflecting the lack of social
conscience that this Government has. They are only following the direction that this
Government has set. This Government, from the time that it was elected in 2008, always
had every intention of privatising our State housing. That is exactly where we are
heading now. It is not about devolving social housing to our community; it is about
devolving responsibility. That Government does not want to be responsible for all the
poor and vulnerable people who actually do need support from the State. The National
Government members can tell us as many times as they want that individuals can make
better choices for themselves. They can tell us as many times as they want that it is up
to the community to decide how they are housed or where they are housed, but at the
end of the day, what we know is that that Government does not want to take
responsibility for looking after some of our most vulnerable people.
The rhetoric in the Speech from the Throne this morning was impressive. But as I
said at the beginning of this speech, what we know as MPs on the ground —and I know
that many of the people sitting across the House who are electorate MPs in particular
know that this is the reality as well —is that that rhetoric does not match the reality. It
does not match the reality of many New Zealanders. It does not match the reality of the
New Zealanders whom we represent. Over the next 3 years our job here in Opposition
will be to hold the Government to account, to ensure that more than 25 percent of New
Zealanders know at the 2017 election that this Government is not there serving their
best interests. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker,
and it is a great privilege to congratulate you as a fellow member of the class of 2005 on
your recent election to that very valuable position of Deputy Speaker. We congratulate
you on behalf of the class of 2005, and I am sure that the support that you will get
around all the parties in this House is really a testament to the way that you are held in
high regard by all the members of this Parliament. So a big congratulations to you, and
90 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
you can be very proud of what you have achieved. David Carter, Lindsay Tisch, and
Trevor Mallard, the other successful Speakers who have been elected for our
Parliament, will in turn also have a very important job in conducting the affairs of this
House in a manner that enables good debate and discussion of ideas.
I just want to take this opportunity, as it is the first debate since the election, to thank
the voters of Hamilton East. Hamilton East is a very diverse electorate. The electors are
smart people who work hard. They know when they are on to a good thing, and they
know that the National Government is good for them and delivers for them. I just want
to congratulate and thank them for making a good choice of me and Tim Macindoe as
the two MPs for Hamilton. We are keeping Hamilton blue, when these seats had been
fought over in the past. It is really, I think, a reflection—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Thank Sue.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, yes, and we thank Sue Moroney as well, as that was a big
part of getting those majorities. The thing is that in the end the public of Hamilton saw
the plan that the National Government had delivered for our city. They saw that it was
working, they saw that they wanted to have more of it, and they voted for it, and that is
the simple fact of the matter. The New Zealand public did the same. They saw that the
plan that the National Government had put in place was a good plan. They saw that the
National Government was extremely well led by the Prime Minister and our Cabinet
and our members of Parliament. They wanted more of that, and they voted for it.
It was a huge election. It was one of the elections that I think was pivotal in New
Zealand’s history going forward, because there was a clear choice. There was a choice
between having a free and open country, where everybody can take advantage of the
opportunities there are in this country, and having a limiting, dependent island at the
bottom of the South Pacific that thinks it is some kind of utopia and does not need to
compete in the world. The public understand the difference. They are smarter than the
people in this room. They understand what actually works, and they voted for that
because they know that what National offers is what this country needs going forward.
To close our country, to isolate ourselves, and to think that we are an island State that
does not need to be part of the world is something that will never succeed, and it is not
the way of the future for New Zealand.
That is what Hamilton stands for. We stand as a city of the future, of course, but we
also understand that there is that bright, bold new world out there, and we want to be
part of that. We want Auckland and Hamilton and Tauranga —and the Coromandel, of
course—to be part of that golden triangle that will take its place alongside Sydney, San
Francisco, Santiago, and Shanghai as the cities of the future. We see that as the new
world order. That is what we are getting and that is good.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: A new world order—a new world order? Oh, my goodness!

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It is. Oh, the Labour members over there. Well, Stuart Nash is
back. That tells you everything about the Labour Party. “Stuart Nash is back.”— he said
it. Those were his very own words half an hour ago. It does not matter about what this
country needs; it does not matter about what the people of Napier need. It is: “Stuart
Nash is back.” Well, Labour has got four other people who are back and they are
fighting over their leadership, so it will be interesting to see who wins that.
I just want to welcome the new members from all sides of this House who are here
today. You will enjoy this place, and make sure you do. It is a great honour to be an
MP, but Parliament is like the sea. You can never quite judge it, and it can be very
unmerciful to you at some stages, but at the same time it can be quite calm and soothing
and an important part of your life. So make sure that you become part of this institution,
and it is good to see so many here tonight to take part in this first debate.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 91
I just want to welcome especially those of our team who have made maiden speeches
today. I think that Chris Bishop’s speech will go down as one of the best maiden
speeches in this Parliament and that many people will be looking at it and reflecting on
it. I think that Barbara Kuriger had her style as well, which showed the dimensions of
the National Party. It is a party that is balanced, a party that is rural and urban, and a
party that represents the new liberal and conservative way going forward. I think that is
something that many new members would want to take note of and look at.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: But her speech was really good. It’s memorable.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It is—it was a very good speech. It is interesting to see that we
have in New Zealand First two members who will be contending for the party
leadership over the next 3 years. So for all those new MPs, look at those two members.
They will be fighting amongst themselves over the next 3 years—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Denis and Ron.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I do not know —do you reckon it will be Denis? No, I do not
think so. This is the leadership battle you will see. While Winston is away, the cats will
play, and that is what you have got in here tonight —the start of that leadership bid by
those two individuals, Ron Mark and Tracey Martin, to take over the reins of New
Zealand First. The problem is —and this is the thing they do not understand —that they
actually think that they themselves are bigger than New Zealand First, and that is not
the case. That party relies on one person and one person alone. So that is something that
they will see.
I just want to say that the residents of Hamilton made a good choice. We had a
choice in Hamilton at this election. National offered to build the Waikato Expressway,
the road of national significance that will link us with Auckland and that will give us
that connection with Tauranga, and there is $1.1 billion of that road that is contracted
out in 2015. The Hamilton and Waikato voters had the most to lose from a change of
Government. That road would not have happened under the parties now in Opposition.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Oh, yes, it would have.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It would not have. Sue Moroney was challenged many times to
promise that. In the end we got this false, hollow promise from the Labour Party, we got
the New Zealand First Party saying: “No, we’re not doing it. We’re not going to spend
that money.”, and Julie Anne Genter, the leader of the Opposition’s transport policy,
said no—no to the people of the Waikato. It was the one thing those parties could have
done for our people to give them the economic vitality that they want going forward,
and they could not even promise it. They could not even promise it to win an election.
That is how much they care about the people of the Waikato and Hamilton, and the
people there knew that. They knew that they wanted that road.
It is also a great day for New Zealand, because there is another thing that came out
today. I have talked about having a free and open New Zealand. Today is a good day
because today we had record immigration numbers. Today we know that over 100,000
people have made New Zealand their home in the last year. They have chosen to come
to New Zealand. We want a free and open and diverse country. We welcome people
from overseas who make New Zealand their home.
A net increase of 45,000 people in the last year is good for New Zealand. It is what
we want to see as we become part of that new world order. It means we have the
population in the north of the North Island and through the rest of the country that can
take advantage of those opportunities. These are young, smart people who want New
Zealand to be their home. They are the people who will build our country going
forward, and their sons and daughters will be the duxes of our schools going forward.
They are the people who will be in this House of Parliament in 20 years’ time. They are
the people who represent the future of this country, and we welcome every one of them,
92 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
unlike the Opposition. The Opposition parties do not welcome new migrants to New
Zealand and that was very clear during the election campaign.
Just before I finish, I want to thank one person from the Opposition, and that is
Kelvin Davis, because Kelvin Davis won his seat and knocked out Dotcom. I tell you
that the public of New Zealand did not want to see that man in this Parliament. They did
not want to see what he stood for —a country that was not open, that was not inclusive,
and that was not free. Kelvin Davis did this country a favour by stopping that man from
getting any political influence in this place. That means that we can go forward as a
country. [Interruption] Do not worry about New Zealand First. Those members can all
talk, but do not worry about it. The only reason they get where they get to is that people
do not vote for Labour; it is not that they vote for them. So in the end Kelvin did us a
favour, and we have that free and open country going forward. Thank you.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: At the outset can I congratulate you, Mr Deputy
Speaker, on your new appointment, and the entire team in the office of Speaker. I think
that we will have a very we ll-run Parliament with the people who have been elected to
those positions. So I congratulate each one of you. I also want to congratulate John Key
and his National Government on their election as the returning Government. It is a third
term.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: That’s generous.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Yes, well, we are generous on this side of the House because that
is a bit what we are like.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: That’s out of your system.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Yes, I have got that out of my system now. So there we go. I also
want to congratulate all new and returning members to this House. It is a great honour
to be one of the 121 people who get the opportunity to be in this Chamber and debate all
the issues, the very many serious issues, that we have in front of us. Can I also place on
record my condolences to the Whitlam family and to the nation of Australia for the loss
of Gough Whitlam. He had a pretty good innings. Not only did he make those most
remarkable, amazing changes to the society in Australia but he lived to the grand age of
98. On both of those counts, if any of us are lucky to do either of those things I think we
would be very pleased with our contribution.
I do want to place on record my concern that we have reduced the proportion of
women in our Parliament after the result of the 2014 election. The 51 st Parliament has
31 percent women, and that has come down from the height of female representation in
our Parliament, the 49 th Parliament—not that many parliaments ago —which comprised
34 percent women. The slide going backwards is something that I think should concern
every single member. But it should particularly concern the Minister for Women, who
was on her feet not that long ago talking about how important it is to have women in
leadership positions but not actually wanting to mention what has happened in our very
own Parliament. I think it is important, because if we are truly to be a House of
Representatives, then it is incumbent on all the parties —all the parties —in this
Parliament to take that seriously. I do find it distressing in terms of the incoming
Government, the new Government, and the opportunity it had. I thought that National
was actually creating for itself an opportunity when it had so many retiring from its
caucus. I think that about 10 or 12 people retired from its caucus at the end of the last
term. I felt certain that National would use that as an opportunity to bring more women
into Parliament. But, sadly, it failed. National now has a lesser proportion of women in
its caucus than it had before. Now it has only two women in its top 10 positions.  That
has gone backwards as well. As I recall, National during the 50 th Parliament had three
women in its top 10, but now only two. So I think that tells us a bit about where the
National Party is heading.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 93
Before the ink was dry on the ballot papers we learnt that the National Party had an
agenda and some things to say, straight after the election, that we did not learn before
the election—before the ink was dry on the ballot papers. Within the first couple of days
of the election being held we learnt that the Prime Minister wants to go to war. He
wants to take this country to war. There may be some valid reasons for that, but why
was that not debated through the election campaign?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Why didn’t he campaign on it?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, that is what I am asking. Why did the Prime Minister not
campaign on it? It has come from his own benches. He should have campaigned on it. I
know from my time in this House that if you mention that within a day or two of the
election there is no way on earth that there were not a lot of official briefings leading up
to that. But there was not a lot of preparatory work done, so the advice and the briefings
would have taken place, but did the Prime Minister mention it on the election campaign
trail? They are shaking their heads because they know that not once did he mention it.
We also learnt within days of the election that the Government has a plan to sell off
State houses —another asset sale stripping of this country. Did National members
mention that once on the election trail? Well, I certainly never heard it. I think they were
at pains to make sure they did not mention it on the election campaign trail. Actually, as
I said just before, in order for them to be making those noises now, they would have had
to have the preparatory work done by officials months ago. They would have already
had that information in front of them. Is that not right, Mr Joyce? He is pretending he is
not listening. He is probably reading the papers, which were already in front of them
well before Parliament rose for the election, about the sell-off of State houses.
What else have we learnt since the election? Well, we learnt, actually within the next
couple of days, that dairy prices were bottoming out. The Fonterra forecast payout, I
think, was announced within 2 days of the election. That was very interesting timing.
We have learnt that $6 billion will be coming out of our economy as a result of that, and
the Government has no plan to address it. I listened very carefully to the Speech from
the Throne today. Not once was there an acknowledgment that there is even going to be
a problem from the low dairy payout. Not once in that speech was an idea put forward
about how that $6 billion hole in our economy is going to be addressed.
One thing that Government members did actually put out a lot of hype about, before
the Speech from the Throne, was that they were going to make announcements about
addressing child poverty. Again, I listened very carefully to that speech today, and
although the words “child poverty” were uttered, there was not one proposal to address
child poverty in that speech. So it was all hype. It was all hype and spin. What I want to
say to John Key is this: children cannot fill their hungry tummies on your spin. They
cannot fill their hungry tummies on your spin. If the Government is going to be serious
about addressing child poverty, then I back up the call from Annette King earlier today
that it will put targets in place, it will make it one of its public service targets, it will
have a plan, and it will have targets and measurements along the way to see how it is
doing in addressing child poverty. Today I read the document Our Children, Our

items.speaker: Choice
items.text: Priorities for Policy . It is from the Child Poverty Action Group. If the Prime
Minister had read this before his speech that was going to address child poverty, I am
sure he could have come out with some great ideas, because in this document there are
several recommendations that ought to be put in place.
I just want to return briefly to the issue about the wholesale sell-off of State housing.
We have seen it before. In fact, the first time that I campaigned in an election campaign,
back in 1996, I joined people in Waharoa, to form a human ring around State houses in
that very, very poor community to stop those houses from being picked up in the middle
of the night, shipped up to Auckland, and sold off at a profit by the National
94 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Government. We have seen this all before. We have seen the same old thing happening.
National is reverting to type. We have seen it before. We have seen the situation where
assets like rest homes have been sold to well-meaning organisations like Presbyterian
Support and like the Salvation Army only to find that within the matter of a few short
years they have been sold on to private corporate interests because those well-meaning
organisations have found that they have not got the resources to actually do it properly.
I predict that that is exactly what is going to happen with housing as well. If those non-
governmental organisations want to be involved in providing social housing, they
should be, but they should be adding to the social housing stock, not just simply
replacing the Government’s responsibility for it. There are going to be many, many
issues on which I look forward to holding that Government to account for the next 3
years.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The honourable member David Clendon —this will be a
split call.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: May I first begin, Mr Deputy Speaker, by saying that
you look very at ease in the Chair and we wish you a very long and enjoyable tenure in
it. Kia ora.
I was intrigued today, listening to the Speech from the Throne, that there was passing
mention of this Government’s promise to focus in the forthcoming Parliament on crime
prevention. There was mention of a 35-year low in the crime rate, with violent crime,
youth crime, and reoffending rates all declining. There was a reference to a stronger
response to preventing family violence, with a focus on gangs and gang lifestyles. These
aspirations are all things that nobody could object to or complain about. These are all
well-intentioned and positive policy directions. I will take just a moment to
acknowledge the former police and corrections Minister Anne Tolley, who, I think, did
a good job of effecting some change in the culture and language.
Police and corrections are two very large, complex, multi-faced institutions. There is
a great deal of inertia within them. We need to put a great deal more effort and energy
into effecting real and positive change in policing in this country and, in particular,
within our prison system because we are failing in our prison system in ways that I will
reference. The Prevention First strategy the police have been rolling out for a couple of
years now is a good strategy. It is an appropriate strategy, but it requires funding and i t
requires resourcing. It is very intensive on staffing. We require a lot of officers who are
well motivated with high morale, and, unfortunately, the police budget over recent years
has been flat at a time when costs are expanding. We need to properly resource the
strategy if it is to succeed, or otherwise it will not succeed, and that would be very
unfortunate.
In terms of reoffending rates, which the Government has taken some credit for, I
have seen some interesting alternative interpretations of the raw data, which suggest that
perhaps the picture the Government is painting about recidivism, about reoffending
rates, may be rather more aspirational than real, shall we say. I do think we need a little
bit more honesty and a little bit more transparency in that, because we will not resolve
problems if we are in denial or if we are trying to disguise the reality, the depth, and the
breadth of those problems.
There is a reference to gangs, and, yes, gangs are a problem in this country. Gangs
are a phenomenon not unique to New Zealand, but New Zealand gangs are different
from gangs elsewhere. I hope this reference to a focus on gangs and gang lifestyles does
not signal a return to the failed approach of being tough on crime, the antagonistic sorts
of street battles that, unfortunately, we saw in the 1970s and 80s between police and
gangs. The resolution of the gang problem is a very complex, multi-faced issue. It
requires a multi-faceted and very sophisticated set of solutions. I am very aware of it,
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 95
living in Northland. There is a serious gang problem. We desperately want and need to
divert our youth away from the gang lifestyles that have been so destructive, but I do
hope that we will take an intelligent, well-resourced, and sophisticated approach to
dealing with that very complex issue.
We heard today that there is an aspiration also to make every prison a working
prison, with every inmate doing 40 hours of rehabilitative, reintegrative activities, be it
work, training, or whatever it might be. Again,  that is something nobody could object
to. That is an excellent project to pursue. We also heard that there would be more
aftercare for released or paroled prisoners who have undertaken drug treatment while in
prison. Again, there is no argument with any of that.
I do think that these rather hopeful propositions do very little to reference or to
acknowledge that we have a very deep-seated problem sitting within our prisons. Our
prisons are de facto mental institutions. They are full of people with serious and less
serious mental health problems, with forms of disability, both visible and not so visible.
We need to acknowledge that something like 7 percent or 8 percent of prison inmates
are so damaged and dangerous that they can never be returned to the community but
that we can do better with the balance —90-plus percent. We need to resolve the very
dysfunctional complaint system within our prison system, which is not working for
inmates or for staff or for the communities. We need to open the doors to enable and
encourage the NGOs who have real solutions to work more freely in the prisons, to
work with inmates to prevent them from going in there, and to deal with their issues at
the time when they are released back into the community.
We cannot do any of this cheaply, but the greatest cost is if we continue to do
nothing, if we pretend our prison system is working and is performing. We need to
address the problem openly, and the Greens are committed to being part of that. Kia ora.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Deputy Speaker, and, like
others, can I begin my contribution by congratulating you and the others in the
Speaker’s team: the Rt Hon David Carter, Lindsay Tisch, and the Hon Trevor Mallard. I
also want to congratulate all of the other members in the House, both those who are
returning and all of the new members. I hope you will enjoy your time in this House and
make the contribution that you came here to make. I look forward, whichever party you
are associated with, to working with you to try to achieve good things.
Chris Bishop gave his maiden speech earlier this afternoon. Chris and I are, I think,
friends and I appreciated his speech. It was good to hear a speech from a new National
member that set out ideas because I look forward to debating ideas against the
Government. There was not much in Chris’ speech that I agreed with. I think that the
ideas that many of the Government’s  policies are based on are the wrong ideas. There
is, for example, the failed ideology of trickle-down— that is, by enriching the already
wealthy, they will somehow lift all boats, and wealth will trickle down to those in the
greatest need. Actually, the reverse has been shown comprehensively to be true.
There is also another idea that I think has characterised the past 6 years of National
Governments, and again it appeared pretty prominent in the Speech from the Throne. It
is the simple false dichotomy that says that whatever the private sector does is good;
