whatever the public sector does is bad. We have seen that again and again in different
realms of Government action over the past 6 years. There was, for example, the
privatisation of energy companies. There was the disastrous foray into charter schools,
which National seems intent on pursuing. Within the conservation portfolio, even, we
have seen conservation activities relying more and more on contributions from the
private sector, despite that being a core function of the State.
In the health sector —an area that I know very well; it is one of my portfolios —in
Westport, which is in the West Coast region where I live, there is to be a new hospital.
96 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
There is to be a new hospital in Westport, but the Government is going to provide
absolutely not one dollar for it to be built. There is a new hospital, provided that it is
entirely privately funded. So in all of these areas of core Government activity, the
Government has, in fact, been withdrawing and shrinking and leaving more and more to
the private sector and to the community sector.
One of my new portfolios is housing, and this shrinking of the State is again apparent
in housing. National’s strategy appears to be essentially twofold. On the one hand, the
Government intends essentially a form of deregulation of the housing market,
apparently having learnt nothing at all from leaky buildings and finance company
collapses and the debacle of—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Victories of the free market.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Yes, exactly—the victories of the free market, as David Cunliffe
says. The other aspect of the Government’s plan appears to be to actually withdraw
from State housing and instead transfer responsibility on to the community sector. That
is the very reverse of what needs to occur, but it is typical of the Dickensian thinking
that says that the role of the Government is smaller and smaller and smaller, individual
citizens are responsible for meeting their own needs, and, if they cannot, then they must
rely on charities. It is a return to the 19th century.
What the Green Party stands for instead is a commitment to the ideas that Michael
Joseph Savage espoused—that the State is the expression of our collective responsibility
to care for each other. Housing, health, education, and conservation —these are core
parts of what the New Zealand public seeks and demands from the State, and we will
hold the Government to account on those fronts.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker.
Can I please offer my congratulations on your ascension to the seat. I offer my
congratulations to the Rt Hon David Carter, to Trevor Mallard, and to the returning
Lindsay Tisch. I hope that nobody took it personally when New Zealand First
nominated our very able colleague Ron Mark to that office. Those who know Ron and
who knew him are thrilled to have him returning with us in this session and will know
that he is very capable, should New Zealand First have been allowed to have some
participation and discussion around those nominated. And that was the point that New
Zealand First was trying to make.
Once again, it is funny coming back here; the more things change —they may be
different faces over there—the more things stay the same. Mr Bennett still does not read
anything before he speaks about it.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Don Clarke’s surname’s still the same.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Mr Sabin still continues to shout out, no matter what anybody
is saying, because Mr Sabin has one role. Now that Mr Henare has gone, now that Tau
has gone, Mr Sabin’s role is to be the shouter. Righty -o. So we will just put that to one
side, New Zealand. That is something we know. This is how it works. They must have
at least two or three.
So the more things change, the more things stay the same. National, once again, has
come into this House and rather than have discussion —let us talk about what the actual
definition of the word “consultation” is, shall we? Please, the new National Party
backbenchers, just absorb what that word actually means. The Oxford Dictionary says
that to consult means “to have discussions with someone, typically before undertaking  a
course of action.” That is what “consultation” means. We have had Ministers who have
not understood that word for the last 3 years. We have had a Minister for Arts, Culture
and Heritage who has not understood it. We have had a Minister of Education who has
not understood it. The word “consultation” does not mean to just put out what we are
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 97
going to do and then say that because we told you, we consulted. So the more things
change, the more they stay the same.
This is a little piece of advice to the backbenchers of the National Party there: if you
do not want to be just fodder, every now and then, stand up inside your caucus and
challenge it. Every now and then at a select committee hearing, do not just shrug your
shoulders and say: “Oh, why not? Because my whips told me to.” Actually challenge it.
Think about what it is that you are voting on. Think about what it is and the direction
that that piece of legislation you are voting on takes the country. Just once, give it a
shot; give it a shot inside of 3 years.
When we had the Speech from the Throne this morning, we, again, had more of the
same. What we got were really nice words, a lovely vision painted —almost, what is it,
colour by dots or something, or colour by numbers—so that New Zealand would remain
calm. That is what National members want you to do, New Zealand. They want you to
think that they won the election with a landslide. Now, New Zealand First members are
exceptionally pleased with our election result.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: No, you—

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Yes, I am, Ms Dean. In 2008 Ms Dean and her colleagues
thought that New Zealand First was dead. They breathed a sigh of relief. They said:
“Phew! Thank goodness those people who actually stand up for New Zealanders here
are gone—gone.” They had 3 years without us and, boy, did they miss us. Boy, did they
miss us. The first thing they said —the ushers and the security people and all the people
who work here —when we came back in in 2011 was: “Oh, thank goodness, Winston’s
back! It’s been so boring without him. Thank goodness, he’s back.” And look at the
team. Look at the team behind me. Look at the team we brought with us. There are 11
of them —11 of them, Ms Dean. And I am sure that Ms Dean and her colleagues
breathed a sigh of relief on election night, too, that they did not actually have to deal
with New Zealand First after the election, because they know that unlike the puppets
they finally signed up over there, it would have been a hard graft. We would have made
sure that the voters for New Zealand First would have actually seen major results from
our being in a position of responsibility.
We are fine with our result. We have brought with us some strong, strong members
of our caucus, like young Darroch Ball. Darroch Ball is from Palmerston North, of
Tongan and Kiribati descent. For a person such as myself, sitting in Warkworth with
one of the largest Kiribati communities in New Zealand, I am thrilled to have a member
of the Kiribati community in our caucus. He is a young man, a solo father, who will go
on to the Social Services Committee and bring a perspective that has not, to my
knowledge, been there before. I am thrilled that Darroch Ball is here. Mahesh Bindra—a
New Zealander of Indian descent who has come through from Mount Roskill to
represent his community. He has worked hard for the New Zealand First Party for the
last 6 years. I am ecstatic that Mr Bindra is here. We have Clayton Mitchell from
Tauranga coming forward with us. Clayton —the Energizer Bunny of New Zealand
First. This man is go, go, go, and he will take on whatever project he has and he will
push the New Zealand First perspective until there is no further to go.
We have Ron Mark returning —Ron Mark and the experience that he brings. And in
the 6 years he has been away from this Parliament, he has gained even more experience
around local government, around settlement issues, and around other issues. We are
thrilled to have Ron back. Pita Paraone —what Pita Paraone does not know about
Māoridom in this country is not wor th knowing. So we are thrilled to have Pita with us
again. Fletcher Tabuteau is from Rotorua, with his commerce understanding. His
background is in commerce and finance and secondary education and tertiary education.
We have never seen such a strong caucus since the early days of New Zealand First.
98 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
Barbara Stewart—one of the rocks of the New Zealand First Party —is back again with
the health portfolio, among other issues. I am very, very proud to have Barbara as a
member of our team.
I am thrilled to be the spokesperson for education from the cradle to the grave once
again. I note that it was mentioned just slightly in the Speech from the Throne. But the
Government members do not want you to talk too much about education in New
Zealand. They do not want you to realise that when they make comments such as that
they are going to reinvest more money in this and put some more money aside for
that—they do not want you to take a moment and think: “Hang on a minute—didn’t
they make those cuts back in 2009? Wasn’t it the National Government that cut that
funding in 2009? Wasn’t it the National Government that shifted all the resource
teachers of learning and behaviour out of the schools? Wasn’t it the National
Government that stopped the teachers of literacy coming int o our schools?”. Why, yes,
it was, and now they are going to put that funding back. Now they are going to say “Pat
us on the back, New Zealand. Pat us on the back, New Zealand, and stay calm.”,
because they do not want you to see the bigger picture, New Zealand.
But I will guarantee you one thing, New Zealand —I will guarantee you one thing.
New Zealand First is here in larger numbers than it has been before, since 2008. New
Zealand First will be back in 2017 in larger numbers again. The National Party cries out
in fear. The National Party cries out in fear because it knows that should New Zealand
First be in a position of holding the balance of responsibility in 2017 —or, perhaps, even
leading the Opposition —then it will get no free ride under New Zealand First. There
will be no free ride under this group, under this caucus. This caucus will hold them to
account for the next 3 years. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant
Speaker Tisch, and can I, like others, extend my congratulations to you on your
appointment as Assistant Speaker with your depth and breadth of knowledge that you
bring to this House, and, of course, congratulations to the Rt Hon David Carter on
returning to his very important role. I want to also just congratulate my electoral
neighbour, the Hon Chester Borrows, Deputy Speaker. He used to be known as DS
Borrows—detective sergeant —but now he is Deputy Speaker. I think that one has
prepared him well for the other as he keeps a firm hand on the misdemeanours of some
who are likable rogues in this House. Speaking of one of those, congratulations to
Trevor Mallard—poacher turned gamekeeper. I think that is one of the beautiful ironies
this House has produced. I think the Hon Trevor Mallard must have been ejected more
than any other member in the last Parliament. Our only hope is that his rulings will be at
least as entertaining. Of course, we must give him credit for his experience and his
knowledge of how this House works. So I think we have an excellent and well-equipped
Speakers team.
I want to also congratulate all our new MPs who have been sworn in —in fact, from
every party. Parliament is a place where you can make a difference, and certainly in
your electorates you can work hard for the people whom you represent. I want to
especially congratulate Chris Bishop and Barbara Kuriger, who this afternoon delivered
their maiden addresses. It was great to hear of the experience and the depth and the
quality that we have in our new National MPs who spoke this afternoon, and, no doubt,
as the rest of our team give their maiden addresses, I think New Zealand will be very
pleased and proud of the people whom they have elected to this place.
Parliament is a place where people from all ways of life and perspective can come
together, and, through debate, we know that the best ideas will win. New Zealand still
thinks the National Party has the best ideas on how to lead this country and
resoundingly gave its vote of support to this effect on 20 September. We have policies
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 99
that are not ethereal but apply to everyday life —policies that are pragmatic, that focus
on people, that bring the concerns that people have to some solution, and that create
aspiration for people who want to build their lives and go somewhere in this fantastic
country of New Zealand. What National represents is not just sound, strategic, and safe
policies but a team that is singly focused. Our goal is to make New Zealand a better,
more successful, and prosperous place. Certainly, we are a progressive party. It is
notable that in this Parliament we have two further women who have joined our ranks,
and of the three new Ministers, two are women. It is great that we are seeing women
take their place through their achievements and not just through allocation.
The Prime Minister continues relentlessly to bring strong leadership that people
continue to be willing to follow. We are a caucus that is not fractious but is unified, and
that supports, respects, and gets on with each other. I think that that is something New
Zealanders have identified with and are pleased to support.
We are a Government with a track record. We have delivered for New Zealanders
and we continue to do what we said we would do. We continue to take Kiwis with us in
the way in which we lead. I think this is a significant difference. We take people with
us. Our steps are not huge, silver-bullet leaps of faith in some ideas like a capital gains
tax or a single-purchaser model for wholesale electricity or 100,000 houses that just are
not achievable at the price point they claim. We take steps that New Zealanders can
follow in. I believe that is the best model for leadership. The best model is someone
who can see over the horizon, who sees what is coming and where we need to go, but
sticks close enough to the people to carry them with them. John Key continues to offer
that type of leadership for New Zealanders. He is a man who not only can walk with
leaders of the world but will walk with everyday New Zealanders in our streets, in our
workplaces, in our towns, and in our rural areas.
Politics is not just about policy; it is about policies that work, that resonate with
people, that people will support, that people will recognise. We are totally focused on
keeping people within our focus. We will continue to work for all New Zealanders. I
would have to say that this is notable not just by what people may say but also by what
is coming out from members on the other side of the House, where people are
concerned that those members have not listened to them and that they are disconnected
from them. We understand that political success is not, essentially, rocket science; it is
listening to people, it is being connected to them, it is finding solutions that will enable
their aspirations to be fulfilled. We have kept to some very fundamental core strategies
and purposes. Essentially, New Zealanders support that. They see that our policies, the
work we have done over the last 6 years, have made a difference in their lives, and they
continue to put their trust in us, and well deservedly, I say.
But our intention, of course, is to remain completely focused on the aspirations and
the ideals that New Zealanders have. We believe that as a country we have got a
significant contribution to make in this world. We have acknowledged that in the fact
that we have been voted on to the United Nations Security Council, and it is good to see
that other nations of the world hold us in significant respect to be able to achieve that
fantastic position. But we must always take these gains with, I think, a circumspect and
humble view and attitude. Whatever we achieve, we achieve in partnership with one
another and with the communities in which we lead. So we continue to work with our
communities to enable them to have the tools necessary for their success. The
tremendous gains that we have been making in education —not without opposition, not
without people disagreeing—and the results that we are seeing are certainly proving to
be recognisable not only here in New Zealand but internationally.
To see our young people coming through the education system with higher levels of
attainment has got to be gratifying not only for us as politicians but for every teacher
100 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
who puts the effort in to change and enable those young people to succeed, and even
more so for every parent who has a hope and a dream for their son or daughter to see the
sorts of achievements that we are gaining through an education system that has been
going through some substantial reform. It is gratifying to see that it is going to have a
great result for our young people. We want to have a world in which our young people
can engage in successfully. We are not just here competing against ourselves but we are
competing against other countries in this global world, and so we need to be fit, we need
to be educated, we need to be men, women, families, and young people, young men and
women, who are able to compete in the workplace and in the arena of ideas if we are to
continue to succeed in this world. We are just a small country a long way away from
every market that we seek to sell our goods in, and so we must be better than just about
every other nation in the world to be able to achieve and keep that leading edge.
What I have learnt as a local MP is that if you listen to people, and if you hear their
heartbeat and their aspirations and you work to fulfil those aspirations, they will support
you. I want to just take a little bit of credit away from my opponent, Mr Little, for my
win. It is not right or fair that all the credit goes to him. The local National MP has just
a little bit to do with his own majority more than doubling and his opponent’s shrinking
by over 10 percent. I want to thank the people of New Plymouth and the 21,500 people
who supported me, and pledge my continual hard work to better their circumstances and
to see our electorate and our region continue to prosper. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: First, can I start by congratulating
the Speaker on his reappointment and the appointment of the Deputy Speaker, Chester
Borrows, and the Assistant Speaker Mr Tisch, whom I look forward to engaging with
through the parliamentary term, and also acknowledging Mr Mallard’s appointment as
Assistant Speaker. Also, like many have done before me through the course of this
debate, I acknowledge those who are new to this House and welcome them here. It was
just 3 short years ago that I arrived here myself and I enjoyed the respect that was paid
to me and the space that was given to me to find my place here before the real robust
debate began. I think that as soon as one steps over the breach and offers firm views,
they come back firmly too from the other side, but until that point new members are
generally welcomed and given the space to broaden out and make their initial
contributions. I look forward to hearing those from new members, engaging in the
debate of ideas, representing the constituents I come here to represent, and hearing the
views that they represent also for their constituents.
Had I known when I woke up this morning that I would be delivering a speech in the
Address in Reply debate today, I might have dressed in something a little bit more
appropriate. I am afraid that today I am, like most MPs here, indulging the inner
wallflower. It rests within each one of us as MPs —some a little more deeply than
others. Yesterday I wore a jacket to the opening formalities that was described by some
as lurid and by others as having panache. I took away from that a lesson about fashion:
that one person’s smart best-dressed is another person’s disco tomato.
I stood here in this House very proud to wear a garment designed by someone in my
own constituency of Dunedin North, a local Dunedin designer Tamsin Cooper. Despite
the considerable attention that it drew and the odd tongue-in -cheek request for a
magazine subscription, I think that the fact that Dunedin has great designers is widely
acknowledged and is a point of admiration across New Zealand. The truth is, though,
that Dunedin designers, like many others in our town, are struggling. They are
struggling because of the hollowing-out of the middle class in our country. They are
doing OK, but they are doing OK —where they are doing OK —against the odds. It is
not the great prosperous industry that many might think goes with the glamour of the
fashion brand.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 101
When I arrived here 3 years ago I was concerned about this growing inequality —the
growing gap between the rich and the rest of us. It featured strongly in my maiden
speech. I discussed the reason that inequalities are both socially bad from a social
justice perspective when we consider the need for every human being to have what they
need to survive, to live with dignity, and to make their best contribution to society, and
also economically bad—the way in which we know that in less equal countries there are
gaps where people could make opportunities but are not able to. We know that children
who go to school hungry do not learn as well as they might otherwise, that kids who
grow up in poverty are more likely to end up in the justice system, and that kids who
grow up in poverty are more likely to end up focusing on earning big bikkies being
hedge-fund managers rather than making a wider contribution through being
neurosurgeons or philosophers.
We know too that investment in infrastructure is lacking in societies that grow big
gaps between rich and poor because the wealthy come to own the political system and
thereby dictate where money gets spent, and it tends not to get spent for the greater
good in the way that it does in more equal societies. Finally, we also know that in less
equal societies, people are less inclined to put their shoulder to the wheel because they
have a sense that a special interest group, be it a corporate sector or another group of
society, is getting a deal that they are not and everyone starts to get out for themselves.
Sadly, in the short time I have been in Parliament I have watched those inequalities
grow. I think that inequalities, no matter how much you debate how fast they are
growing, have been too high for too long. We see housing affordability running away.
In the first 6 months of loan-to -value ratios being introduced we saw homeownership
drop by 3 percent in my home town of Dunedin. Now we see a housing sell-off from
this Government that will see people in need unable to get into safe and secure State
housing. I raised the issue of a State housing sell-off in Dunedin in May of this year.
The Minister of Housing Dr Smith described my description of the proposal to sell off
one-third of the State housing in Dunedin as deliberate scaremongering by the Labour
Party on the basis of outdated figures. Now we learn there is a plan to sell them all off,
not just one-third. Then Dr Smith said there is a huge difference between a projection
and a plan. Well, there clearly was a plan; it just was not one that was being spoken
about before the election.
This Government will be held to account on these decisions it is making now. It is
beyond the point where it can say that it is the fault of a previous Government for
anything that is going on. This Government will now be held to account and it will wear
the decisions that it is now making in the next election.
I also wanted to branch out and talk a little, in the realm of inequalities, about a
YouTube video that I have seen recently that is by a fellow called CGP Grey. I would
encourage those watching on television at home or listening on the wireless to get on
the YouTube channel by CGP Grey and have a look for a video called “Humans Need
Not Apply”. It has had nearly 3 million views in the 2 months that it has been online.
This video makes the point that work as we know it today will not be around forever.
This is not a new thesis, but the video itself makes a very compelling case in 15 short
minutes for rapid change in the future of work in the Western World and, in fact, for 45
percent of the jobs in America being on the way out in the current period —that the
technologies exist to replace the human workforce by up to 45 percent in the near
future.
This dystopian view creates a very unsettling prospect for policy makers and
politicians in the years ahead. We in this House have a responsibility to address these
social changes and look to create the kind of society that is fair for everybody and that
provides everybody with the opportunity to make a contribution. I do not believe that
102 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
we are discussing in this House yet in the depth and detail that we ought to be how we
are going to handle these changes that are not too far ahead. This short YouTube clip
makes the point that horses not so long ago did a huge amount of manual labour for us
human beings and that when the automobile came along, they were swiftly replaced.
Peak horse was early in the 20th century and it has been downhill for them since then.
The changes in technology that are occurring are changes in intellectual muscle. The
human brain has long thought that it could create new jobs for itself to do that would
occupy a new and emerging workforce, but this video presents a dystopia where that is
no longer the case to the same extent. Indeed, in a very short space of time we can
expect many, many jobs to go by the by. How, then, do we share the fruits of a
productive society —a more efficient society, no doubt —fairly to create the kind of
society we would all wish to live in? I want to suggest that we in this House have a
responsibility to tackle these problems. We do need to be thinking about redistribution.
We need to be thinking about ideas like a basic income. We need to be considering
changes in our tax system. We need to consider how it is that we can make sure that
people can be rewarded for the types of labours that they might want to contribute so
that we are encouraging everybody to make a contribution, not letting people lose hope
as they see the kinds of jobs that they have trained for disappearing rapidly from the
workforce.
Finally, I would like to just say a word about the local election result in my part of
town. It was no doubt a very disappointing result across the country. In Dunedin North I
want to thank the supporters who helped with my campaign and also those people who
voted Labour. Dunedin North was National’s fifth-worst result. I can only think that that
is thanks to the intelligence and insight of the voters of Dunedin North, and I look
forward to seeing a brighter result overall for the Labour Party in the next election.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: It is such a privilege and an honour to stand in the
House today as a member of this John Key - led Government. I would like to begin my
contribution tonight by joining the many speakers before me by congratulating you, Mr
Assistant Speaker. May you be blessed with the wisdom and patience to watch over the
proceedings in this House and this Chamber, which at times can be very challenging.
Over the last term of Parliament when I have been sitting here when you have been
presiding over the House, you have been nothing but fair. So, congratulations once
again on your return to the Assistant Speaker’s position, and hopefully you will be a
good adviser to the new colleagues who join you in the Chair. I am particularly just a
tad concerned about the Hon Trevor Mallard. I do not know how he is actually going to
go as the new Assistant Speaker with his performance in the House, but no doubt he
knows the procedures probably better than anybody else, and I hope that he will be very
fair as well. His colleagues actually attest to that.
I know that many members have ended their speeches by thanking the people in their
electorate. I would like to begin my speech by thanking the people of Mt Albert.
Although I am actually not the elected member of the Mt Albert electorate, more than
14,359 voters gave their party vote to National, which meant that in the very, very
strong Labour seat of the former Labour Prime Minister Rt Hon Helen Clark and the
former Labour leader David Shearer, National actually won the party vote. As one of
our National Party stalwarts, a former deputy mayor of Mt Albert Alice Wylie actually
said: “Darling, we have never won anything in Mt Albert but we have this time round.”
So I would like to thank the people of Mt Albert for giving us their party vote. The
candidate vote also improved from 7,400 in the previous election to more than 10,000,
so we did, I think, quite well. I would like to thank all of our volunteers who actually
helped us get there, tirelessly delivering tens of thousands of pamphlets, making
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 103
thousands upon thousands of phone calls, and door-knocking rain, hail, or shine. Thank
you all for making it happen.
The last 2 days have been full of pomp and ceremony, and I feel very privileged to
be sitting in this House of Representatives for the 51 st Parliament. I welcome my new
colleagues right across the House and I echo the Prime Minister’s advice to enjoy your
time here. You have fought hard to get here, and 3 years actually flies by very, very
quickly. Make it count. Make your stay here count, and may you be returned in the next
term of Parliament as well. On that score I would like to acknowledge the return of
Kelvin Davis and his colleagues who are actually returning to Parliament —particularly
you, Kelvin Davis. Mate, I do not know of any other—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Just Kelvin?

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: No, no, no —particularly Kelvin Davis because I do not know any
other Labour MP who got such resounding applause on a National election campaign
night apart from you, mate, for winning your seat and preventing the other people from
coming into this Parliament, so well done. Carmel Sepuloni, I welcome you back. It is
nice to see you back. Stuart Nash and Ron Mark—congratulations once again.
The general election in 2014 has given the National Party a very strong mandate to
govern for the next 3 years. Together with our partners the ACT Party, United Future,
and the Māori Party, we will continue to give New Zealanders a stable, effective, and
inclusive Government. We are focused on returning to surplus, and a long-term fiscal
objective remains to reduce core Crown debt to 20 percent of GDP by 2020. We will
keep Government spending under control. Around $1 billion of the operating allowance
in each Budget will be used to increase spending, with the remainder set aside for tax
reductions and further debt repayment, depending on economic and fiscal conditions.
We plan to build a more productive and competitive economy, supporting more jobs
and higher incomes. This is set out in the Business Growth Agenda, which contains
about 350 individual initiatives that will be progressed and more added during this term
of Parliament. This business agenda is doing a great job of giving companies the
confidence to invest and grow jobs in New Zealand while carefully managing the
environmental impacts.
This National-led Government will continue to pursue high-quality trade agreements,
including negotiations with my birth country, Korea, and the Trans-Pacific Partnership,
while ensuring that New Ze aland’s best interests are always served. We want our
exporters to be able to compete on an equal footing with other economies and further
lift our exports. We want to increase our international footprint so we will make more
investments in New Zealand Trade and Enterprise to expand the number of businesses
that it works with. The kind of benefit that New Zealand will reap from a free-trade
agreement such as the one that we are hoping to get from Korea is currently New
Zealand exporters are paying in excess of 89 percent tariff for such things like butter.
They are paying more than 45 percent in tariff for kiwifruit. They are paying more than
40 percent in tariff for beef exports to Korea. They are not competing with Korean
products. They are competing with products from places like Chile, where Chile already
has a free-trade agreement with Korea and their tariffs are coming down. Unless we
secure a free-trade agreement with Korea our products will no longer be competitive in
a market in Korea. So our exporters may not be able to export to Korea because our
produce will be too expensive for Korean people to purchase.
It is imperative, therefore, that we secure these free-trade agreement deals so that our
export markets are secured and also diversified, that we are not putting all of our eggs in
one basket, and that our markets are all over the world, including Asia, where there is a
growing middle class. Even in the previous term I have talked about the growth in
population in countries like Indonesia. More than 150 million people live in Indonesia
104 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
and its growth of population is the whole of New Zealand. Every year 4.5 million
people are born in Indonesia.
A big focus over the next 3 years for this National-led Government is about
rewarding New Zealanders for their hard work. We will be further reducing ACC levies,
which will be the equivalent of a tax cut for households and businesses. I am very happy
about that, because reducing income taxes for lower and middle income earners in 2017,
if fiscal conditions actually allow, is, I am sure, welcome news for everybody. New
Zealand’s economy grew by 3.9 percent in the year to 30 June. While some countries
are struggling, we have had an economy that has been growing. Some people have
called it a role model for the world economy. For me, it is the fact that our average wage
has grown by $2,500 in the past 2 years and has been forecast to grow even more. An
estimated 83,000 jobs were created in the past year and Treasury forecasts around
150,000 more jobs to be created by mid-2018. Unemployment is coming down.
Treasury forecasts that it will fall to 4.5 percent by mid-2018, from 5.6 percent now and
well over 6 percent a year ago. That is achievement. That is the result that this National-
led Government has delivered to New Zealanders.
Mortgage interest rates are also interesting because they are to remain lower for
longer than they did in 2008. Back in 2008 they were somewhere around the 11 percent
mark, which is slightly lower, I guess, than when I first bought my own house. On my
first home I think I paid an interest rate in excess of 18 percent. I know which one I
would rather have—the rate that is currently offered now, which is around 5.2 percent,
rather than the 18 percent that we paid back when I bought my first house, or back in
2008 when Labour was in Government and the rate was around 11 percent.
The new KiwiSaver Homestart grant will be introduced next year to double the
support a first-home buyer can get if they are buying or building their new home. It has
to be welcomed by first-home buyers. I never knew this until I owned my own home,
but having a quarter-acre section, which people talk about, is the dream that all Kiwis
have. It may not be the quarter-acre section now —it may be an apartment that they
prefer because it is smaller and easier to maintain —but owning their own home is a
possibility under this National Government. I commend this.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to be
back in the House, even if I was being interrupted by the senior Government whip at the
time that you called me. Mr Assistant Speaker, can I join other colleagues in
acknowledging your re-election to your role as Assistant Speaker and also your new
colleague, Trevor Mallard. We are all very excited to see the poacher turned
gamekeeper. We also acknowledge Chester Borrows as Deputy Speaker and the re-
election of the Rt Hon David Carter as Speaker. We look forward to working alongside
you. For those returning presiding officers, we look forward to your continued fair and
firm presiding over this House.
It is a pleasure to be back in this House representing the fine city of Palmerston
North. It was a mighty challenge at election time. The National Party threw everything
it had at us. You could see the money swimming around our electorate. National chose
the best candidate it could, and put an enormous effort into taking Palmerston North.
This is not new for me. At every election my demise has been predicted by iPredict and
various other pundits out there, and, yet, I keep coming back. It is very, very pleasing to
be back here. I would like to thank the voters of Palmerston North for continuing their
confidence in me to be their representative, to be their strong voice here in Parliament. I
would also like to thank and acknowledge the hundreds of people who worked so very
hard on our campaign in Palmerston North. We are very pleased with the party vote
result we managed to get, in the circumstances. We are very pleased with the
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 105
contribution we made to the party votes that Labour did get across the country, and we
are also very pleased to be able to hold the seat.
Although the people of Palmerston North chose to elect a Labour member of
Parliament to be their representative here, they have very, very high expectations of this
Government. Now more than ever the people of Palmerston North desperately need a
Government that is going to work in their interests and support them to play to their
strengths. Today, just this very day, we had new data out that spells out some of the
concerns that Palmerston North has to face. In the year to September 2014 there has
been a 6.6 percent increase in the number of people receiving the job seeker benefit in
Palmerston North. Although this Government may be pleased with its efforts to reduce
the number of people on the job seeker benefit by 2.6 percent across the country —
although those of us on this side of the House are dubious about whether or not those
people are going from being on a benefit to actually being in work —the truth is that in
my city there has been an increase over the last year in the number of people stuck on
the unemployment benefit.
There was a 9 percent increase in the number of 18 to 24-year-olds on the
unemployment benefit, and there was an 11 percent increase in the number of 25 to 39-
year-olds on the unemployment benefit in my city. Overall, there was an increase of just
0.7 percent, but an increase, nevertheless, in the total number of people receiving a
benefit in my region, and that compares with a 3.3 percent decline across the country.
My province of Manawatū, and my city of Palmerston North, like many provinces
around the country, is being left behind by this Government. The economic growth that
may or may not be occurring across the country is certainly not being felt in my
electorate.

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: That was before you were working hard for your city.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I hear Ian McKelvie interjecting. Mr McKelvie, the
statistics do not lie. You should be standing up for your region as well, because the
picture is not pretty in the Rangitīkei either. We are being left behind by this
Government. Now more than ever we need a Government that really is working for the
provinces. We need a Government that has a real plan. When you walk around my city
right now, what you see is empty land where there used to be houses, empty land where
there used to be businesses, and empty shops where there used to be a thriving retail
sector. That is the truth. That is what is happening in my city right now. We need this
Government to work much harder for the provinces than it is right now.
But what does this Government have planned for my city? Right at the top of its plan
is to reduce the number of State houses we have by 500. Right now, this very day, more
houses have been torn down in Palmerston North and there is no plan at all to replace
those State houses. Seven years ago houses were removed from Botanical Road. They
have never been replaced by this Government. Last year houses were removed from
Rugby Street. There is no plan for that empty land. Now there are at least four different
locations around the city where this Government plans to tear down houses, and it has
absolutely no plan for what to do with that land. We all know what the Government is
thinking—that land is going to be sold off and those houses will never be replaced. That
is this Government’s plan for State and social housing in my city, and that is not what
my constituents want.
I heard it loud and clear through the election campaign that we need social housing in
our city. There is a need. Homelessness is real. There are people living in garages.
There are people relying on their parents to look after them, their children, and their
grandchildren. There are people who have no home, no place to call home. They rely on
friends. They couch surf from one friend to another. That is what housing insecurity
looks like. That is why we need a decent State house provision, to ensure that people
106 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
who are in desperate need of accommodation can turn to the State, can turn to their
community, in their time of need and know that they will have a roof put over their
heads.
But what is this Government doing for my city? The Government’s plan is to reduce
the amount of State and social housing that we have by 500. The Government has no
plan for one of our biggest State assets, one of our most important assets. Regardless of
what you think about the need to provide social housing, why on earth would you leave
land sitting empty, year after year? Why would you leave houses sitting empty? Why
would this Government leave houses sitting empty, for the windows to be broken, for
the hot-water cylinders to be raided for the copper or to be stolen, and for that asset to
be run down, when this Government is supposed to be the Government of sound
economic management? It just does not make sense.
In some of the parts of my city that have been most affected by this removal and
destruction of State houses we have another serious concern, and that is access to
primary health care. It is as true in my electorate as it is in just about any other
electorate around the country that those most impoverished areas, those most in need of
access to primary health care, have the least provision. So it is my goal and my aim to
see, in the suburb of Highbury and the suburb of Roslyn, integrated primary health care
services located in those suburbs, because those are the places that need them most. Yet,
we are seeing integrated primary health care being developed in the areas that already
have the most health provision. Highbury continues to be overlooked. Roslyn continues
to be overlooked. So it is my aim —and I am happy to work across the House to make
this happen —to see integrated primary health services provided to those in my
electorate who need them the most.
There is one other aim that I want to talk about tonight, and that is around the
environment. We all know the stories about the Manawatū River. We all know that it
desperately needs to be cleaned up. We need to set standards in this Parliament that
actually ensure that our waterways will not be degraded further—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: That’s what we’ve done.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: —and that they will be cleaned up over the next
generation. Jacqui Dean says that they have already done that. No, Jacqui Dean, the
standards have been set so that water that is perfectly clean right now could actually be
degraded under the standards set by this Government. So this Government has actually
said that it wants to set standards that will allow water to be degraded. I am sick and
tired of hearing about this false dichotomy between the economy and the environment.
Our economy is built on our environment. Saving our environment is not about saving
the planet; it is about making sure that there are jobs and that there is a lifestyle and that
we can grow food and that people can live well in the future. It is not about raping and
pillaging our planet now so that future generations have not got the opportunity to live
the life that we take for granted.
Those are the challenges ahead of us, that is what my constituents expect from this
Government, and that is what I am going to be pressing it for over this term of
Parliament.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The previous speaker, Iain
Lees-Galloway, obviously has a prophecy. He is concerned about Manawatū being left
behind. The mighty Hawke’s Bay Magpies may well leave Manawatū very, very far
behind in the game that they are going to play. It is actually the Ranfurly Shield -
winning Hawke’s Bay Magpies team, ladies and gentlemen, and you will notice the
badge that I wear, with honour, of the Ranfurly Shield.
Congratulations to returning members and welcome to new members, of course,
across the House. Some returning members might have been away for a wee while. It is
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 107
good to see you back and we will have some battles across the House, as we always do,
but those members and colleagues whom I value the most are those whom I can go and
have a beer with afterwards and talk tactics and talk rugby and things like that, and get
on with the real job of governing the country. I do enjoy that kind of company.
I do note, though, particularly that there is a message for some of our new MPs here.
It will probably happen only once, but I noticed that they were listening quite intently to
Mr Peters earlier when he was giving his dissertation. Well, I can tell them that it is the
only time that they need to listen to that because it is the same speech he will give, time
and time and time again. I have heard that speech many, many times. It is quite
interesting to watch, but I see Mr Mark over there. I know what you are thinking, Mr
Mark. I know that you are thinking a year or two out. I know what you are doing, and it
will be interesting to watch from this side of the House. I wish you well in your
ambitions, be it for whip, for leadership, or for whatever. Let us just see what happens
there. That will be interesting.
Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, I also acknowledge your appointment, as I do the
election of Mr Speaker and, of course, the appointment as Deputy Speaker of the Hon
Chester Borrows, the first from our glorious National Party class of 2005 to sit in the
Speaker’s Chair. I am sure that the Hon Chester Borrows will always be well prepared
for any emergencies as they may arise.
Can I also acknowledge particularly a very good and moving speech from Mr Kelvin
Davis earlier, which spoke to the heart, I think, of why many of us are here and what
drives us. There is a lot more beyond that than law, legislation, and regulation. There is
love, there is passion, there is concern, and there is an outright focus on a better New
Zealand for some of those who have no idea how good things could be and who are
stuck in very unfortunate circumstances. So I salute you, actually, for what you were
saying earlier.
Can I also thank my Tukituki team. This is the first opportunity that I have had to
speak in the House, of course, since the election. We did very, very well in Tukituki,
Hawke’s Bay— home of the Ranfurly Shield. My National Party campaign team did
very, very well there. In fact, in Tukituki we achieved the highest National Party vote
ever, and, in fact, across Hawke’s Bay we achieved the highest National Party vote ever.
In Tukituki and Napier over 36,000 voters voted for the policies of the National Party
and now the policies of the National Government. In fact, we increased the Tukituki
party vote by about 1,000 this election, but I make the point that those policies that were
laid out before Hawke’s Bay included water storage, irrigation,  Ruataniwha, oil and gas
exploration, the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband, and exploring some of the wonderful
opportunities and potential we do have in Hawke’s Bay. I did note an earlier speech
from one of the returning members, which I will come back to later on.
How did we increase that majority? We stayed relentlessly positive, absolutely
positive, for the ambitions and potential for Hawke’s Bay and for New Zealand. We had
a faith—an ongoing faith—in the positive nature of the silent majority of Hawke ’s Bay
and New Zealand, and they came out and voted for us in spades. We earned that. I am
very, very humbled and proud of what we managed to achieve there because there are
plenty of people out there trying to distract us with the negative, with attacks, with dirty
politics, or whatever you might call it.
In fact, we had a very, very motivated team. One thing that motivated our team more
than any other incident in the election —and, in fact, I would allege that it motivated
many, many voters to actually make sure that they voted and that their vote counted —
was, in fact, one night when we had a huge number of our billboards smashed,
hammered away at, graffitied, and destroyed. There was no pattern to it. It was
everywhere—absolutely everywhere. At the time it knocked our team around a fair bit
108 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
because we raised a fair bit of money to put them up, but not only did that motivate our
team to do more and to absolutely win and win well across Hawke’s Bay but also it
motivated voters, who saw the danger of the anti-democratic, disgusting, disgraceful
tactics that were brought into and arrived in Hawke’s Bay.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Anti-democratic? That party knows all about anti-democratic.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: So the member over there may be interested in the purely
coincidental nature, I think, of the fact that that was the night that the Internet Mana
Party had a meeting in Hastings, which was an interesting coincidence I am sure.
I acknowledge and congratulate Mr Nash on his win in Napier. He is back now. I did
note his speech earlier, so well done him and I wish him well in his tenure as an MP. Of
course, I will be doing my thing on my side of the national political fence but I am sure
we will have some common ground in some things.
But I do note one thing with Mr Nash. He did run a very good local campaign —a
very good localised campaign for, as he said, a couple of years or so, and that is
probably about right; a couple of years of a very local campaign. But I was quite
interested that 5 minutes after he won the seat he was talking about being leader, and
then not too long after that he was talking about not being leader. Then he was going on
all the chat shows and the talk shows and then he was going to be in the mix again for
being leader and then he was not going to be in the mix again for being leader, while at
the same time being the local guy, 10 minutes or so after winning Napier. So that was
an interesting observation, I would humbly say. But I do wish him well and we do seem
to share many acquaintances or people I know, in fact, people from my electorate.
People such as Mr Simon Lusk lives in the Tukituki electorate, as does Jordan
Williams, who comes from Hastings, and I am quite interested that we seem to know
certain people. I was quite interested.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Did you get that from the book?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Well, I do not know. I have not looked up my own name in it,
but I might look up his. But, anyway, I do find that interesting.
But we saw tonight, or earlier on, an interesting Labour speech, the speech from
Annette King. Actually, I think that Annette King and Kelvin Davis should run as a
team, because that was one of the better Labour speeches from the Acting Acting
Deputy Deputy Leader, or whatever she is at the moment. But the way that was
delivered and the support from her colleagues—I have not seen that in a long, long time.
So quite why she is not in that mix, I do not know, but that was a very, very good
speech.
I do note, and to be fair again, I would just like to acknowledge —and it might be
surprising to some of my colleagues —David Cunliffe. Not many people, regardless of
your politics, get to lead a political party and have a go to be Prime Minister. So ,
regardless of the result, I acknowledge anybody and I acknowledge him for what he
went through to try to become the Prime Minister of the country. I think that is the right
thing to do and I wish him well with whatever he chooses to do after this.
But we do have an interesting contest over there. We have Mr Parker, Mr Robertson,
Mr Little, and Nanaia Mahuta. It is very interesting and we will watch with interest as
we pull the popcorn out of the pot. We saw this when the Labour Party changed its
voting procedure a year ago. I watched Mr Hipkins and I watched Mr Mallard, Assistant
Speaker now actually, at the time on the TV running around their conference trying to
stop this new process, because they could see how it was going to play out, and it is
playing out right now. It is quite interesting and we are quite happy over on the National
side to watch that play out in public —the contest between the contest; the contest of
these four people who all choose to be, or think they could be, the leader and the Prime
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 109
Minister of the country one day. We will watch with interest. I am sure it will be very,
very interesting.
One thing again, about the speech from the previous member —I have heard that
speech before. It was the Labour Party’s campaign speech around the  hustings. I have
heard that one in Hawke’s Bay. Well, a couple of points on Hawke’s Bay. There are
opportunities—200 new jobs with Kiwibank in Hastings; 200 new jobs. Ultra-fast
broadband across the country enables those jobs.
In our policy manifesto, in our profile, we talked about encouraging oil and gas
exploration and, hopefully, a commercial find across Hawke’s Bay, endorsed by the
people of Hawke’s Bay. It was refuted, voted down by the Labour Party, which used to
be in favour of jobs and now its members are against oil and gas. I do not think they
will be saying the same thing over in Taranaki, funnily enough though. But it will be
interesting to see what Andrew Little says about some of the earlier speeches, actually.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: One thing here; another thing elsewhere.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Another thing elsewhere —that is right. So, it depends what
audience it is.
Also there is the Ruataniwha Water Storage Scheme. I was very interested to hear the
Napier MP thank some of his team, which was fair enough, but actually some of his
team are quite strong advocates against the Ruataniwha Water Storage Scheme and the
incredible job opportunities that can create for the bay. Watch this space. There are
many other opportunities quite soon, perhaps, for the Hawke’s Bay. Thank you.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. E ngā
mana, e ngā reo, e ngā rangatira mā, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa. I would
like to take this opportunity to, firstly, congratulate you on your reselection as Assistant
Speaker in this House of Parliament. I find that you have always been very fair and I
look forward to working with you and your colleagues, the Rt Hon David Carter, the
Hon Chester Borrows—and I want to acknowledge that this is a new role for him —and
also my colleague the Hon Trevor Mallard.
I would also like to congratulate all members across the House, but particularly new
members. This is an opportunity that you cannot pay for. It is an opportunity that you
earn through hard work and connection with your communities —those of you who are
electorate MPs.
I also want to take the opportunity to congratulate all the political parties on what
was a pretty intense campaign. National has worked hard and has secured a mandate. I
respect that the people of New Zealand have spoken, and I wish you all very well in the
role in terms of governing our country.
I also want to acknowledge all the new Ministers and all the new select committee
chairs, because we want to be constructive in terms of the work that this House does. I
would also like to specifically acknowledge the Hon Te Ururoa Flavell in his role as
Minister for Māori Development and acknowledge a new tikanga that he established,
which was to have a karakia on Monday morning with Te Ātiawa in Matangireia, and it
was a privilege to actually be part of what is a new tikanga. And I also want to
acknowledge and thank the House for its agreement to my colleague Su’a William Sio
taking the Oath of Allegiance in his heritage language in addition to taking the Oath in
English because, whether or not we realise it, we have changed and created a tikanga
that I hope will enable in the future any New Zealander who has a heritage language to
be able to take the Oath in either Māori or English and also in their heritage language.
So I am really proud of what this House has managed to achieve already.
I want to focus on what the Government’s agenda is within the next 3 years and its
relevance to my electorate of Manurewa. I want to thank the people of Manurewa for
empowering me with the responsibility to be their spokesperson and, in doing so, I want
110 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
to acknowledge all the other people who put their hands up to be the spokesperson for
Manurewa. I am incredibly privileged to be in this position. So for me, when I look at
the agenda that the Government has set out for the country, of course I am going to
think about what it means for the people of my electorate.
One of the policies that the Government has signalled that it will prioritise is
extending flexible working arrangements. I guess that as a member of the Service and
Food Workers Union—a proud member of the Service and Food Workers Union, which
represents the lowest-paid people in our country —I obviously want to understand what
the implications for flexible working arrangements may mean. For me, a flexible
working arrangement means decreasing the power of the unions, and obviously unions
collaborate with workers to make sure that the conditions of workers enable them to get
a fair day’s pay for a fair day’s work. What does that pay do? It pays for their power. It
pays for their rent. Hopefully, it pays for their mortgages, for some of them. But what it
does is enable people to live independent lives. So when we look at equality of
opportunity, obviously the equality of opportunity does not happen within a vacuum. It
happens within a context. What I am hoping is that those flexible working arrangements
are going to enable working New Zealanders to be able to put a roof over their heads
and food on the table, and enable their children to have a good quality of life, whether it
be in sports, or the arts, or whatever.
What I do not want to see in terms of the consequences of the legislation that this
Government has prioritised is an erosion of the value of wages, because if we see an
erosion of the value of wages, what does it mean in electorates like mine? Actually, it
means people living in cars, people living in tents, people living on the streets, and
people living in circumstances where 18 people in a two-bedroom home or a three-
bedroom home has actually become normal. It means children living in garages. That
context for the people of my electorate in Manurewa is something that I am incredibly
focused on because I cannot do my job unless the Government does its job, and I am
sure that the Government has not got a deliberate intention to put families and children
on the streets, living in cars and living in garages.
The other thing that I do not want to see through the extension of flexible working
arrangements is an expansion of the low-paid service sector. We want to see people
being paid enough and not having to work 60-hour, 70-hour, 80-hour, or 90-hour weeks
to be able to live the New Zealand dream, which is actually about working hard and
then having a quality of life that means that you can then play sport and you can take
your kids to the beach. You know, you should not have to work 6 or 7 days a week. The
other thing I do not want to see is that it increases temporary and part-time employment.
Again, what does that erode? It erodes the ability of families and parents to provide the
basics for their children.
My focus on homelessness is timely because the Parliamentary Library research unit
put out a paper in July, and it is entitled Homelessness in New Zealand —the reality of
homelessness in New Zealand—and I am going to outline the people who are homeless
in New Zealand. The University of Otago did some research and, basically, people who
are homeless in New Zealand are new migrants, Pasifika or north Asian. More than half
of them are people younger than 25 years old. Half of them are children under the age of
15 years, and most of them are Māori and Pasifika. The relevance of these statistics to
my electorate is that there I have 32 percent Pasifika, I have 28 percent Māori, and I
have 23.4 percent Indian. So for me, I live in an electorate where I have high
concentrations of specific ethnic groups who do not own their own homes, and actually
the State and the social housing providers and the landlords who are going to provide
accommodation to my constituents are incredibly important.
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 111
Homeownership rates in New Zealand are now at less than 50 percent, but if you are
Māori they are 28 percent, and if you are Pasifika they are 18.5 percent. So one of the
concerns I have—and this is another priority for this Government —is that we are going
to sell 22,000 State houses. We currently have 68,000 State houses. The mandate of
Housing New Zealand is to provide rental housing for those who need it most. I guess
that when I look at the definition of those who need it most, I would have thought that
that included people living in cars, people living in tents, people living on the streets,
and people living in two and three-bedroom houses where there are three, four, or five
families living together in crowded conditions.
When I look at my electorate I see that we have houses sitting empty at the moment,
so what Iain Lees-Galloway is experiencing in Palmerston North, what Carmel Sepuloni
is experiencing in Kelston, what Megan Woods is experiencing in Wigram, and what I
would contend quite a few other electorate MPs across this House are experiencing is
that they are meeting people who are in need of what I would say is the basic necessity
of life—that is, to be able go to work, for kids to be able to go to school, and for ou r
children to have the aspirations and the dreams that we all want them to have. So when I
look at a priority of selling 22,000 State houses within a context of underprovision, it
makes no sense to me—it makes no sense to me.
So I want to call this Government to account. There will be some houses in some
places where, actually, selling the house and using that money more effectively makes
sense, but I call for a moratorium on the selling of State houses in areas like Manurewa,
South Auckland, Christchurch, and west Auckland, where we have people who are
living in cars and living on the streets. They have nowhere to live. So if the Government
is true to what it said in terms of addressing child poverty, one of the things I would like
it to do is to tell us—tell New Zealand—where these 22,000 houses are and to guarantee
that in areas where we do not have the provision, the Government will not sell them. I
think that if this Government wants to work constructively and meet the needs of New
Zealanders, it would do that. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is a great
privilege—an unalloyed privilege —to be speaking in this the 51 st Parliament in New
Zealand’s history, to be returned as the MP for Tauranga, and to be part of this National
Government, which comes back into this Parliament with a renewed sense of vigour,
purpose, and determination, really, to govern for all New Zealanders to the best of our
abilities.
Can I congratulate you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, on your return in your fine
electorate, very close to mine, and also on the service you provide this Parliament along
with the Rt Hon David Carter, who, of course, was returned. As everyone has done, but
I think it is worth doing again, I also heartily congratulate Chester Borrows and Trevor
Mallard, who are —and for one of them at least I use this phrase advisedly —great
parliamentarians. Again, in one case, I would not say I enjoyed it, but I have had close
interactions with both men. In Chester Borrows’ case it was on the Justice and Electoral
Committee, where he showed what a bipartisan person he can be in the House, and in
the case of Trevor Mallard my very clear recollection of first speaking in this House
was of him putting me through my paces. That is something I suppose that all new MPs,
whom I also congratulate, have to look forward to as they earn their stripes in this great
House and serve this country very well.
I was really proud to listen to our Prime Minister this afternoon, firstly, as he talked
about the United Nations Security Council, and the privilege, really, it is for us as a
small country to be represented temporarily on it, and then as he talked about the flag
and that important debate that we are going to have as a country. I think that both of
those issues show that New Zealand, albeit a small country in the South Pacific, is very
112 Address in Reply 21 Oct 2014
much an outward-looking one and an optimistic one. For all the talk of that big country
near us being the lucky country, we are a lucky country that has a great future and that
we should be proud of and actually very patriotic about. I am looking forward to that
flag debate. I think it really speaks about what we can be as a country.
This party at least is a party that is outward looking, that believes in free trade, that
knows that our prosperity is tied to the rest of the world and that we can face those
issues, if you like, with confidence and optimism, not with fear, and knows that,
actually, foreign investment is something that, if we manage it right, makes a real
difference to this country and to our standard of living, and that we should really
embrace the rest of the world.
I was also proud to be a member of the National Party on election night, not because
of the great result that we got —if not historic then certainly the very strong result on
election night —but because of the Prime Minister’s speech, and I think it was a fine
speech, where he made clear that this party along with our supply and confidence
partners is here to govern for all New Zealanders. I know that is something that this side
of the House takes very seriously indeed. We are going to resist arrogance. It is not a
“Stuart Nash is back” attitude on this side of the  House. We take our role seriously and
we are going to govern for all New Zealanders. We are going to stay in touch with our
electorates, and I know that is something you have done with aplomb for some time, Mr
Assistant Speaker. I know in Tauranga that it is very important that we stay close, that
we listen, and that we continue to get out into various sectors of our communities in
order to know what it is that they want from us, as we are now in our third term.
We have, yes, got a proud and a great track record as a party in Government that has
achieved strong economic management, better public services, very strong public
services, is bringing down the deficit into surplus, and is this term offering tax cuts at
the end of it all. But we are not out of ideas. We have got fresh ideas and things that we
will be putting to this country to ensure that our track record continues, but there is
more and better to come: a strong economy, better public services, and a clean
environment.
I am really excited about the portfolios that I have both been in as a Minister in John
Key’s Government and that I take up as new portfolios. It is interesting to listen to
Louisa Wall, and I think she is genuine in everything she said, but we have heard a lot
of scaremongering in this House, actually over years, about employment reform in this
country and the Employment Relations Amendment Bill in particular. I have been really
privileged to be part of that, to have been the Minister of Labour for National. Now I
think it is the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, Michael Woodhouse, who is
going to do a great job. Actually what we have done there has been about delivering
more opportunities for more people —more opportunities for more people. We are pro-
jobs and we are not going to see the kind of people that Louisa Wall talked about out of
jobs.
I think it is really sad, actually, to see parties on the other side campaigning against
the 90-day trial and campaigning against the youth start-out wage, because they are
policies that employers have told us in the independent ministry surveys have created
more jobs and have seen employers give young people a go whom they would not have
otherwise given a go and kept them in a job. We recognise, unlike the Labour Party, that
New Zealand predominantly is a country of small and medium sized enterprises, which
do not take on employees just to fire them. They take them on to give them a go and to
pay them the best that they can. I am really proud of the work we have done in that area.
I am really proud, actually, of the work that we are going to do in minimum
employment standards—actually, that we have done with the minimum wage. We have
lifted the minimum wage every single year we have been in office, so it is now the
21 Oct 2014 Address in Reply 113
highest in the world relative to average wages, actually. That is not something to be
sniffed at. As for paid parental leave, there is great work there and Michael Woodhouse
is going to do a great job to ensure not only that we increase the entitlements to 18
weeks but also that we widen it to ensure that it goes to more people than ever.
In transport—roads of national significance, regional roads —we are making sure we
have got efficient, safer roads for people to travel on while also ensuring better public
services than ever before in this country. Actually, I am really proud of, in electorates
like Louisa Wall’s, the $1.7 billion investment in rail in Auckland.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.
